sources.news_title: Social Security is running out of money. Benefits are rising 3.6% next year anyway.
sources.text:
Social Security Is Running Out of Money. Benefits Are Rising 3.6% Next Year Anyway.
Congress has yet to address a looming funding shortfall that could leave the retirement program unable to pay 22 percent of scheduled benefits by 2032.
With Social Security barreling toward insolvency, the government is increasing benefits in January.
On Wednesday, the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced that retirees will receive a 3.6 percent increase in Social Security benefits next year. The raise, which was unveiled shortly after the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported consumer prices rose 3.7 percent year over year in September, will amount to an increase of $75 per month for the average beneficiary. It also represents a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) that will be 0.8 percentage points higher than last year's, which was 2.8 percent, and 0.9 percentage points higher than what was projected by the Social Security Trustees, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," said SSA Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano in a press release. "Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people."
But the announcement comes as Social Security faces a looming funding cliff.
The program has been spending considerably more than it receives for years, thanks in large part to the U.S. demographic problem: Birth rates have collapsed, life expectancy has risen, and there are fewer working-age people paying taxes to fund retirees. In 2025, the program collected $1.45 trillion in revenue and spent $1.61 trillion, leaving a $160 billion shortfall. Trust fund reserves covered the gap, but they are rapidly dwindling. In June, Social Security's Trustees projected that, without legislative changes, incoming revenue would cover only 78 percent of scheduled retirement and survivor benefits by late 2032—a 22 percent shortfall. Combined retirement and disability funds are expected to run out by 2034. There are a handful of fixes, including raising the retirement age, reducing benefits, raising the cap on earnings, means-testing the program, privatizing it, or getting rid of it altogether.
While many lawmakers have acknowledged reality, Congress remains divided on how to address the issue. In August, Sen. Ron Wyden (D–Ore.) blocked a proposal from Sen. Bill Cassidy (R–La.) to establish a congressional process to consider reforms, arguing that it would slash retiree benefits and help billionaires "avoid paying their fair share."
"People are objecting to doing their job," Cassidy complained in September. "Congress needs to fix Social Security this year."
What makes Wednesday's increase even more unjustified is the fact that older Americans are already among the wealthiest age groups in the country. According to the Federal Reserve's latest Survey of Consumer Finances released last week, households headed by someone aged 75 or older had a median net worth of $504,900 in 2025, compared with just $33,000 for households headed by someone under 35. Despite their relative wealth compared to working-age people, retirees are getting a COLA increase that is greater than the average worker, whose wages have risen by 3 percent in the last year.
For the very wealthiest beneficiaries, the 2027 COLA will constitute an enormous increase. According to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, the highest-earning couples who retired this year will receive a combined increase of $3,600, meaning that their combined benefits would exceed $100,000 next year. However, without congressional action, Social Security recipients could expect a 22 percent cut that, in 2032, would wipe out the previous nine years' COLAs all at once.
Despite years of warnings about Social Security's deteriorating finances, Congress has yet to enact reforms to avert the looming shortfall. For now, beneficiaries can look forward to larger checks in January, even as the program moves closer to the day when it can no longer pay the benefits it has promised.

sources.news_title: As Inflation Climbs, Social Security Payments Get a Boost
sources.text:
Photo: Adobe Stock
PODCAST
October 15, 2026 ~ Patrick Anderson, Principle and CEO of Anderson Economic Group. Inflation was up in September. Social Security Administration announces 3.6% COLA increase.
WASHINGTON ~ Rising prices at the gas pump and for everyday essentials continued to put pressure on household budgets in September, as inflation rose 3.7% from a year earlier. The higher costs are being felt by many retirees and other Americans living on fixed incomes who closely watch changes in their monthly expenses.
In response, the Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for 2027, increasing benefits for more than 72 million Americans. For many seniors, the larger payments will help offset rising costs for necessities such as groceries, fuel and health care.

sources.news_title: Social Security announces 3.6-percent benefit increase for 2027 | The Highland County Press
sources.text:
Social Security announces 3.6-percent benefit increase for 2027
The Social Security Administration (SSA) this week announced a 3.6-percent benefit increase for 2027. Social Security benefits include Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI), and Supplemental Security Income (SSI). On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month.
Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2027. Increased payments to about 7.3 million people receiving SSI will begin on December 31, 2026. (Note: Some people receive both Social Security benefits and SSI).
“Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” said Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano. “Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people."
Individuals with personal my Social Security accounts can view their COLA notice online starting in late November—up to three weeks earlier than receiving a paper notice in the mail. Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account’s Message Center. Individuals who do not have a personal account will need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see their COLA notice online. Create an account today at www.ssa.gov/myaccount.
Individuals who have not enrolled in paperless notices in my Social Security will receive their COLA notice by mail in December.
Social Security beneficiaries will receive a simplified, one-page COLA notice, which uses plain and personalized language, and provides exact dates and dollar amounts of an individual’s new benefit amount and any deductions.
Information about Medicare changes for 2027 will be available at www.medicare.gov. For Medicare enrollees, the 2027 premium amount will be available via my Social Security Message Center starting in late November. Individuals who have not opted to receive messages online will receive their COLA notice by mail in December.
The Social Security Act provides for how the COLA is calculated. The Social Security Act ties the annual COLA to the increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) as determined by the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics.

sources.news_title: Boomers Get A Bigger Check While The Rest Of Us Pay The Price
sources.text:
The Social Security Administration announced its annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) on Wednesday. Nearly 72 million retirees will receive a 3.6 percent increase in benefits next year.
Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said the increase, which averages out to an extra $75 in benefits per month, will give retirees and disabled workers “greater financial stability.” The annual COLA is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, which the Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) determines. (RELATED: It’s Harder For Zoomers To Afford These Five Mainstays Of Life That Boomers Could When They Were Their Age)
BLS data released Wednesday showed that the Consumer Price Index increased 3.7 percent annually, up from August’s 3.4 percent rate. A 9.1 percent surge in gasoline prices in September accounted for more than half of the month-over-month consumer price gains. Year-over-year, gas prices stood 34.2 percent higher, while fuel oil costs spiked by 74.2 percent.
Social Security is a pay-as-you-go system. Payroll taxes collected from today’s active workers are not saved or invested in an individual account for them. Rather, they are used immediately to pay current benefits to retirees and disabled workers. Taxes that are not immediately paid out in monthly benefits stay in federal trust funds, managed by the U.S. Treasury, and get invested in special-issue Treasury bonds.
As older generations receive more in benefits, inflation continues to eat away at wage gains for working Americans.
A chart shared by Navy Federal Credit Union chief economist Heather Long showed that wage growth in the U.S. has dropped to a five-year low. Long said that wage increases for typical workers have been entirely offset by inflation since April.
The financial pain is real: Wage growth fell to 3% (y/y) in September. That’s the lowest in 5 years. Wage growth: 3% Inflation: ~3.4% Inflation has eaten up all wage gains for the average worker since April. Many people are having to make hard choices about what to buy and what to skimp on right now. Yes, consumption is still strong (mainly due to wealthier Americans and people dipping into savings or credit cards), but a lot of people have to think hard about every dollar they spend. Notable: Wages only ticked up 0.1% in the month of September. That was the weakest monthly gain since December 2025.
— Heather Long (@byHeatherLong) October 2, 2026
Long also noted that while overall consumer spending remains “still strong,” this activity is largely driven by higher-income households, credit card usage, and depleted savings, leaving most people to carefully evaluate every purchase.
A separate chart posted by Jack Salmon, a research fellow at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University, showed median household net worth by age beginning in 1989. Data from the Survey of Consumer Finances and the Federal Reserve found that older Americans over the age of 75 have seen their net worth steadily climb. But younger generations under 35 have largely stagnated.
If you solution to Social Security insolvency involves raising taxes on the blue line to give more benefits to the orange line, you should at least acknowledge the profound intergenerational injustice involved. https://t.co/BoebdMK5TX
— Jack Salmon (@_JackSalmon_) October 13, 2026
Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the economic divide between wealthy Americans and the rest of the country has expanded, according to a Federal Reserve report released earlier in October.
The Fed’s 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances found that overall median family net worth ticked up 2 percent to nearly $216,000 between 2022 and 2025. However, stark generational disparities emerged over the same period: the median net worth for individuals under 35 plunged 23 percent to approximately $33,000, whereas for those aged 75 and older, it jumped 37 percent to roughly $504,900.

sources.news_title: It's the largest COLA hike in years. Some say it isn't enough
Social Security recipients to get 3.6% cost of living boost, an average of $75 per month - American Press
sources.text:
Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported Wednesday that inflation accelerated in September, with the consumer price index rising 3.7% in September compared with a year ago and gas prices have spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Nancy Altman, president of the Social Security Works advocacy group, said the latest inflation data shows that “as important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices.”
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans’ healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance,” given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.

sources.news_title: Social Security Administration approves 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027
sources.text:
Monthly Social Security payments and Supplemental Security Income benefits for roughly 76 million Americans will expand by 3.6 percent in 2027, the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday. The boost, which reflects persistent inflation trends tracked by federal labor metrics, is set to elevate typical monthly checks for retired workers by approximately $75, raising the average payment from $2,088 to $2,163 starting in January.
The cost-of-living adjustment, determined by comparing third-quarter inflation indices from consecutive years, surpasses the 2.8 percent increase implemented in 2026. Under federal guidelines, the rate calculation relies specifically on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers monitored by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Alongside the benefit expansion, federal officials noted that the maximum amount of earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes will rise to $192,300, up from $184,500.
Financial policy analysts observed that while the bump helps offset everyday expenses, the distribution impacts households differently depending on baseline earnings. According to the nonpartisan Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, the 3.6% COLA “will boost average benefits by about $900 per retiree but would provide an over $2,200 increase for the very richest beneficiaries.” The research group further highlighted that “The highest earning couples who retired this year at their normal retirement age will enjoy a $3,600 combined increase – enough to push their combined benefits above $100,000 annually”.
Payment schedules will begin reflecting the updated numbers at the turn of the year, though nearly 7.3 million Supplemental Security Income recipients will receive their initial expanded checks on Dec. 31, 2026, due to New Year’s Day falling on a federal holiday. Beneficiaries registered for paperless alerts on their online accounts will be able to review individual notice figures by late November, while physical mailings will be dispatched through December.

sources.news_title: Social Security says retirees will get a 3.6% raise for 2027
sources.text:
Social Security says retirees will get a 3.6% raise for 2027
Published 12:05 am Thursday, October 15, 2026
Retirees and other beneficiaries will receive the largest annual cost-of-living adjustment since 2023 in their Social Security checks next year, driven mainly by persistently high inflation.
The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% annual cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, on Wednesday after the release of government inflation data for September. The COLA is determined using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W. The index values for July, August and September are averaged to produce the official adjustment figure.
For the average Social Security beneficiary, the COLA will translate to a $75 monthly increase, the government said. However, the actual amount for any retiree enrolled in Medicare will vary. The Part B premium, which covers outpatient care, is usually deducted from Social Security benefits, changing net COLAs. Separately, Social Security said the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax would rise to $192,300, up from $184,500 this year.
The Medicare board of trustees has projected that the monthly Part B premium will rise $6.60 in 2027 to $209.50. The final figure will be released this fall, but if the projection holds, most beneficiaries will receive net COLAs of at least 3%.
Other Medicare costs are rising, too. Monthly premiums for some prescription drug plans, which are known as Part D, will jump $50 or more next year — although plenty of lower-cost options are available for people who shop the market during the annual enrollment period that begins Thursday. In addition, costs will rise and supplemental benefits will be reduced in private Medicare Advantage plans next year.
The CPI-W reflects price changes for goods and services that working people buy and use, and it is under-weighted for healthcare costs, which have an outsize impact on older Americans. The health spending burden for people enrolled in Medicare is more than twice as large as that of other households, accounting for 14% of total spending in 2024, according to KFF, a healthcare research nonprofit.
The COLA announcement comes at a time when Americans are feeling less confident that they will have enough money to live comfortably in retirement. An annual survey released this year by the Employee Benefit Research Institute found that 61% of workers were confident they will have enough money to be comfortable in retirement, down from 72% in 2021; retiree confidence fell to 73% from 80% during the same period.
“For retirees who aren’t confident, inflation and the rising cost of living are overwhelmingly the top reason,” said Craig Copeland, director of wealth benefits research at EBRI.
The automatic COLA is one of Social Security’s most valuable features, but some advocates have long argued that it isn’t adequate to help seniors cope with inflation — and that the CPI-W should be replaced by a yardstick that does a better job measuring the inflation that affects retirees.
A new AARP survey found that just 23% of adults over age 50 think a 3.5% COLA keeps up with rising prices. “For most people, the COLA just isn’t enough to keep up with what they see as rising costs in their life,” said Bill Sweeney, AARP’s senior vice president for government affairs. “When they go to the grocery store or fill up their tank with gas or get a notice that their rent is going up, it’s almost always higher than those numbers.”
Worries about the future of Social Security itself also are eroding confidence.
Social Security’s trustees projected in June that the retirement trust fund would be exhausted in 2032 — just six years from now. The combined retirement and disability funds are projected to run dry in 2034.

sources.news_title: US retirees to get 3.6% Social Security bump
Big News for Retirees: Your Social Security Checks Are Growing in 2027!
sources.text:
If you count on Social Security, there is great news today. The Social Security Administration officially announced a 3.6% benefit increase for 2027. This annual cost-of-living adjustment is widely known as the COLA. About 72 million retirees and beneficiaries will see this bump in their monthly payments. Supplemental Security Income recipients will also see their checks go up.
What does this change mean for your everyday bank account? For the average retired worker, benefits will rise by roughly $75 each month. Average monthly checks will climb from about $2,088 to roughly $2,163. That adds up to more than $900 in extra cash across the entire year. Couples who both receive benefits will enjoy an even larger combined boost. This 2027 raise is noticeably higher than the 2.8 percent adjustment seen in 2026.
How did the federal government settle on this specific percentage? Every year, officials track the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners. They measure price changes during the third quarter of the current year. Rising grocery bills, gasoline prices, and utility expenses drove inflation higher this past summer. Because living costs jumped 3.6 percent, benefit amounts must keep pace.
Higher earners will also notice key tax adjustments in 2027. The maximum wage base subject to Social Security taxes will climb to $192,300. That’s up from the previous cap of $184,500.
When can you expect this fresh cash to land in your pocket? Most retirees will see the increase in their payments starting in January 2027. Your exact payment date depends on your birthday. If you receive Supplemental Security Income, your larger check arrives even earlier. Those funds will arrive on December 31, 2026. You will receive an official notice by mail or online this December.
While this raise helps, seniors still face rising costs across the board. Advocates note that medical bills and prescription prices continue to rise rapidly. Medicare Part B premiums might also absorb part of this monthly increase. Even so, this 3.6 percent jump gives millions real breathing room.
To make the most of this boost, review your household budget right now. Log into your personal online Social Security account to verify your updated numbers. Staying informed helps you protect your financial future. Every extra dollar helps when you are managing everyday retirement living. Plan ahead today and enjoy your well-deserved raise in 2027. Enjoy this positive update as the new year approaches.

Republicans traditionally have criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy.
The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the payroll tax cap would add roughly $3 trillion to the program over the next 10 years.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program.
The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax-and-spending bill, gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and older, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren’t able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults, who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold.
And former President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

Here's what experts say you need to know Economy Updated on Oct 14, 2026 8:56 PM EDT — Published on Oct 14, 2026 6:31 PM EDT Social Security checks will increase by roughly $76 per month for the average retired worker in 2027, the federal government announced Wednesday. The payment jump is due to the Social Security Administration's annual COLA, or cost-of-living adjustment, which has been determined each fall for decades. Next year's increase is 3.6%, based on inflation data, amounting to a little more than $900 next year. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The COLA is really one of the only things in most people's retirement portfolios that is inflation-adjusted," said Bill Sweeney, senior vice president for government affairs at AARP. "That really means that Social Security becomes an increasingly important part of your retirement portfolio as you get older." People 62 or older and those with a disability or blindness can receive Social Security benefits. Some dependents or surviving spouses of people who have died can also collect payments. Here's what experts say Social Security beneficiaries need to know about the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027. What is the COLA and how is it calculated? Next year's cost-of-living adjustment of 3.6% is the highest since 2023, when payments increased 8.7% from the prior year's already higher 5.9% jump. The COLA is a mathematical formula tied to consumer prices. For more than 50 years, Social Security beneficiaries have gotten annual adjustments to keep up with inflation. If inflation is low, so too are COLAs, but when inflation spikes, as it has on-and-off for the past six years, the COLAs can be big jumps. Next year's adjustment is "not wildly outside of the norm," said Shai Akabas, vice president for economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center. Because inflation has remained above the Federal Reserve's target of 2% year over year since 2021, COLAs have generally also been higher than that, he said. The Bureau of Labor Statistics calculates the adjustment by finding the percent change between the average consumer price index for workers for July through September of the current year and the same figure for the previous year. If the percent change is negative, there's no adjustment for the following year. Because inflation has been so volatile sector by sector, it may be hard to predict what a COLA will feel like when it takes effect in January, Akabas said. But the adjustment isn't necessarily meant to be a perfect fix. "It's meant to be as close to an approximation and current a measure as can be done," Akabas said, that then "needs to be incorporated into millions and millions of benefit payments and be communicated throughout the system." What does next year's COLA mean for people who receive Social Security? The 3.6% increase is "a significant amount of money," Sweeney said. But with rising costs, it can still be hard for consumers to keep up, he said. READ MORE: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% as midterm elections near An AARP poll of some 1,000 adults aged 50 and older found that 76% of respondents said a projected increase of 3.5% would not be enough to keep up with rising prices. That includes 80% of Social Security recipients. Instead, about 7 in 10 of older adults said an increase between 5% and 8% would be "sufficient" to help Social Security recipients afford expenses — a number that has remained relatively consistent over the past three years AARP has conducted its poll. Over time, older Americans lose buying power, said Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst who receives benefits herself. That's partly because older adults spend more on healthcare than younger adults, while the COLA is based on the costs of urban wage earners, which does not include retired people. People 65 and older spent nearly 2.5 times the amount working-age people spent on healthcare in 2020, according to the government. Next year's COLA may also be undercut by a rise in Medicare Part B premiums, which wasn't the case when Social Security recipients got a huge COLA in 2023. That could take a bite out of people's COLA increases, Akabas said, though recent estimates put premium increases at probably less than $20 per month, he added. The effect of the Social Security payment increase will also vary from household to household, Akabas said. Gas has remained particularly elevated recently, he added, so the COLA may overcompensate for people who use less gas and be insufficient for those who fill up more frequently. Even within the older population, there's spending nuance, Akabas said. When Johnson tracked her own budget in 2025 and 2026, for example, she saw spending spikes that exceeded 3.5% in every category, including medical and dental insurance, electricity, groceries and property taxes. There's debate on how and whether the Social Security Administration should change its formula for calculating COLAs, but a perfect solution may be elusive. "It's difficult to create one cost-of-living index that applies to everybody in a group as diverse and large as Social Security beneficiaries," Akabas said. sources.news_title: Social Security says retirees will get a 3.6% raise for 2027 | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Social Security says retirees will get a 3.6% raise for 2027
Retirees and other beneficiaries will receive the largest annual cost-of-living adjustment since 2023 in their Social Security checks next year, driven mainly by persistently high inflation.
The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% annual cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, today after the release of government inflation data for September. The COLA is determined using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W. The index values for July, August and September are averaged to produce the official adjustment figure.
For the average Social Security beneficiary, the COLA will translate to a $75 monthly increase, the government said. However, the actual amount for any retiree enrolled in Medicare will vary. The Part B premium, which covers outpatient care, is usually deducted from Social Security benefits, changing net COLAs. Separately, Social Security said the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax would rise to $192,300, up from $184,500 this year.
The Medicare board of trustees has projected that the monthly Part B premium will rise $6.60 in 2027 to $209.50. The final figure will be released this fall, but if the projection holds, most beneficiaries will receive net COLAs of at least 3%.
Other Medicare costs are rising, too. Monthly premiums for some prescription drug plans, which are known as Part D, will jump $50 or more next year — although plenty of lower-cost options are available for people who shop the market during the annual enrollment period that begins Thursday. In addition, costs will rise and supplemental benefits will be reduced in private Medicare Advantage plans next year.
The CPI-W reflects price changes for goods and services that working people buy and use, and it is under-weighted for healthcare costs, which have an outsize impact on older Americans. The health spending burden for people enrolled in Medicare is more than twice as large as that of other households, accounting for 14% of total spending in 2024, according to KFF, a healthcare research nonprofit.

Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
The COLA announcement comes at a time when Americans are feeling less confident that they will have enough money to live comfortably in retirement. An annual survey released this year by the Employee Benefit Research Institute found that 61% of workers were confident they will have enough money to be comfortable in retirement, down from 72% in 2021; retiree confidence fell to 73% from 80% during the same period.
“For retirees who aren’t confident, inflation and the rising cost of living are overwhelmingly the top reason,” said Craig Copeland, director of wealth benefits research at EBRI.
The automatic COLA is one of Social Security’s most valuable features, but some advocates have long argued that it isn’t adequate to help seniors cope with inflation — and that the CPI-W should be replaced by a yardstick that does a better job measuring the inflation that affects retirees.
A new AARP survey found that just 23% of adults over age 50 think a 3.5% COLA keeps up with rising prices. “For most people, the COLA just isn’t enough to keep up with what they see as rising costs in their life,” said Bill Sweeney, AARP’s senior vice president for government affairs. “When they go to the grocery store or fill up their tank with gas or get a notice that their rent is going up, it’s almost always higher than those numbers.”
Worries about the future of Social Security itself also are eroding confidence.
Social Security’s trustees projected in June that the retirement trust fund would be exhausted in 2032 — just six years from now. The combined retirement and disability funds are projected to run dry in 2034. Those are likely best-case projections, as key underlying factors have deteriorated over the past year, including lower long-range assumptions about the size of the U.S. population, which were affected by lower projections on the number of children women will have.
Trust fund exhaustion does not mean Social Security would stop paying benefits altogether, but it would set off an across-the-board cut of about 22% for retirement benefits in 2032, absent congressional action, according to the Social Security trustees. The top concern for retirees in this year’s EBRI survey was possible government changes.
“People are realizing that they’re going to have to make adjustments in their expectations of what the benefits are going to be in the future,” Copeland said.
The AARP survey found that 46% would cut back on dining out if benefits were reduced 5% — but a nearly equal share, 45%, said they would have to cut back on groceries and basic household items.
Retirement savings and investments can help plug the gap in meeting living costs, but those savings are available mainly to higher-income people. Among households ages 55 to 64 that have a 401(k) account, the median balance for the lowest fifth in 2022 was just $25,000 — and $220,000 in the third fifth, according to the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College.
At the same time, poverty rates for the lowest-income households are rising. The Census Bureau reported recently that the rate of poverty for Americans 65 and older rose to 15.4% in 2025 — the highest rate for all age groups, and up sharply from 12% in 2019.
The Social Security Administration will notify recipients about their new benefit amounts by mail and online starting in early December, and the COLA will be added in January to the benefits of millions of Americans, a group that includes retirees and their spouses and survivors, as well as those who receive disability benefits and Supplemental Security Income.
Some older people also will receive a separate one-time payment of $90 this month from the government. Characterized by the Trump administration as a Part B “premium rebate,” the payment will be sent by direct deposit or check to 21 million people enrolled in Part B under traditional fee-for-service Medicare. The payments, before the midterm elections, were described by the White House as a “historic action to help senior citizens,” but KFF noted that the 2027 projected Part B premium increase alone would consume most of the $90 — and that less than half of all beneficiaries will get it, since Medicare Advantage enrollees are ineligible.
“An extra $90 in the bank won’t hurt,” said Juliette Cubanski, vice president and director of the program on Medicare policy at KFF. “But it’s not likely to stretch very far to cover higher costs for everyday essentials like putting food on the table, filling up the gas tank and paying the utility bill.”

sources.news_title: Social Security COLA 2027: 3.6% increase adds $75 a month, but retirees say it’s not enough
sources.text:
The Social Security Administration has projected a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for older adults and people with disabilities in 2027, translating to an estimated additional $75 a month for beneficiaries. However, some retirees say the increase will do little to offset rising food, healthcare, gasoline and housing costs.
The adjustment will affect nearly 72 million people receiving monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries enrolled in Supplemental Security Income (SSI), according to the announcement.
The projection comes as inflationary pressures weigh on American households and businesses, with the United States also approaching midterm elections. The government reported on Wednesday that the consumer price index rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, as renewed fighting between the United States and Iran pushed up gasoline prices.
Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano said the adjustment would provide beneficiaries with “greater financial stability”.
However, advocates for older Americans argue that rising living costs could erode the value of the increase before it reaches retirees’ pockets.
Nancy Altman, president of the Social Security Works advocacy group, said the latest inflation figures highlighted the limitations of the adjustment.
“As important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices,” she said.
For many older Americans living on fixed incomes, the projected increase comes amid mounting expenses, particularly for healthcare and prescription medicines.
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree living outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the adjustment would not make a meaningful difference to her household’s healthcare costs.
Ufkin expects her premiums and prescription expenses to rise after a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy programme that has helped offset premiums ends at the close of the year. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people, but Ufkin said her household faces steeper costs.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
She said one medication taken by both her and her husband was expected to increase from $11 per month per prescription to $200 per month per prescription.
She described the expected increase as “catastrophic”.
Senior advocacy groups have warned that such expenses could absorb much of the additional money retirees receive through the annual adjustment.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” AARP CEO Dr Myechia Minter-Jordan said.
Rising living expenses are also forcing some older Americans to reconsider retirement.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York, who retired at 55, has recently returned to work to help cover his expenses, particularly rising property taxes.
He said the projected 3.6% COLA would be offset by inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the adjustment “a pittance”, pointing to the cost of food, healthcare and gasoline.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
His experience reflects concerns among retirees that an increase in monthly benefits does not necessarily translate into greater purchasing power when essential expenses are rising at a similar or faster pace.
Concerns about the adequacy of the adjustment extend beyond individual households.
An AARP poll conducted in September found that about three-quarters of Americans aged 50 and older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% Social Security COLA in 2027 would be sufficient to keep pace with rising prices.
The findings underscore the financial pressure facing older Americans who depend heavily on Social Security to cover everyday expenses.
The impact of the adjustment will vary from beneficiary to beneficiary, depending on their existing benefits, household expenses and healthcare costs.
The COLA announcement also comes alongside a projected increase in the maximum annual earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes.
The wage cap is set to rise to $192,300 in 2027 from $184,500 in 2026. Social Security benefits are financed through payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, subject to the annual earnings limit.
The annual COLA is intended to help benefits keep pace with inflation, protecting beneficiaries’ purchasing power as the cost of goods and services rises.
However, advocates argue that the adjustment may not fully reflect the spending patterns of older Americans, particularly those facing substantial medical expenses.
Beyond the immediate question of whether the 2027 increase will be sufficient, the programme faces a longer-term funding challenge.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report projected that the combined Social Security trust funds, which cover retirement and disability benefits, would be unable to pay full scheduled benefits beginning in 2034 if Congress does not address the funding shortfall.
After that point, incoming revenue would be sufficient to cover about 83% of scheduled benefits, according to the report.
The projection does not mean Social Security payments would stop entirely in 2034. Instead, beneficiaries could face reductions in the amounts payable under the programme if the shortfall remains unresolved.
For retirees already struggling with rising household expenses, the combination of near-term inflation and uncertainty over Social Security’s long-term finances adds to concerns about their financial security.

sources.news_title: Government To Increase Payments To 6.8M Californians: See How Much And When
sources.text:
Politics & Government
Government To Increase Payments To 6.8M Californians: See How Much And When
A boost in benefits is coming for Social Security recipients. But experts say it's not enough to keep up with the cost of living.
Millions of Californians will see their Social Security checks grow next year after federal officials announced a 3.6 percent increase in benefits Wednesday. It's an increase that some experts say doesn't go far enough in cover soaring costs of living — especially in the Golden State.
The increase will amount to an additional $75 per month for the average retiree, according to the Social Security Administration. That will raise average monthly benefits $2,095 to $2,170. Higher payments begin in January, although increases in Medicare premiums could consume some of that additional money.
About 6.8 million Californians receive Social Security benefits.
Find out what's happening in Los Angelesfor free with the latest updates from Patch.
Nationally, nearly 72 million Social Security recipients will receive the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, beginning in January 2027. Another 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income will see their payments increase beginning Dec. 31. Some people receive both benefits.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
Find out what's happening in Los Angelesfor free with the latest updates from Patch.
Higher Costs In California
The increase comes as inflation continues to strain household budgets, particularly in California, where residents face some of the highest housing, transportation and other living expenses in the nation.
The Social Security Administration calculates its annual benefit adjustment using the Consumer Price Index, a federal measure of inflation.
The 3.6 percent increase will apply nationwide, regardless of differences in living costs between states.
California was ranked the state with the highest cost of living by U.S. News & World Report, with housing among the biggest factors.
According to Redfin, the national median rent was $1,785 last month. In Los Angeles, it was nearly $1,000 higher.
The disparity is even more pronounced at the gas pump.
As of Wednesday, the average price of a gallon of gasoline in California was $6.26, according to AAA. That's about 45 percent higher than the national average of $4.33 and nearly 67 percent higher than the $3.75 average in North Carolina.
And those costs continue to rise.
Inflation accelerated in September, with consumer prices increasing 3.7 percent compared with a year earlier, up from 3.4 percent in August, according to federal data.
Gasoline prices alone jumped 9.1 percent between August and September. Airfares rose 22 percent compared with a year earlier.
20 Percent Have No Retirement Savings
Senior advocacy groups highlight the COLA as a sign of older Americans' financial strain.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan told The AP.
Jaime Jakubczak, 68, of Buffalo, New York, retired at 55 but returned to work to cover rising property taxes. He called the 3.6 percent COLA “a pittance,” saying high inflation, steep food and gas prices, and a local tax hike swallow it.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he told The AP.
A September AARP poll shows most older adults agree: roughly three-quarters aged 50+ doubted a 3.5 percent 2027 COLA would keep pace with rising costs.
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree living near Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA fails to address her escalating health care expenses. These costs are expected to rise further at the end of the year as the Trump administration phases out a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program designed to soften premium increases.
Ufkin said that her premiums and drug costs are also expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA “doesn't even meet what they're going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans' healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”
Social Security Faces Funding Shortfall
Social Security faces a funding shortfall that could reduce benefits unless Congress acts. According to the 2026 trustees' report, the combined retirement and disability trust funds are projected to run out of reserves in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83 percent of scheduled benefits.
The outlook is more urgent for retirees. The trust fund that pays retirement and survivor benefits is projected to exhaust its reserves in 2032, leaving enough revenue to cover just 78 percent of promised payments. Benefits would not disappear, but recipients could face substantial cuts.
Congress has yet to agree on a solution. One proposal would eliminate the cap on earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes, requiring higher earners to contribute more. The Peterson Foundation estimates the change could generate roughly $3 trillion over 10 years.
Recent legislation has also affected Social Security's finances. A law signed by President Joe Biden in January 2025 expanded benefits for about 2.8 million former public workers, while President Donald Trump's 2025 tax law provided temporary tax deductions for eligible adults 65 and older. Both measures improved finances for some older Americans but added to the program's long-term funding pressures.

sources.news_title: Social Security benefits increase will hit 3.6% in 2027 • Oklahoma Voice
sources.text:
Social Security benefits increase will hit 3.6% in 2027
The Social Security Administration field office in Whitehall, Ohio. (Photo by Marty Schladen, Ohio Capital Journal.)
WASHINGTON — The Social Security Administration announced on Wednesday that recipients will receive a 3.6% increase in benefits in 2027.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, will begin for 72 million Social Security beneficiaries in January. It will apply for Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, recipients beginning on Dec. 31.
Some individuals receive both types of benefits. SSI provides payments to 7.3 million people with limited income and resources.
The COLA is based on continuing inflation, as recorded in the Consumer Price Index from the third quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026.
On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by about $75 a month, the agency said.
Tax rates to fund the program will stay virtually unchanged, at 6.2% of income up to a certain amount. The cap will increase slightly from $184,500 this year to $192,300 in 2027.
Social Security is facing a shortfall, with payments to recipients outpacing tax collections.
Without congressional action, that will mean benefits will automatically begin to decrease in 2032. Candidates in key U.S. Senate races this year, whose six-year terms would mean they’ll be in office when the benefits cliff arrives, have stayed relatively quiet on the issue.

sources.news_title: Social Security announces 3.6% benefit increase for 2027
sources.text:
ALEXANDRIA — On Oct. 14, the Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% benefit increase for 2027. Benefits include Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance, and Supplemental Security Income. On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month.
Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment beginning in January. Increased payments to about 7.3 million people receiving SSI will begin on Dec. 31.
ADVERTISEMENT
Individuals with personal my Social Security accounts can view their COLA notice online starting in late November — up to three weeks earlier than receiving a paper notice in the mail.
Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account’s Message Center. Individuals who do not have a personal account will need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by Nov. 18 to see their COLA notice online.
Individuals who have not enrolled in paperless notices in my Social Security will receive their COLA notice by mail in December.
Social Security beneficiaries will receive a simplified, one-page COLA notice, which provides exact dates and dollar amounts of an individual’s new benefit amount and any deductions.
Information about Medicare changes for 2027 will be available at www.medicare.gov . For Medicare enrollees, the premium amount will be available via my Social Security Message Center starting in late November.
For additional information, visit www.ssa.gov/cola .
For more information about Social Security’s services, visit www.ssa.gov .

sources.news_title: Hoosiers to get $75 more in Social Security
sources.text:
Hoosiers to get $75 more in Social Security
INDIANAPOLIS — Social Security recipients will receive larger monthly payments beginning in January, but an advocate for older Hoosiers says the increase may not be enough to keep pace with rising living costs.
Benefits will increase by 3.6% in 2027, giving the average retired worker about $75 more per month, or roughly $900 over the year. Nearly 72 million people will receive higher Social Security payments, while Supplemental Security Income recipients will see the increase beginning Dec. 31.
Jason Tomcsi, communications director for AARP Indiana, said the increase will help people facing higher costs for groceries, utilities and health care.
“The adjustment is welcome news for Hoosiers facing higher prices, but our data does show that most people feel that they would need a 5% to 7% increase just to keep up with inflation,” Tomcsi said.
He said rising expenses can make it difficult for older adults living on fixed incomes to cover their basic needs.
“Everything’s more expensive, and so any little bit is going to help, but whether or not it’s going to be enough, I don’t know,” Tomcsi said.
How much the increase helps will depend on each recipient’s financial situation, he said. Some may use the additional money for groceries or utility bills, while others may need it for medical expenses.
Tomcsi said more than one in five Indiana residents receives some form of Social Security benefits, making the annual adjustment important to households across the state.
He also emphasized the importance of maintaining annual cost-of-living adjustments, known as COLAs, as recipients face rising expenses.
“The proposal that maybe people are pushing that would cut or reduce Social Security is not something that Hoosiers want,” Tomcsi said.

sources.text:
Social Security benefits will increase 3.6% beginning in January for more than 70 million recipients, the Social Security Administration (SSA) said on Wednesday.
The cost-of-living adjustment for 2027, known as COLA, came in markedly higher than the prior year’s hike of 2.8%.
The annual uptick in Social Security benefits aims to keep payments on pace with inflation, which surged in the spring after the outbreak of the Iran war.
The rise in Social Security payments for 2027 amounts to an average increase of about $75 a month for each recipient, the SSA said.
The announcement on Wednesday came after inflation data for September showed price hikes had climbed to a four-month high due in large part to a surge in gasoline costs. The fresh reading marked the final piece of data necessary for SSA to calculate COLA for 2027.
“Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a statement.
The agency will also hike the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax, elevating the taxable income limit from $184,500 to $192,300.
Recipients can check their online accounts with Social Security for notifications of their new benefit amount beginning in late November, the agency said. Notices will be sent to recipients by mail starting in early December.

sources.news_title: Social Security Recipients to Get 3.6% Cost of Living Increase
sources.text:
Social security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living (COLA) increase in their monthly benefit checks in 2027. The COLA increase follows a 2.5% increase in Social Security payments in 2025 and a 2.8% increase in 2026.
The Social Security Administration (SSA) announced Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for senior citizens and people with disabilities (SSI) will increase by 3.6% beginning in January 2027.

The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from employees and their employers.
Nancy Altman, president of the Social Security Works advocacy group, said the cost of living increase “is not keeping up with prices.”
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree told the Associated Press the COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare.”

sources.news_title: Social Security Announces 3.6% COLA for 2027 — Here’s How Much More Retirees Will Get – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Jack
sources.text:
Social Security’s 2027 cost-of-living adjustment is official — and millions of Americans now know exactly how much relief is headed their way.
The Social Security Administration announced Wednesday that benefits will rise 3.6% next year, lifting the average retirement check by roughly $75 per month.
That is real money for families living on fixed incomes.
But it is also a reminder of just how stubborn inflation remains.
The Associated Press broke the news shortly after the agency released the final number:
BREAKING: Social Security recipients will get a 3.6% cost-of-living boost in 2027, reflecting an average increase of $75 per month. https://t.co/cXKYCcco56
— The Associated Press (@AP) October 14, 2026
The increase will begin with January 2027 benefits for nearly 72 million Social Security recipients.
About 7.3 million people who receive Supplemental Security Income will see their higher payments arrive on December 31, 2026.
Some Americans receive both programs, so the combined total is about 76 million people rather than the sum of those two groups.
The Social Security Administration says the average retirement benefit will climb by about $75 a month. That works out to roughly $900 over a full year, though each person’s actual increase depends on the size of his or her current benefit.
A retiree receiving $1,500 per month would see a gross increase of about $54.
A $2,000 monthly benefit would rise by about $72, while a $3,000 benefit would increase by roughly $108.
The agency says nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will receive the adjustment beginning in January. Increased payments for roughly 7.3 million SSI recipients will begin one day earlier, on December 31, because January 1 is a federal holiday.
Individual COLA notices will begin appearing online in late November. Beneficiaries who use a personal “my Social Security” account can review the exact new benefit amount there instead of estimating from the national average.
The agency’s own announcement put the scale of the adjustment in plain terms:
❗BREAKING❗76 million Americans will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in their monthly Social Security benefits and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments in 2027. Learn more: https://t.co/ZFjSgZZqm4
— Social Security (@SocialSecurity) October 14, 2026
The 3.6% adjustment is larger than the 2.8% increase beneficiaries received for 2026. It is also the biggest annual Social Security increase since the 8.7% surge that took effect in 2023.
Federal law ties the annual COLA to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, better known as the CPI-W.
Officials compare the average CPI-W reading from July, August and September with the average from the same three months one year earlier. If prices rise, benefits rise by the same percentage, rounded to the nearest tenth of one percent.
That formula is automatic. Congress does not take a fresh vote on the increase each year.
The final piece arrived Wednesday morning, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the broader consumer price index was up 3.7% over the year ending in September. The CPI-W rose 3.9% over that same 12-month span, although the COLA calculation uses the three-month quarterly averages rather than one month’s year-over-year reading.
That distinction matters.
A 3.6% COLA does not mean every price rose exactly 3.6%, and it does not guarantee that every retiree will feel 3.6% better off.
Housing, food, electricity, insurance and medical costs can hit seniors much harder than the national average. When those essentials rise faster than the formula, the extra money can disappear before it ever feels like a raise.
CBS News summarized the enormous reach of Wednesday’s announcement:
More than 75 million Americans will get a 3.6% boost to their monthly Social Security benefits next year, due to a cost-of-living adjustment announced Wednesday by the Social Security Administration. https://t.co/1WTQaba8XT
— CBS News (@CBSNews) October 14, 2026
There is another number beneficiaries should watch: the 2027 Medicare Part B premium.
For many retirees, that premium is deducted directly from their Social Security payment. The announced COLA is a gross benefit increase, so a higher Part B premium can reduce how much of the raise actually lands in a recipient’s pocket.
Social Security will begin posting individual COLA notices online in late November through personal “my Social Security” accounts. Paper notices will follow by mail.
The agency’s 2027 fact sheet also confirms several other changes that will affect workers and beneficiaries.
The maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax will increase from $184,500 in 2026 to $192,300 in 2027.
Workers younger than full retirement age who claim benefits can earn up to $25,560 next year before the retirement earnings test begins withholding benefits. Social Security deducts $1 in benefits for every $2 earned above that limit.
For people who reach full retirement age during 2027, the earnings limit rises to $67,920. The withholding rate for earnings above that threshold is $1 for every $3 until the month full retirement age is reached.
The maximum federal SSI payment will increase to $1,029 per month for an eligible individual and $1,544 for an eligible couple, before any reductions for countable income.
Those details make Wednesday’s announcement bigger than one headline number.
The COLA changes checks. The taxable maximum changes how much higher-income workers pay into the system.
The earnings limits change the math for people who continue working while collecting retirement benefits.
For recipients, the smartest next step is simple: check the personalized notice when it arrives, compare the new gross benefit with any Medicare deduction, and build the 2027 budget around the net amount.
A $75 average increase will be welcome.
After years of elevated prices, however, nobody should confuse an inflation adjustment with a windfall.
This is a Guest Post from our friends over at WLTReport. View the original article here.

sources.news_title: Social Security Benefits to Rise 3.6% in 2027 as Inflation Pushes Up Living Costs
sources.text:
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
Social Security Benefits to Rise 3.6% in 2027 as Inflation Pushes Up Living Costs
Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment in 2027, increasing average retirement benefits by approximately $75 per month as Americans continue to face rising prices for gasoline, housing and other necessities.
The Social Security Administration announced the increase on October 14, saying nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will receive higher payments beginning in January 2027. Approximately 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) will see increased payments beginning December 31, 2026. Some individuals receive both types of benefits.
According to the Social Security Administration, the adjustment will affect approximately 76 million Americans across the two programs. The agency said the increase is designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation.
The Associated Press reported that the adjustment comes as many older Americans continue to struggle with the cost of everyday expenses and question whether annual benefit increases adequately reflect their actual living costs.
Social Security Increase Follows Higher Inflation
The adjustment is tied to inflation data collected by the U.S. Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics. Under federal law, Social Security’s annual cost-of-living adjustment is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on October 14 that consumer prices increased 3.7% over the 12 months ending in September 2026. Prices rose 0.6% in September alone, following a 0.4% increase in August.
Gasoline prices were a major factor in the latest monthly increase. The BLS reported that gasoline prices climbed 9.1% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly increase in the overall consumer price index. The broader energy index rose 5.2% during the month.
Over the 12 months ending in September, the energy index increased 20.4%, while food prices rose 2.5%. Shelter costs increased 3.2% over the same period.
Reuters also reported on October 14 that the 2027 adjustment would be larger than the 2.8% increase implemented for 2026. The increase reflects inflation measured during the third quarter, rather than simply matching the overall September inflation rate.
How Much More Will Retirees Receive?
The Social Security Administration estimates that the average monthly benefit for retired workers will increase from $2,095 before the adjustment to $2,170 in January 2027.
That represents an increase of approximately $75 per month, or $900 annually, for someone receiving the projected average benefit throughout the year.
Other beneficiaries will see different increases depending on their current payments. Because the adjustment is percentage-based, recipients with larger benefits generally receive larger dollar increases, while those receiving smaller payments receive less.
The agency’s projections also show that the average monthly benefit for an aged couple in which both spouses receive Social Security will rise from $3,238 to $3,355.
These figures are averages, not guarantees of the amount every household will receive. Individual payments depend on benefit amounts and other applicable adjustments or deductions.
The Social Security Administration said beneficiaries with personal my Social Security accounts can view their cost-of-living notices online beginning in late November. Recipients who receive paper notices are expected to receive them in December.
Will the Increase Keep Up With the Cost of Living?
Although the adjustment will put more money into monthly benefit checks, the increase does not necessarily mean retirees will have greater purchasing power.
The cost-of-living formula measures changes in a particular basket of consumer prices. Individual retirees may face different expenses, particularly if a large share of their income goes toward medical care, prescription drugs, housing, insurance or transportation.
The Associated Press has reported on concerns among older Americans that annual Social Security adjustments do not fully cover their rising expenses. For retirees who rely heavily on Social Security, even a substantial percentage increase can be absorbed by higher bills.
The latest BLS figures illustrate the challenge. While food prices rose 2.5% over the year, energy prices increased much more sharply. Gasoline prices rose 34.2% over the 12 months ending in September, according to the agency’s report.
That disparity means the effect of inflation varies considerably from household to household. A retiree who drives frequently or pays substantial heating costs may experience a different financial impact from someone whose expenses are concentrated elsewhere.
Other Social Security Changes Coming in 2027
The Social Security Administration also announced changes to several program limits for 2027.
The maximum amount of annual earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes will increase from $184,500 in 2026 to $192,300 in 2027.
For workers younger than full retirement age, the annual earnings limit will rise to $25,560. Social Security generally withholds $1 in benefits for every $2 earned above that limit. A separate, higher limit applies during the year a worker reaches full retirement age.
The agency’s published figures also project that the maximum monthly retirement benefit for someone retiring at full retirement age will rise from $4,152 in 2026 to $4,188 in 2027.
The 3.6% adjustment provides an increase in benefits as inflation continues to affect household budgets. However, the amount recipients ultimately gain in purchasing power will depend on how their personal expenses change during the coming year.

US Social Security benefits to rise by 3.6 percent in 2027
sources.text:
US Social Security benefits to rise by 3.6 percent in 2027
Retired Americans will see a $75 boost in monthly cheques as benefits rise amid widespread inflation challenges.
United States Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6 percent beginning in 2027, marking one of the largest cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) of the decade.
On Wednesday, the Social Security Administration announced the hike after the Bureau of Labor Statistics published the Consumer Price Index for September. The alteration represents a four-year high, boosting average monthly cheques by $75 for older adults and people with disabilities.
The benefit bump will roll out in January for 72 million Social Security recipients, and on December 31, for nearly 73 million Supplemental Security Income (SSI) beneficiaries.
Starting in 2027, the maximum limit for a taxable wage base, or income cap, is slated to increase to $192,300, up from $184,500 in 2026.
The social security programme is the largest federal social insurance framework in the country. The entitlement programme provides financial support for older adults and disabled people, as well as benefits for survivors of families of workers who have passed away. Funded through dedicated payroll taxes, it serves primarily as a federal pension system that replaces a portion of an individual’s pre-retirement income upon leaving the workforce.
The agency bases the annual increase, closely watched by retirees and others receiving benefits, on the average of the annual increase in the CPI for urban wage earners and clerical workers, also known as the CPI-W index. That index rose 3.9 percent in September and averaged about 3.6 percent for the three months of July, August and September. For 2026, the increase was 2.8 percent.
The announcement comes as high US inflation continues to remain a persistent economic headwind, fuelled primarily by energy shocks from the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran, which have caused global energy market turmoil that has sent crude oil prices above $100 a barrel.
More recently, refined petroleum products like diesel fuel have climbed to record highs and have contributed to a widening of inflationary pressures.
Most older adults in the US believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5 percent COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.

Social Security announces 3.6% COLA increase for 2027
sources.text:
Social Security retirement benefits will rise by an average of $75 a month in January 2027 under a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment, the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday.
The increase will also apply to Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments — with adjustments reaching about 7.3 million recipients beginning Dec. 31.
In total, roughly 76 million Americans will receive higher Social Security or SSI payments.
The annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation and rising household expenses. Despite the 2027 increase being the largest in four years, senior advocates and recent surveys say it falls short of what’s needed.
“Another year, another COLA that falls short of expectations,” said Senior Citizens League Executive Director Shannon Benton. “Seniors will find themselves disappointed today when they look up the COLA announcement in the news. The reality is that millions depend on Social Security to retire with dignity, and today’s announcement puts that ideal in jeopardy for millions.
“When inflation spikes due to a geopolitical event like the Iran war, seniors pay the price. Prices go up today, but benefits stay the same for months due to an outdated COLA methodology. Working people can request a raise or seek a higher-paying position, but seniors have to make lifestyle cuts or drain their savings until the next COLA.”
The Senior Citizens league projected a 3.6% increase in August — down from a 3.9% prediction from earlier this year.
AARP recently conducted a survey showing that most adults age 50-plus don’t think a 3.5% COLA keeps pace with increased costs. In three straight AARP surveys, roughly 75% of that demographic reported the same belief.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings and more people feel financially insecure this year than last,” said Myechia Minter-Jordan, CEO of AARP. “That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) critically important. It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, health care and other everyday expenses.
“Yet special interests in Washington still want to weaken or eliminate the COLA, which would amount to cutting tens of thousands of dollars for middle-class seniors. We will not let that happen.”
The COLA formula is based on changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, as measured by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Other Social Security provisions will also change in 2027.
The maximum amount of annual earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes is scheduled to increase to $192,300 — up from $184,500 in 2026. The taxable earnings limit is based on changes in average wages.
Beneficiaries will be able to review their updated payment amounts through their personal Social Security accounts beginning in late November. Account holders can opt to receive text or email alerts when new notices become available in their online message center, officials added.
People who do not have an account must create one by Nov. 18 to access their COLA notice online. The agency plans to mail notices to recipients who have not opted for paperless communications during December.
Medicare beneficiaries will also be able to view their 2027 Social Security benefit amounts in their online accounts beginning in late November.
Information about changes to Medicare for 2027 will be available through Medicare.gov.
Individual benefit increases will vary based on current payment amounts and applicable deductions — including Medicare premiums, the Social Security Administration said.
