sources.news_title: Social Security will jump 3.6% next year. How far does that really go in Maine?
sources.text:
The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities — including about 400,000 people in Maine — will go up by 3.6% next year.
Some say it’s not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment, which accounts mostly for inflation, translates to an average of $75 extra per month for the 73 million people nationwide who receive monthly Social Security benefits and the nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
In all, the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries will add about $360 million to Mainers’ pockets next year, and the Social Security Administration’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
But most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices. The adjustment for this year was 2.8%, following 2.5% in 2025, 3.2% in 2024 and a historically large 8.7% jump in 2023.
And these are top issues for older Mainers, a key, high-turnout demographic in the upcoming midterm elections: Another AARP poll of older Maine voters found that their top concerns were affordability and Social Security and Medicare.
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits facing many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — 1 in 5 have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last,” AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan said.
AARP Maine State Director Noël Bonam said there is a flaw in the Social Security annual adjustment system, which is based on year-on-year measures by the Bureau of Labor Standards: It simply does not account for the true cost of living.
The recent national AARP poll found that almost 40% of Social Security recipients planned to reduce their expenses on everyday needs, including groceries and medication. The more accurate annual increase, those respondents said, would be 5% to 8%.
The cost of goods such as heating oil have rocketed well past the pace of inflation since the start the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran this spring. Those costs reached an all-time high last month, and the Natural Resources Council of Maine found families in Maine will spend an additional $1,200, at least, this winter filling their tanks.
Jess Maurer, the executive director of the Maine Council on Aging, said it cost 60% more to fill her tank this year than it did last fall.
That’s untenable for the one-third of Mainers age 65 and older who have no major savings or other income than Social Security, she said. Many, Maurer said, will have tough decisions to make this winter: medication or food or fuel.
“A 3.6% cost of living increase for people who already don’t have enough money to meet their basic needs — $75 a month isn’t going to cut it,” Maurer said. “It may, in fact, cover the increased cost of food, but it won’t cover the increased cost of goods and of fuel oil for the winter.”
Maurer said older women, especially those living alone, will be among the hardest hit by the disconnect between increases in Social Security benefits and the cost of living. Maine women, she said, are more likely to have worked in lower-paying careers or to have left work to become caregivers. That often means they paid less into Social Security over their working years.
“It is definitely women who get caught in that circle more than men, and it’s been women who have fewer resources later in life,” she said. “They’re the folks who are getting squeezed right now.”
Meanwhile, the Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old-age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Massachusetts, and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. The COLA is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” Warren and Moreno wrote in The New York Times. The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the cap would add roughly $3 trillion to the program over the next 10 years.
The solution will require tons of new money, Maurer said — but it’s necessary.
“It is about survival, not thriving, at this point for a lot of older Mainers,” she said.
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

sources.text:
Americans collecting Social Security will see a boost in 2027.
Nearly 72 million people will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) increase next year, the Social Security Administration announced on Wednesday.
The COLA’s figures for 2027 were calculated after the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics released its September inflation report earlier Wednesday. The Consumer Price Index rose at an annual rate of 3.7% last month.
The Social Security increase is the largest since 2023, according to CBS News.
The new benefits will be paid out beginning in January, the SSA said. Increased payments to approximately 7.3 Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients will begin on Dec. 31, 2026.
According to the agency, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax will rise to $192,300. The earnings limit for workers younger than full retirement age will also increase to $25,560. The SSA deducts $1 from benefits for every $2 earned above that amount.
❗BREAKING❗76 million Americans will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in their monthly Social Security benefits and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments in 2027. Learn more: https://t.co/ZFjSgZZqm4 https://t.co/xJ7MqRajxT
— Social Security (@SocialSecurity) October 14, 2026
Meanwhile, the earnings limit for people reaching their full retirement age in 2027 will increase to $67,920, the SSA said. The agency said that there will be a $1 deduction for every $3 earned above that threshold.
There is no limit on earnings for workers who have reached full retirement age or older for the entire year.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: One in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last,” AARP Chief Executive Myechia Minter-Jordan told USA Today. “That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important. It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, health care and other everyday expenses.”
According to the AARP, the average benefit check of $2,087.52 will rise to $2,162.67 each month. That is an increase of $75.15 per month and $901.81 annually, USA Today reported.

sources.news_title: Social Security COLA 2027 is 3.6%: Here’s how much more money you will get each month
Social Security Announces 3.6 Percent Cost of Living Boost to Payments in 2027
sources.text:
Tens of millions of retirees will see their Social Security benefits increase by 3.6 percent under a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) that goes into effect next year, the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced on Wednesday morning.
The new COLA will begin for the nearly 72 million Social Security recipients starting in January 2027, the agency said. The around 7 million people who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) will also receive a 3.6 percent increase, and it goes into effect on Dec. 31, 2026.
The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month, the SSA said in a news release.
“Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” SSA Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement published on Wednesday. “Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people.”
The 2027 COLA is the largest annual increase for Social Security and SSI recipients in four years. The adjustment factors in federal inflation metrics recorded by the Department of Labor in July, August, and September.
In 2023, a whopping 8.7 percent COLA for Social Security recipients went into effect due to surging inflation amid the COVID-19 pandemic. A year before that, a 5.9 percent COLA was imposed under similar pretexts.
Last year, the SSA announced a 2.8 percent COLA that went into effect for payments sent out throughout 2026.
The COLA is designed to assist retired people and those with disabilities on fixed incomes to deal with rising prices of food, medicine, services, and other goods.
The COLA is specifically based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W, a metric under the broader CPI, reported by the Labor Department every month.
In an emailed news release to The Epoch Times on Wednesday in response to the announcement, the chief executive of the American Association of Retired Persons (AARP) said that “there’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last.”
“That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important. It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, health care, and other everyday expenses,” AARP Chief Executive Officer Myechia Minter-Jordan said in the statement.
Most older adults believe the COLA doesn’t adequately keep up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September included in the news release. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5 percent COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
Other advocates for older Americans have argued that the COLA should be based on a separate CPI that is used for elderly people.
According to the SSA, people with personal “my Social Security accounts” can evaluate their COLA notice online starting next month, or three weeks earlier than getting a paper notice sent in the mail.

The following is a statement from Nancy Altman, President of Social Security Works, on Social Security’s 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), which will be 3.6 percent:
“Every year, Social Security’s benefits are automatically adjusted to account for inflation. This is an essential feature of the system, which prevents benefits from eroding over time.
Next year’s COLA can’t come soon enough for many Social Security beneficiaries. The Trump administration's war of choice with Iran and tariff chaos have driven gasoline prices up nearly 40 percent, and caused grocery costs to skyrocket.
The COLA adjustment will help. But it doesn’t fully account for the costs that Social Security beneficiaries face. That’s because the measure used to calculate it, the CPI-W, is designed to reflect the costs of working people — not retirees, who spend a higher percentage of their income on healthcare, housing, and other bare necessities.
Democrats in both the House and Senate have plans to improve the COLA, by switching to a more accurate measure, the CPI-E. Meanwhile, Republicans complain that the current COLA measure is too generous.
Many Republicans, including Speaker Mike Johnson, have endorsed plans to use a stingier measure, the chained CPI. That’s a cut to the American people’s hard-earned benefits.
Over time, switching to the chained CPI, as the Republicans have proposed, would shrink yearly benefits by hundreds and even thousands of dollars. Switching to the CPI-E, as the Democrats propose, would increase benefits. This would particularly impact women and Hispanics, who have longer average life expectancies.
In 2032, within the six-year terms of U.S. Senators elected this November, Social Security is projected to face a funding shortfall. The vast majority of Republicans refuse to support a single penny in revenue increases, even from the ultra-wealthy, to address the shortfall. That leaves benefit cuts, including less generous COLAs, as their only option.
The bottom line: Social Security’s future is on the ballot this November, and that includes the size of annual COLA adjustments.”
Social Security Works' mission is to: Protect and improve the economic security of disadvantaged and at-risk populations; Safeguard the economic security of those dependent, now or in the future, on Social Security; and Maintain Social Security as a vehicle of social justice.

A report released Thursday details how the family of President Donald Trump "pocketed more than $2.9 billion"—including "in cash and gifts from crypto ventures, legal settlements, a luxury jet from a foreign government, and corporate deals"—while Republican cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program left millions of Americans without critical food aid.

The shooter is dead, and "children are among the victims" of a Thursday shooting at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, according to a police spokesperson.

California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said DOJ was “demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians' right to vote, based on unverifiable information."
In what one former election official called a significant "escalation" of President Donald Trump's interference in the midterm elections, his Department of Justice sued California on Thursday for not disqualifying over 20,000 mail ballots from voters it claims could be noncitizens.
The suit comes two days after acting Deputy US Attorney General Trent McCotter sent a letter demanding that, within 48 hours, state election officials set aside ballots from a list of voters it determined were ineligible to vote using federal databases administered by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS)—systems that have previously been shown to regularly spit out errors.
When other states, like Nevada, Texas, and Missouri, have used the DHS system to vet their voter rolls for noncitizens, investigations have found that it incorrectly flagged hundreds of US citizens as ineligible to vote.
California officials have said the list of names was provided to them on a thumb drive, which came with a password written on a sticky note. They did not consider this to be a secure device and refused to open it. The letter was sent more than a week after California began sending mail ballots to 23 million registered voters.
The state refused to set the ballots aside, saying that the administration had not provided credible evidence that the voters were not citizens and that eligible voters could be disenfranchised. In its complaint Thursday, the DOJ called on the court to stop the ballots from being tallied until the citizenship status of each voter could be independently verified. It also requested that the state not send a ballot to anyone who has not yet received one.
The DOJ's batch of roughly 20,000 supposedly ineligible voters is a significant reduction from the 190,000 that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin alleged were registered in the state back in July. When California asked for the underlying data and methodology for that figure, DHS declined to provide it.
"What happened to those 170,000?" said California Attorney General Rob Bonta at a press conference on Thursday. "They just got those wrong."
This highlights the concerns states have expressed about using the DHS system to purge their voter rolls. In refusing the DOJ's request, state officials have noted that in Nevada, the system flagged 185 voters as possible noncitizens only for state officials to determine that every single one of them was a US citizen.
California Secretary of State Shirley Weber responded to the DOJ's lawsuit with a sharply worded letter, accusing it of “demanding unprecedented measures that threaten thousands of Californians' right to vote, based on unverifiable information or methodology that you still fail to explain or provide.”
Weber described it as an effort to block “thousands of Californians’ right to vote” weeks before an election and said, “The extraordinary measures you demand are contrary to both federal and state law.” Federal law prohibits states from systematically purging voter rolls within 90 days of an election.
“We are not impressed with the federal government’s letter. We are not impressed with its lawsuit," Bonta said. “This is what the federal government does. They lie, they advance misinformation, disinformation, they advance conspiracy theories. They try to sow distrust with those lies."
“Their timing is rife with and smacks of and reeks of desperation and bad faith, to do this during an election,” he said.
Stephen Richer, the former Republican Maricopa County recorder in Arizona, described the government's lawsuit as "a real escalation by the federal government."
"I've mostly said 'Calm, calm. It's going to be OK' with respect to federal involvement in election administration," he wrote on social media. "This lawsuit—in October, in the middle of early voting—that asks election officials to disqualify certain voters based on suspect databases, not conclusive evidence, which definitely could have been alleged before early voting began... This does represent an escalation."
The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Voting Rights Project filed an emergency brief on Thursday seeking to stop the DOJ from using its list to withhold ballots.
"With voting already underway, eligible citizens should not have their ballots withheld based on a federal list they have never seen and have had no opportunity to challenge," said its director, Chad Dunn. "We are asking the court to intervene before voters suffer harm that cannot be corrected after Election Day."
Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) said in a statement that the Trump DOJ "is now actively trying to interfere in the 2026 elections and strong-arm California into purging names from our voter rolls and blocking mail ballots based purely on vague allegations less than three weeks before Election Day."
He added, "This lawsuit has no legal basis or evidence behind it and is nothing more than a blatant abuse of power designed to sow distrust in our elections and threaten Americans’ right to vote."

A Palestinian toddler watched, screaming in horror, as her mother was burned alive in an Israeli airstrike on their Gaza City home early Wednesday that left the wounded girl orphaned—and received almost no coverage in US corporate media.
Reem Asaad Awad was killed when an Israeli helicopter attacked her family's apartment in the Rimal neighborhood at approximately 3:48 am local time Wednesday, the Palestinian Center for Human Rights reported.
Trapped inside the burning apartment was Awad's daughter, Maryam Ahmed Ghanem, whose age has been reported as between 2 and 4 years old. Prominent Palestinian author Mosab Abu Toha said family friends confirmed the child was born in February 2024.
Palestinian journalist Ali al-Jaafrawi witnessed and recorded the immediate aftermath of the strike.
"There are children are screaming alive inside," al-Jaafrawi is heard saying as he approached the building.

"I went back to rescue others and to document what happened, but I suffocated and lost consciousness because of the thick smoke," he added. "I saw a woman on fire inside the apartment."

Abu Toha, who saw Ghanem in the hospital, said the child "kept repeating the same heartbreaking words: 'I want my mum. My body hurts. There was a lot of fire.'"
Ghanem—whose father, Ahmad Ghanem, was reportedly killed by Israeli forces early in their genocidal assault—has joined the ranks of the more than 56,000 Gaza children who have lost at least one of their parents in the war, according to the United Nations Children's Fund.
"Reem and Ahmad had waited four years to conceive Maryam," Abu Toha wrote. "Four years of waiting and hoping to bring a child into this world. Ahmad never lived to see his daughter’s face. The horrific footage of the strike's fiery aftermath evoked imagery from earlier in Israel's onslaught, including video of a 7-year-old girl trying to escape an inferno caused by bombing that killed dozens of Palestinians—among them her mother and siblings—and a teenager photographed burning alive after Israeli forces bombed a tent encampment.

"Members of Congress must condemn this atrocity and demand an immediate end to all US support for Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza," the group added.
The US has provided Israel with tens of billions of dollars in armed aid, as well as diplomatic cover, including repeated vetoes of a series of United Nations Security Council ceasefire resolutions, throughout the three-year annihilation of Gaza, which has left more than 250,000 Palestinians dead or wounded.
Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, weighed in on the attack on Bluesky.

Even 67% of Republican voters think states should be allowed to sue oil companies for climate damage. But Trump and GOP lawmakers are pushing to kill these suits for good.
President Donald Trump and Republicans in Congress have sought to stop state-level lawsuits aimed at holding oil and gas companies responsible for climate-related damage. But most voters don't think they should be immune from accountability.
In a poll released last week by Data for Progress, 75% of likely voters said they would oppose legislation that would give fossil fuel companies "legal immunity from having to pay for the damages they have caused by worsening climate change."
Just 20% said they would either "somewhat" or "strongly" support such legislation. Meanwhile, more than half (53%) said they would "strongly" oppose it.
Opposition was strong across political affiliations: 83% of Democrats and 76% of independents said they opposed giving oil companies immunity from lawsuits, but so did 67% of Republicans.
(Graphic by Data for Progress)
In recent years, states and municipalities have sued fossil fuel companies over their well-documented history of misleading the public about their products' role in warming the planet. These lawsuits have sought compensation for damages from worsening floods, wildfires, droughts, and other climate-related disasters.
Eleven US states—California, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, Rhode Island, and Vermont—as well as the District of Columbia, have active lawsuits, as do at least two tribal governments and dozens of municipalities around the country, according to a tracker by the Center for Climate Integrity.
The new poll suggests voters are even more opposed to shielding oil companies from these lawsuits than they were five months ago. Another Data for Progress poll in May showed just 65% opposed legislation to shield oil companies, compared with 75% now.
"Big Oil is desperate to secure legal immunity and escape accountability for its role in the climate crisis—and the billions of dollars of damages that have followed," said Iyla Shornstein, the political director at the Center for Climate Integrity. "These poll results show that Americans across the political spectrum are opposed to putting Big Oil above the law.”
Protesters hold a banner outside the US Supreme Court as it considers the Suncor v. Boulder case in Washington, DC, on October 5, 2026. (Photo by Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)
The oil industry's lobbying arm, the American Petroleum Institute, has described stopping state climate lawsuits as a top priority for 2026. Their Republican allies have pushed at all levels of government to advance that goal.
In April, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and several GOP cosponsors joined Rep. Harriet Hageman (R-Wyo.) to introduce legislation that would shield fossil fuel companies from any climate-related lawsuits, dismiss pending cases, and overturn state "superfund" laws requiring the industry to pay for climate damages.
That bill failed to pass out of the House Judiciary Committee last month but could be brought forth again during the "lame-duck" session after the midterm elections in November.
ProPublica has identified at least 15 bills across 11 states that have either been enacted or proposed to shield companies, either by granting them broad immunity from liability for greenhouse gas emissions or restricting the ability of communities to sue over climate-related damages. Groups linked to Leonard Leo, the co-chair of the right-wing Federalist Society, have coordinated many of these efforts.
Republican attorneys general in 16 states have proposed creating a "liability shield" for fossil fuel companies modeled on the one that protects gun manufacturers from liability for the misuse of their products. The American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC), a leading conservative policy shop, approved a model bill in August aiming to establish this shield in state legislatures nationwide.
The oil industry has also pushed for the right-wing Supreme Court to step in to block these lawsuits. Earlier this month, during oral arguments, oil giants ExxonMobil and Suncor urged the court to block a lawsuit brought by Boulder, Colorado, that accused oil companies of deceiving the public about climate change and sought to hold them financially responsible.
If the court blocks the Boulder suit before it gets to trial, it could set a precedent that derails dozens of similar lawsuits around the country.
Meanwhile, Trump, who pledged to help Big Oil executives in exchange for their donations to his presidential campaign, signed an executive order last year directing the Department of Justice (DOJ) to identify and challenge state lawsuits that seek to impose financial penalties on fossil fuel companies.
His DOJ has weighed in on the Suncor v. Boulder case on the side of the oil industry and has sued at least five states that have sought to hold fossil fuel companies accountable.
The question about climate lawsuits was part of a broader set of questions Data for Progress asked voters about rising insurance costs and corporate accountability in partnership with the Insurance Fairness Project. Other results showed that many Americans want legal recourse against insurers and other companies that impose costs on consumers.
"As rising home insurance costs directly threaten housing affordability for the majority of Americans, voters are tired of their prices rising while insurance companies, energy providers, and the oil and gas industry go unchecked," said Grace Adcox, senior climate strategist for the Insurance Fairness Project. "There is a strong appetite for holding corporations accountable, both for their role in driving up costs and their role in contributing to the climate crisis."
"Under Donald Trump, there’s a two-tiered justice system," said one watchdog leader. "Big Tech plays by a different set of rules because they bought their way in."
A newly revealed list of companies and billionaire CEOs who donated millions of dollars to President Donald Trump's ballroom construction project shows that Big Tech, according to one government watchdog, "bankrolled it fully expecting a return on their investment."
The list, first reported by The Washington Post, doesn't just show the $25 million donations from tech giant Apple, the pro-Israel Adelson Family Foundation, and microchip firm Nvidia—the latter of which requested anonymity.

The 57 donors whose names were published by the Post had committed to contributing at least $100,000 to the ballroom construction project, which is proceeding for now following a Supreme Court ruling in August.
The list shows a total of $333 million contributed from private donors, but does not include Trump's name, though the president has said the demolition of the White House's East Wing and the construction of the ballroom would be "paid for a hundred percent by me and some friends of mine."
It also falls short of the $600 million projected price tag; according to the Post, taxpayer funds have been used to partially fund the project, along with donations from companies with business before the government.

sources.news_title: Social Security 2027 COLA Set at 3.6%, Largest Increase in Four Years
sources.text:
The Social Security Administration has announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027, affecting more than 75 million beneficiaries. This increase, the largest in four years, is designed to address inflation driven by rising fuel prices and other economic pressures, following a Consumer Price Index (CPI) increase of 3.7% in September.
While the 3.6% boost increases the nominal amount of monthly checks, it does not necessarily restore the purchasing power lost during previous years. The 2026 adjustment of 2.8% lagged behind the CPI for seven consecutive months, meaning many seniors entered the current cycle already facing a deficit in their real income. Consequently, the 2027 COLA functions as a mechanism to track current inflation rather than a recovery tool for previous losses.
The Social Security Administration determines the COLA using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), tracking price changes from July through September. Critics argue that this specific metric fails to reflect the actual spending patterns of older Americans, who allocate a higher proportion of their income to healthcare-a sector where costs often rise faster than the general inflation rate.
Advocacy groups have proposed switching to the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E) through legislative efforts like the Social Security Expansion Act and the Social Security 2100 Act. The CPI-E is designed to more accurately weight the costs specific to senior citizens, potentially providing a higher adjustment than the current CPI-W formula.
Despite Social Security serving as the primary antipoverty program in the U. S., the senior poverty rate rose to 15.4% last year from 14.2% in 2022. This trend is linked to insufficient private retirement savings-with one in five older adults possessing no savings-and healthcare costs that outpace benefit adjustments.
Beyond immediate inflation, the program faces a structural solvency risk. Current projections suggest the Social Security trust fund could become insolvent within six years. Without legislative intervention, this insolvency would result in a benefit reduction of more than 20% for all recipients starting in 2032.

sources.news_title: Here’s how much more Social Security recipients will get from a cost-of-living boost
sources.text:
Here’s how much more Social Security recipients will get from a cost-of-living boost
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, with some recipients complaining that is not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
The agency’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
Older adults feel the bite of rising costs
Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported Wednesday that inflation accelerated in September, with the consumer price index rising 3.7% in September compared with a year ago and gas prices have spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Nancy Altman, president of the Social Security Works advocacy group, said the latest inflation data shows that “as important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices.”
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans’ healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance,” given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
Social Security faces a looming funding shortfall
The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times.
The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy.
The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the payroll tax cap would add roughly $3 trillion into the program over the next 10 years.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program.
The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax and spending bill, gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren’t able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold.
Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

sources.news_title: Social Security benefits get big bump? – The Horn News
sources.text:
Social Security monthly payments are going up next year by the biggest amount since 2023.
The Social Security Administration announced Wednesday that benefits will rise 3.6% starting in January 2027. That works out to about $75 a month increase for the average retiree.
But is that enough? Critics say no.
The raise will reach about 76 million Americans, including retirees, people with disabilities and those who receive Supplemental Security Income.
Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano credited the Trump administration.
“Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” Bisignano said. “Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people.”
Not every senior is celebrating. Prices for gas, food and health care have climbed this year. Inflation sped up in August as gas prices spiked after renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Jaime Jakubczak, 68, of Buffalo, New York, retired at 55 but recently went back to work to keep up with rising property taxes. He told The Associated Press the raise is too small to matter.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
AARP said many older Americans are struggling and need more in their monthly budget.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
An AARP poll in September found about three out of four Americans 50 and older didn’t think a 3.5% raise would be enough to keep up with prices.
Seniors have gotten help from the Trump administration in other ways. The Republican tax and spending bill gave Americans 65 and older a new tax deduction that applies to all of their income, not just Social Security. Some seniors can’t use it, including the lowest-income retirees who already don’t pay taxes on their benefits.
The bigger problem is the program itself. Social Security is simply running out of money.
The June 2026 trustees’ report says the program’s combined trust funds will be unable to pay full benefits starting in 2034. After that, incoming money would cover only about 83% of what retirees are promised.
Washington has helped speed up the clock. In 2024, President Joe Biden repealed two rules on Social Security payments for about 2.8 million people, most of them former public workers. That moved insolvency closer.
One fix on the table is a tax hike. In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, proposed removing the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax. Right now, that cap is $184,500. It is set to rise to $192,300 in 2027.
The Peterson Foundation estimates lifting the cap would bring in about $3 trillion over 10 years.
The COLA news comes just weeks before the midterm elections, with rising prices at the top of voters’ minds.
Beneficiaries will find out their exact new benefit amount in December. Those with an online my Social Security account can see their notice starting in late November.

sources.news_title: Social Security announces cost-of-living adjustment for 2027
sources.text:
Social Security announces cost-of-living adjustment for 2027
The SSA said the new COLA will be 3.6% in 2027
The Social Security Administration on Wednesday announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027.
The COLA is determined using the consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers (CPI-W) data for the third quarter of the year, including the months of July, August and September. It aims to ensure that the purchasing power of Social Security benefits isn't eroded by inflation.
On average, the COLA will increase Social Security retirement benefits by $75 per month.
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," said Commissioner Frank Bisignano.
SOCIAL SECURITY CHIEF BISIGNANO SAYS PROGRAM WILL ‘BE AROUND FOR ANOTHER 90 YEARS’
The COLA will take effect for benefits paid for the month of January 2027, including Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) and Supplemental Security Income (SSI).
The 2027 COLA is the largest since 2023, when benefits got an 8.7% boost to account for the spike in CPI inflation that had occurred.
As inflation eased in the past three years, the COLA shrank accordingly and came in at 3.2% in 2024, 2.5% in 2025 and 2.8% in 2026.
CONSUMER INFLATION ROSE FASTER THAN EXPECTED IN SEPTEMBER, CPI REPORT SHOWS
The larger COLA for 2027 was driven in part by the rise in energy prices this year, which surged following the outbreak of the Iran war and have remained elevated due to disruptions in the oil and gasoline supply chain.
AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement that there's "a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last."
"That makes Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) critically important. It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, healthcare and everyday expenses," Minter-Jordan added.

sources.news_title: Social Security 2027 COLA increase: 3.6% benefit raise
sources.text:
The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 on Wednesday, raising benefits for nearly 72 million recipients beginning in January.
The adjustment, the largest since 2023, will raise the average retirement benefit by $75 per month beginning in January
The increase, tied to inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, will lift the average Social Security retirement benefit by $75 per month, the agency said. The adjustment is the largest since 2023, when benefits rose 8.7% amid a surge in inflation, according to CNBC. In 2026, beneficiaries received a 2.8% increase.
About 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income will see higher payments beginning December 31, 2026, the agency said. Some recipients collect both Social Security and SSI.
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a statement.
At 3.6%, the adjustment exceeds the 2.6% average COLA recorded over the prior two decades, according to MarketWatch. Still, the increase may not fully offset costs for many recipients. More than three-quarters of adults 50 and older said a projected 3.5% adjustment would not be enough, according to an AARP survey cited by CNBC. AARP fielded the survey among 1,023 respondents aged 50 and older from September 17 through 21, with a margin of error of 4.25%.
Rising Medicare costs could further reduce the effective value of the benefit boost. Medicare Part B premiums, which are generally withheld directly from beneficiaries' Social Security payments, are expected to climb to $209.50 a month in 2027, up from the current $202.90, according to CNBC.
Beneficiaries with a personal my Social Security account can view their COLA notice online beginning in late November, up to three weeks before paper notices arrive by mail, the agency said. Those who have not enrolled in paperless notices must create an account and opt in by November 18 to receive the notice online. Information about 2027 Medicare premium changes will be available at www.medicare.gov.

sources.text:
Social Security is upping monthly payments by $75 to counter inflation.
About 7.3 million seniors will see increased payments starting in December, and over 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see the $75 monthly adjustment starting in January 2027, the administration announced on Wednesday.
“Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” said Social Security Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano. “Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people.”

Social Security recipients to get 3.6% cost of living boost, an average of $75 per month
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, with some recipients complaining that is not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the 73 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
The agency’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
Older adults feel the bite of rising costs
Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans’ healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance,” given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
Social Security faces a looming funding shortfall
The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times.
The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy.
The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the payroll tax cap would add roughly $3 trillion into the program over the next 10 years.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program.
The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax and spending bill, gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren’t able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold.
Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

sources.news_title: Social Security checks will go up by about $75 a month to offset inflation
Social Security recipients get a 3.6% COLA increase in 2027. Here's what that means for monthly checks.
sources.text:
Older Americans just learned how much to expect in monthly Social Security checks next year.
The Social Security Administration announced its latest cost-of-living adjustment on the heels of Wednesday's September inflation report. SSA beneficiaries, who are mostly 65 and older, are now set to receive a 3.6% raise in their benefits in 2027.
That's higher than the 2026 increase of 2.8% and will amount to a $900 annual boost for recipients, according to AARP calculations — an average monthly check increase of $75.
The consumer price index, which tracks how much prices have changed, is key in determining just how much Social Security checks should go up. The adjustment is calculated based on the increase in prices during the third quarter of this year compared to a year ago for urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The Social Security Administration said it will start notifying people about their amount in November via its online portal.
While a check bump will likely be a welcome development for many older Americans, it might still amount to a drop in the financial bucket. Over the past few years, Americans 65 and older have increasingly been slipping into poverty after adjusting for transfers like taxes and government programs.
Social Security alone is a formidable anti-poverty program, keeping nearly 21 million of those older Americans from poverty, per the Census Bureau. And for many older Americans, Social Security goes beyond a poverty lifter; it's a key financial lifeline. An August AARP survey of 1,085 Americans ages 50 and up found just over half of recipients say Social Security is their main source of income; among those who said they were highly reliant on it, 82% said it helps them cover basic expenses like housing, food, and healthcare.
Looming over all of that is the concern that Social Security won't be able to pay out full benefits in just a few years; the latest accounting from the fund's trustees found that, unless funding is replenished, the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Fund will stop being able to pay out full benefits at the end of 2032.
Are you an older American living on Social Security? How will the new cost-of-living adjustment affect your finances? Reach out to these reporters at jkaplan@businessinsider.com and mhoff@businessinsider.com.

sources.news_title: Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living increase in 2027
sources.text:
Social Security recipients will receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment next year of 3.6%, one of the largest increases this decade. But advocates say it’s still unlikely to go far enough for many struggling older adults.
It’s the largest adjustment since 2022 and will amount to an additional $75.15 per month on average, according to the Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group for older Americans.
Elevated inflation continues to bedevil the U.S. economy, with rising energy and gas prices sparked by the Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars as the primary culprits. Yet even without the added cost of gas, so-called core inflation — which excludes volatile energy and food prices — has remained stuck at about 2.5%, well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target.
For older adults, who are the majority of Social Security retirement benefit recipients, next year’s increase will be welcome, but it will still come up short given rising costs, said Shannon Benton, the league’s executive director.
“Seniors have spent years watching their expenses outpacing their benefits,” Benton said. “This provides a little breathing room but won’t undo the damage of what we’ve seen this decade.”
The league found in a survey that 89% of older Americans thought the cost-of-living adjustment that kicked in this year, 2.8%, was inadequate given rising costs in the economy. About 44% of older adults draw all their income from Social Security, the survey found.

The annual adjustment is typically calculated using inflation data from July, August and September. “They need Social Security benefits to cover the cost of living, and it’s just not happening,” she said.

sources.news_title: US retirees to receive 3.6% Social Security increase in 2027
Social Security COLA Revealed: What 3.6% Increase Means for Retirees
sources.text:
Millions of Americans receiving Social Security benefits will see their monthly payments rise by 3.6 percent in 2027, following the announcement of the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) today.
The Social Security Administration (SSA) has said average benefits will increase by around $75 per month, though this will vary based on the type of benefit claimed and how much recipients already receive. The average benefit will rise from $2,095 per month to $2,170, though individual payments will vary.
“Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” Social Security Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said. “Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people."
The adjustment follows a 2.8 percent increase in 2026 and is intended to help protect the purchasing power of Social Security benefits as Americans contend with rising living costs.
More than 70 million people rely on Social Security benefits, with the new COLA impacting all payments starting in 2027.
How Is the Social Security COLA Calculated?
The COLA is an annual adjustment designed to prevent Social Security benefits from losing purchasing power as prices rise. The adjustment is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which measures changes in the prices of goods and services purchased by working Americans.
The Social Security Administration (SSA) compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August and September with the corresponding three-month average from the previous year. The percentage increase determines the following year's COLA, rounded to the nearest tenth of a percentage point.
Because the calculation uses third-quarter inflation figures, the adjustment is announced in October, once September's data have been published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
How Much Will Benefits Rise By?
According to the SSA, the 3.6 percent COLA will increase the average monthly benefit for retired workers by approximately $75, from $2,095 to $2,170 in January 2027. For an elderly couple both receiving benefits, the average combined monthly payment will rise by $117, from $3,238 to $3,355.
Disabled workers will receive an average of $59 more in their pockets per month, taking their payments from $1,642 to $1,701, while widows and widowers living alone will see their average benefit increase by $69, from $1,936 to $2,005.
Disabled workers will receive an average of $59 more per month, taking their payments from $1,642 to $1,701, while widows and widowers living alone will see their average benefit increase by $69, from $1,936 to $2,005.
These are averages, and individual benefit payments vary from person to person.
Which Benefits Will Increase?
The adjustment affects all SSA-administered payment programs. These are:
- Social Security retirement benefits: Monthly payments to retired workers, including those who claimed benefits before or after full retirement age.
- Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI): Benefits paid to eligible workers with qualifying disabilities and certain family members.
- Social Security survivor benefits: Payments to eligible surviving spouses, children and other qualifying family members of deceased workers.
- Social Security spousal and dependent benefits: Payments to qualifying spouses and dependents of eligible workers.
- Supplemental Security Income (SSI): Payments to eligible people with limited income and resources who are aged 65 or older, blind or disabled.
Is The COLA Enough?
U.S. inflation accelerated to 3.7 percent in September, up from 3.4 percent in August, according to the BLS. Consumer prices rose 0.6 percent over the month on a seasonally adjusted basis, driven largely by higher energy costs, with gas prices surging 9.1 percent in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly increase, while overall energy costs climbed 5.2 percent.
The CPI-W rose 3.9 percent over the year and 0.7 percent in September before seasonal adjustment.
The 2027 COLA comes amid widespread concern among older Americans that the annual increase will do little to ease the financial pressures they face, particularly in a year when inflation has been running hot. The year-over-year inflation rate was 3.7 percent through September 2026, still well above the 2 percent Federal Reserve target.
A new nationwide AARP survey, published prior to the COLA announcement, found that 76 percent of adults aged 50 and older believed a projected 3.5 percent COLA would be insufficient to keep up with rising prices. Among current Social Security recipients, that figure increased to 80 percent.
Meanwhile, 71 percent of respondents said an increase of between 5 and 8 percent would be needed to help beneficiaries afford everyday expenses. The poll surveyed 1,023 adults aged 50 and older between September 17 and 21.
The findings were consistent across political affiliations, with similarly large proportions of Republicans, Democrats and independents expressing dissatisfaction with the projected adjustment.
The over 50s advocacy organization has documented similar concerns in previous years, with more than three-quarters of older Americans surveyed in each of the past three years saying the projected increase would be inadequate.
Patrick Sabol, a senior lead planner at investment and financial planning firm Facet, said that while the COLA is certainly helpful, over the years it hasn't "fully kept pace with what retirees are actually spending."
"The adjustments have softened the impact of the rising costs we’re all seeing every day, but they haven’t 100 percent solved for inflationary pressures, so many retirees’ purchasing power has slipped," he told Newsweek. "If retirees don’t have other income to rely on, they will likely have to cut costs somewhere in their budget to stay whole."
Lower income retirees are more likely to continue facing financial strain, even though their benefits have been boosted beyond what they've received in recent years.
"Because the COLA is a percentage increase, retirees who already receive higher benefits will see the biggest raise in dollar terms. But since those retirees often had higher earnings during their careers and, in many cases, saved more in 401(k)s and IRAs, they may not rely on the COLA as much," Sabol said. "Unfortunately, retirees with lower benefits and lower earning histories will see smaller dollar increases, even though they tend to depend on Social Security the most. They’re the ones most likely to keep facing financial strain."
The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan think tank, reports the 3.6 percent increase will boost average benefits "by about $900 per retiree," but that it would "provide an over $2,200 increase for the very richest beneficiaries."
"The highest earning couples who retired this year at their normal retirement age will enjoy a $3,600 combined increase – enough to push their combined benefits above $100,000 annually," the organization said.
Senior advocacy groups have said that while the boost is certainly welcome, it won't soften the blow of heightened inflation for many recipients.
“People are getting crushed by prices," Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works said following this morning's announcement. "In fact, the All Items Index for the fiscal year ending September 30 is higher than the COLA, at 3.7 percent, a reminder that Social Security beneficiaries are falling behind as their benefits erode as inflation continues to skyrocket. As important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices.”
When Will the Social Security COLA Take Effect?
The 3.6 percent increase will be reflected in Social Security retirement, disability and survivor benefit payments beginning in January 2027. Recipients of Supplemental Security Income will receive their first increased payment on December 31, 2026, because January 1 is a federal holiday.
The SSA will notify beneficiaries of their new payment amounts in December. Recipients with a personal my Social Security account can also access their COLA notices online.

sources.news_title: Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027
sources.text:
The Social Security cost-of-living adjustment will be 3.6% in 2027, the Social Security Administration said Wednesday.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, provides an annual inflation adjustment to both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, benefits.
Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month on average, the agency said.
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a statement.
Around 72 million Social Security recipients will see the benefit increases in January, according to SSA. About 7.3 million SSI beneficiaries will receive higher payments starting Dec. 31, the agency said.
The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is in line with Social Security experts' projections, which last month forecast an increase of 3.5% to 3.6%.
Bigger COLA comes amid higher inflation
The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is the largest increase to benefits since 2023. That year, beneficiaries received an 8.7% benefit boost — the highest in four decades — in response to rising inflation.
The 2026 COLA was 2.8%.
New government inflation data released Wednesday shows consumer price increases are accelerating. The consumer price index rose 3.7% over the past 12 months, as gas prices jumped.
About 40% of Social Security beneficiaries ages 65 and over rely on the program for at least half of their income, according to AARP.
A recent AARP survey found 76% of respondents said a 3.5% COLA would not be enough.
The Social Security COLA is "critically important" because it helps millions of Americans cover rising everyday costs, including groceries, routine bills and health care, AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement.
"There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last," Minter-Jordan said.
How to calculate your 3.6% benefit increase
Beneficiaries can multiply their current monthly benefit amount by 3.6%, or 0.036, to estimate the increase to their checks for 2027.
However, keep in mind that increases to Medicare Part B or Part D premiums for 2027 — which may be deducted directly from benefit checks — can affect the size of beneficiaries' monthly payments.
Standard monthly premiums for Medicare Part B are projected to be $209.50 in 2027, up from $202.90 in 2026, according to a report from Medicare trustees. Some beneficiaries may pay extra surcharges, known as Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amounts, or IRMAAs, if they have higher incomes. Medicare Part B covers medically necessary and preventive services.
Meanwhile, Medicare Part D prescription drug plans may see modest premium increases in 2027, according to an analysis by KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group.
The Social Security Administration will send beneficiaries notices about the COLA changes. The notices will include specific information about their 2027 benefits, including exact payment dates and dollar amounts as well as any deductions.
Individuals who have created online My Social Security accounts can access that information starting in late November, according to the agency. Beneficiaries without an online account who want to see their COLA notice online must create an account and opt into paperless notices by Nov. 18.
Beneficiaries who have not signed up to receive online notices will get mailed COLA statements in December. Those individuals should make sure the address the agency has on file is up to date, according to SSA.
Medicare premium amounts for 2027 will also be available online through the My Social Security message center starting in late November, the agency said.
How the Social Security COLA is calculated
The COLA is based on the percentage increase of one specific government inflation measure — the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W — from the third quarter of the previous year to the third quarter of the current year.
The CPI-W is a subset of the consumer price index that tracks the average change in prices for goods and services purchased by urban households.
The CPI-W rose 3.9% over the past 12 months, according to September data the Bureau of Labor Statistics released Wednesday.
Policymakers and advocates have proposed alternatives to the CPI-W for calculating the annual COLA. One alternative is the chained CPI, an index that accounts for changes in buying habits as prices rise. However, a recent AARP analysis found that switching to that measure would "substantially lower benefits over time."
Others have proposed using the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly, or CPI-E, an experimental index that tracks spending for individuals ages 62 and over. However, some experts say the CPI-E does not necessarily grow much faster than the current measure used to calculate benefit increases.
Switching to a different COLA measure is among the changes lawmakers may consider in upcoming Social Security reform.
"Social Security's future is on the ballot this November, and that includes the size of annual COLA adjustments," said Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group focused on expanding Social Security.

sources.news_title: Social Security sets its 2027 COLA increase at 3.6%. Here's what that means for your benefits.
sources.text:
Social Security sets its 2027 COLA increase at 3.6%. Here's what that means for your benefits.
More than 75 million Americans will get a 3.6% boost to their monthly Social Security benefits next year, due to a cost-of-living adjustment announced Wednesday by the Social Security Administration.
The 2027 cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, represents the largest annual boost for Social Security recipients in four years. The bigger increase is meant to keep pace with higher inflation this year, driven in part by soaring fuel prices sparked by the war in Iran.
Starting in January, next year's COLA will increase the average Social Security payment by roughly $75 to $2,170 a month, the Social Security Administration said.
The Labor Department said Wednesday that the Consumer Price Index, a closely watched inflation gauge, rose at an annual rate of 3.7% in September.
The annual COLA helps older Americans, people with disabilities and other Social Security beneficiaries stay ahead of rising prices, ensuring their benefits don't lose purchasing power. Yet critics say the measure may fall short for many seniors struggling to cope with rising costs following a 2.8% benefits adjustment in 2026 — a rate that has lagged the CPI for the last seven months.
"While a 3.6% COLA is certainly welcome, it wouldn't necessarily restore the purchasing power seniors have already lost," Shannon Benton, executive director of the advocacy group Senior Citizens League, told CBS News. "The COLAs are designed to keep pace with inflation, not make up for years of falling behind."
She added, "The bottom line is that seniors aren't getting ahead. They're getting a slightly bigger check to pay bills that have gotten even bigger."
About 7.3 million people who receive Supplemental Security Income will see the new COLA reflected starting on Dec. 31, 2026, the agency said.
The 3.6% COLA lags September's inflation data, noted Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group for the program.
"People are getting crushed by prices," Altman said in an email. "As important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices."
How Social Security calculates the COLA
Each fall, the Social Security Administration announces its inflation adjustment based on a metric known as the "Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers," or CPI-W, which tracks the average change in prices paid by workers for a basket of commonly purchased goods and services.
The COLA is based on that inflation data from July through September. However, some advocates for senior citizens say that the CPI-W doesn't accurately reflect spending by older Americans, who tend to spend more on healthcare than younger people. Those costs have tended to rise faster than overall inflation.
As such, some experts support using different measures to make Social Security's annual adjustment.
"We favor the adoption of the CPI-E (Consumer Price Index for the Elderly), which calculates the impact of inflation on seniors' true living costs," Max Richtman, president of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, told CBS News.
The advocacy group has endorsed two congressional bills — the Social Security Expansion Act and the Social Security 2100 Act — that would make the switch to the CPI-E.
"Without adopting a more adequate COLA formula, seniors likely will continue to tread water or fall behind rather than 'catch up,'" Richtman said.
Medicare has not yet announced its 2027 premiums, which could eat into Social Security's inflation adjustment, experts said. Part B premiums, which pay for doctor visits and outpatient care, are automatically deducted from seniors' monthly Social Security checks.
"For some retirees, a significant portion of their COLA increase can be absorbed by healthcare costs before they even have a chance to spend it elsewhere," Tyler End, a certified financial planner and CEO of retirement planning firm Retirable, told CBS News.
End added, "Healthcare inflation runs 5.8% annually, while COLA averages 2.4%. Even on paper, a 3.6% COLA only goes so far if the costs retirees face most heavily continue to rise faster than their benefits."
More senior citizens in poverty
Social Security is the largest antipoverty program in the U.S., the Census Bureau said last month. However, the poverty rate among seniors has been inching higher for several years, rising to 15.4% last year from 14.2% in 2022, according to government data. Experts attribute that increase partly to issues such as rising healthcare costs, lagging Social Security benefits and insufficient retirement savings.
In an AARP survey taken ahead of the COLA announcement, about three-quarters of older Americans said a 3.5% inflation adjustment in their Social Security benefits wouldn't be enough to keep up with rising prices.
"There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: 1 in 5 have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last," AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement on Wednesday.
At the same time, Social Security's trust fund is projected to become insolvent in six years. Unless lawmakers agree on remedies, all Social Security recipients will see a benefit cut of more than 20% in 2032.
"Americans cannot afford cuts to the benefits they have earned, whether through changes to their hard-earned payments or the COLA," Minter-Jordan said.

sources.news_title: Social Security recipients will get a 3.6% bump in benefits in 2027
sources.text:
(CNN) — Senior citizens and other Social Security beneficiaries will receive a 3.6% boost in their monthly payments in 2027, the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday, making it the largest cost of living adjustment since 2023.
Monthly payments for retired workers will rise by about $75 to an estimated average of $2,170 starting in January, the agency said. Nearly 72 million senior citizens, people with disabilities and others receive Social Security benefits.
The roughly 7.3 million lower-income people who receive Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, will also receive a 3.6% bump. Some people receive both Social Security benefits and SSI.
Social Security monthly payments are a key source of income for many senior citizens. That makes the annual adjustment “critically important,” Myechia Minter-Jordan, CEO of AARP, a powerful advocacy organization for older Americans, said in a statement.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last,” she said. The annual raise “helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, health care and other everyday expenses.”
However, many older Americans say the annual adjustments, known as COLAs, haven’t been enough to cover their ever-rising expenses.
Inflation has ticked up this year amid the ongoing war with Iran, which has sent gas and diesel prices soaring. But Social Security recipients only received a 2.8% cost-of-living adjustment for 2026.
The COLA is based on an inflation metric from the third quarter of the prior year. A related metric, the Consumer Price Index, rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Bureau of Labor Statistics announced Wednesday.
In 2023, Social Security beneficiaries saw an 8.7% increase, following the surge in inflation the year before.
Part of beneficiaries’ COLA for 2027 will be eaten up by an increase in Medicare Part B premiums, which should be released in the coming weeks. The monthly premium for 2027 is expected to rise to $209.50, up $6.60 from this year, according to Medicare’s most recent trustees report. That’s much smaller than the nearly $18 jump in premiums for this year.
Crucial annual raise
Many senior citizens and their advocates have pushed for changes to the COLA to have it better reflect their actual cost of living.
The inflation measure used to calculate the COLA is designed to reflect the costs for working Americans, not retirees, said Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group. Older Americans spend a larger share of their income on healthcare, housing and other necessities.
“The COLA adjustment will help. But it doesn’t fully account for the costs that Social Security beneficiaries face,” said Altman, who supports switching to another inflation measure geared to spending by the elderly.
Social Security benefits have lost 13.7% of their buying power over the past decade, according to a recent analysis by The Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group. Put another way, a dollar of benefits in 2016 is only worth 86 cents today.
Payments would have to jump by nearly $296 a month, or about $3,550 annually, to restore their buying power for the average beneficiary, the analysis found.
Others, however, would like to reduce the COLA’s generosity – particularly for better-off retirees – to help stabilize Social Security’s finances.
Those collecting the maximum monthly Social Security benefit will enjoy a boost of more than $2,200 for next year, compared to a roughly $900 annual uptick for the average retiree, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a watchdog group. It noted that Social Security’s trust fund will be drained in six years, which will result in a benefit cut of 22%.
“To help restore Social Security solvency, lawmakers should consider reforming future COLAs,” the committee said in a blog post.
This story has been updated with additional information.
