sources.text:
Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 will be 3.6%. Is that enough for retirees?
The cost-of-living adjustment will kick in December 31, 2026
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Join today
Already a member? Log in
Retirees will see their federal retirement payments go up nearly 4 percent next year, the government announced Wednesday.
The annual Social Security cost-of-living adjustment, known as COLA, will be 3.6 percent, up from 2.8 percent in 2026, the Social Security Administration said.
The yearly adjustment, meant to account for inflation, will kick in December 31, 2026. It will be the third-biggest increase in the past 9 years - but experts aren’t convinced it’s enough.
”The thing to remember about this increase is that it’s simply bringing people up to where they should be based on inflation,” Scott Siff, founder of 55-and-over job matching platform Pivoters, told The Independent in an email. “People have already lost this money due to inflation and been paying the extra expenses month after month. Now they’re just caught up to where they were a year ago.”
When applied to the average Social Security payment of $1,941.76 in August - the most recent federal data - the 2027 COLA would boost that figure to $2011.66.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, called the 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance,” given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said
Beyond 2027, the country’s retirement system faces serious challenges. A key funding source for Social Security payments, the Old Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, is projected to run out in 2032.
If that happens, payments would drop by 22 percent, according to federal experts. A cut that big would reduce the average Social Security payment from $1,941.76 to $1,514.57.
The shortfall is on the horizon for two main reasons, according to nonpartisan think-tank Peter G. Peterson Foundation. Americans are living longer which means the system has to support more payments per person, on average. The gap between workers paying into the system and retirees taking payments from the system has also dropped from 3.9-to-1 in 1966 to 2.6-to-1 this year.
“If lawmakers act soon to address the trust fund shortfalls, they will be able to phase in changes gradually and responsibly in a way that does not harm vulnerable populations,” the foundation said in June. “However, delaying reform would require larger changes to the program.”
Little progress has been made in Congress to remedy the situation, even though experts have been sounding the alarm on Social Security for years.
One possible remedy is eliminating the income cap on Social Security tax payments. Under current Internal Revenue Service regulations, workers pay Social Security tax on up to $192,300 in 2027.
Removing that cap could extend the Old Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund’s solvency by as much as 35 years, according to the Foundation.
“Increasing or eliminating the Social Security tax cap is just one of many solutions for improving Social Security’s financial outlook - but it’s clear that some sort of action must be taken to ensure the future of this vitally important program,” the group stated.
With additional reporting from The Associated Press

The numbers are out for the Cost-of-Living Adjustments for Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance and Supplemental Security Income.
By Wolf Richter for WOLF STREET.
The 71.5 million Social Security beneficiaries will see their benefit increase by 3.6% in the calendar year 2027, according to the Social Security Administration, based on today’s somewhat ugly inflation data for September. It will be the largest Cost-of-Living Adjustment since 2023 (8.7%).
The new COLA will be applied to Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) benefits paid starting in January 2027.
The COLA is based on the average of the year-over-year increases of the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), not seasonally adjusted, for July (3.40%), August (3.52%), and September (3.93%, released today), by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The COLA also applies to Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments.
Because the applied COLAs are based on inflation data for July, August, and September of the prior year, they reflect past inflation. So in years when inflation surges, the COLAs, reflecting the cooler inflation in the prior year, lag behind and beneficiaries lose purchasing power. And in years when inflation cools, the COLAs, reflecting the hotter inflation in the prior year, catch back up, and recipients regain some of that lost purchasing power.
Social Security was designed to protect people from descending into abject poverty when they retire, after having worked all their lives. It’s a safety net and old-age insurance. And it more or less does that.
But Social Security benefits are not enough to retire on comfortably unless recipients do a lot of belt-tightening because the benefits are far smaller than the beneficiary’s peak income was.
In addition, CPI-W may not fully capture the increases in actual costs of living that beneficiaries may experience. These effects are cumulative and erode the purchasing power of those benefits a little more every year. And that adds up.
To prepare for a long comfortable retirement, people need to build additional resources over the course of their working lives, with Social Security being only the bottom layer.
Obviously, if you love the work you do and if you can keep doing it, the best retirement may be no retirement for as long as possible. It keeps the brain challenged and the body active. Our politicians have figured this out; they’re working into their 80s, or longer, and they’re having a blast, whether we like it or not. sources.news_title: When will the 2027 COLA increase take effect? Here's when you'll get more money
sources.text:
- Personal Finance. COLA Increase 2027: What is the adjustment for next year and how much extra payment you'll get in your Social Security?
- Personal Finance. 2027 tax refund: How families with two children could qualify for up to $7,316
Millions of Americans receiving Social Security are preparing for the next annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), which is designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation.
While the Social Security Administration is expected to announce the 2027 adjustment on October 14, 2026, recipients will have to wait until the new year to see the increase reflected in their regular retirement payments.
The timing is important for retirees, people receiving disability benefits and others who rely on Social Security to cover everyday expenses.
The annual adjustment changes monthly benefit amounts rather than delivering a separate one-time bonus, meaning eligible recipients generally receive a higher payment each month once the new rates take effect.
The Senior Citizens League has projected a 3.5% COLA for 2027. If that estimate is confirmed, it would exceed the 2.8% adjustment that took effect in January 2026.
However, the projection is not the final decision: the official increase depends on inflation data used by the government to calculate the adjustment.
For most people receiving retirement benefits, January 2027 will be the first month covered by the higher payment rate.
The exact date the money arrives in a bank account depends on the Social Security payment schedule, which generally varies according to a recipient's birth date and, in some cases, when they first began receiving benefits.
It is therefore important to distinguish between the month the higher benefit applies to and the date the money reaches an individual's account. Although the increase takes effect for January benefits, not every beneficiary will receive their payment on January 1.
When will the higher Social Security payment arrive?
The first increased payments are scheduled for January 2027. Social Security retirement benefits are typically paid on Wednesdays, with the specific Wednesday determined by the beneficiary's birth date.
Under the usual schedule, people born from the 1st through the 10th of a month generally receive their payments on the second Wednesday.
Those born from the 11th through the 20th are usually paid on the third Wednesday, while beneficiaries born from the 21st through the 31st generally receive their money on the fourth Wednesday.
That means many retirement beneficiaries should expect their first payment reflecting the 2027 COLA on a Wednesday in January. The precise date will depend on their payment group and the official calendar.
There are exceptions. People who began receiving Social Security before May 1997, as well as certain recipients who receive both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI), may follow a different payment schedule.
SSI payments are normally issued at the beginning of the month, and the January 2027 payment calendar may differ if a scheduled date falls on a weekend or federal holiday. Beneficiaries should check their individual schedules rather than assume everyone will receive the increase on the same day.
The adjustment is calculated using inflation data from the third quarter of the year.
The government compares the average Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) for July, August and September with the corresponding period used for the previous calculation. The resulting percentage determines how much monthly Social Security benefits rise.
The September inflation report is therefore a key part of the process. Forecasts can give beneficiaries an idea of what to expect, but the official adjustment cannot be established until the relevant data are available and the Social Security Administration announces its decision.

sources.news_title: Social Security's 2027 COLA Is Officially the 5th-Largest in 35 Years -- but This Doesn't Tell the Full Story
sources.text:
Arguably, the most important day of the year has arrived for Social Security's more than 71 million traditional beneficiaries. Given that most retirees rely on their Social Security income, in some capacity, to make ends meet, the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) reveal is of great importance.
Put simply, Social Security's COLA is the near-annual "raise" passed on to beneficiaries that accounts for inflation (rising prices). If, for example, a broad basket of goods and services regularly purchased by seniors increases in price by 3% from one year to the next, Social Security benefits would also need to rise by 3% to ensure no loss of buying power. Social Security's COLA is the tool that attempts to keep benefits in line with inflation each year.
Today, Oct. 14, at 08:30 a.m. ET, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics released the September inflation report, providing the final data point needed to calculate Social Security's 2027 COLA.
Image source: Getty Images.
Retired workers, workers with disabilities, and survivors of deceased workers are set to receive one of the largest raises since 1993. What's more, tens of millions of retirees are on track for Social Security's first silver lining since 2023.
It's official: Social Security's fifth-largest COLA in 35 years is on its way
According to the Social Security Administration, beneficiaries will see their monthly payouts climb by 3.6% in 2027. This represents a tie for the fifth-largest Social Security COLA over the last 35 years, bested only by raises of 4.1% (2006), 5.8% (2009), 5.9% (2022), and 8.7% (2023), the latter of which was the largest since 1982.
Furthermore, it's the sixth consecutive year in which payouts have grown by at least 2.5%: 5.9% (2022), 8.7% (2023), 3.2% (2024), 2.5% (2025), 2.8% (2026), and 3.6% (2027). The last time Social Security recipients enjoyed six straight years with COLAs of at least 2.5% was from 1988 through 1997.
Based on the average payouts listed in Social Security's August 2026 snapshot, a 3.6% COLA translates into an extra $75 per month for the typical retired-worker beneficiary in 2027. As for the average worker with a disability and the average survivor beneficiary, their monthly payouts will each rise by roughly $59 next year.
Given that Social Security's COLA is designed to combat inflation, one of the largest raises since 1993 means the prevailing rate of inflation is also above average. Federal Reserve policymakers have homed in on three factors responsible for persistently elevated inflation and, thus, Social Security's outsize 2027 COLA.
Price changes over last year (September CPI report) Fuel Oil: +74.0% Gasoline: +34.2% Gas Utilities: +5.0% Electricity: +4.4% Overall CPI: +3.7% Food away from home: +3.5% Apparel: +3.4% Shelter: +3.2% Transportation: +2.7% Medical Care: +2.5% Food at home: +1.8% New Cars: +0.6% Used Cars: -1.5%
— Charlie Bilello (@charliebilello) October 14, 2026
Firstly, policymakers have pointed to President Donald Trump's tariff and trade policy as a source of inflation. When duties are added to imported goods used to manufacture products in the U.S., it can increase production costs, which are then passed on to consumers.
Secondly, Federal Reserve officials have singled out the Iran war as a source of higher consumer prices. The ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz has led to the largest energy supply disruption in modern history, sending fuel prices soaring.
Finally, Fed officials recognize that the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out is increasing consumer prices. The combination of insatiable demand for AI hardware and persistent supply shortages for AI chips and memory has increased prices for consumers on everything from laptops to smartphones.
Yes, Social Security beneficiaries are receiving an outsize raise in 2027, but it's designed to offset higher-than-normal inflation.
Image source: Getty Images.
Tens of millions of retirees are on track for a welcome silver lining in 2027
While today's headlines will be focused on one of the largest Social Security raises in more than three decades, there's an even bigger story brewing for tens of millions of retirees currently enrolled in traditional Medicare.
Traditional Medicare consists of:
- Part A: Inpatient hospital care
- Part B: Outpatient services
- Part D: Prescription drugs
Whereas Part A has no monthly premium for roughly 99% of workers, Parts B and D have a standard monthly premium. The standard Part B premium of $202.90 per month in 2026 is typically deducted from a retiree's Social Security payout.
Part B premiums have been a consistent sore spot for the nearly 29 million retirees enrolled in traditional Medicare. In most years, the annual percentage increase in Part B premiums has vastly outpaced Social Security's yearly COLA. For instance, the 3.2%, 2.5%, and 2.8% respective COLAs passed on to beneficiaries from 2024 to 2026 were met by Medicare Part B premium hikes of 5.9% (2024), 5.9% (2025), and 9.7% (2026).
BREAKING: 71 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 2.8% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2026. The average annual increase over the last decade: 3.1%. https://t.co/l5IYmkf6Ih https://t.co/pgqtPLgqMB
— Charlie Bilello (@charliebilello) October 24, 2025
When annual increases to the Part B premium are notably higher than Social Security's COLA, it can offset some or all of a beneficiary's raise.
But here's where the aforementioned silver lining comes into play for these individuals. According to the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report, the projected increase in the monthly Part B premium for 2027 is just $6.60, or 3.25%, to $209.50. If this estimate proves accurate, it would mark the first time since 2023 that Social Security's COLA (3.6%) will be larger than the increase in Medicare's Part B premium (3.25%).
For the tens of millions of retirees enrolled in traditional Medicare, it means the odds have risen that they'll be able to retain more of next year's COLA, as opposed to losing it to a higher monthly Part B premium. That's a silver lining to celebrate.

sources.news_title: 'A pittance': Social Security benefits will rise 3.6% in 2027, about $75 a month for the average retiree, but some say it’s not enough
sources.text:
The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, with some recipients complaining that is not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
The agency’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
Older adults feel the bite of rising costs
Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported Wednesday that inflation accelerated in September, with the consumer price index rising 3.7% in September compared with a year ago and gas prices have spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Nancy Altman, president of the Social Security Works advocacy group, said the latest inflation data shows that “as important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices.”
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans’ healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance,” given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
Social Security faces a looming funding shortfall
The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times.
The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy.
The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the payroll tax cap would add roughly $3 trillion into the program over the next 10 years.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program.
The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax and spending bill, gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren’t able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold.
Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

sources.news_title: Social Security benefits set for a boost next year
sources.text:
Social Security benefits set for a boost next year
Benefits will increase by 3.6 percent in 2027
Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6 percent in 2027, a jump from the 2.8 percent cost-of-living adjustment provided this year, the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday.
Monthly benefits for nearly 72 million recipients are set to increase by an average of $75 for all retirees beginning in January, the agency said. Increased payments to about 7.3 million Supplemental Security Income recipients are set to begin on Dec. 31 this year.
The new cost-of-living adjustment, while largely in line with forecasts from groups like the AARP, is the highest increase since 2023, when monthly benefits spiked by 8.7 percent in the wake of an inflation surge during the coronavirus pandemic.
Inflation, as measured by the consumer price index, rose by 3.7 percent for the 12 months ending in September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics announced Wednesday. That was up from 3.4 percent over the previous 12 months ending in August.
Average monthly benefits for all retired workers will be $2,170, up from $2,095.
And the maximum amount of earning subject to Social Security tax is set to jump to $192,300, up from $184,500.
“Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a release. “Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people.”
But the increase in benefits puts further strain on a program that already faces insolvency in coming years.
Social Security is projected to become insolvent by the end of 2032, according to a June report from the program’s Board of Trustees. Absent changes to the program, participants would at that point see a 22 percent cut to their monthly benefits.
Some lawmakers have floated various proposals for changes to the program to ensure it doesn’t become insolvent. But nothing has gained traction for legislative action.
“With the insolvency of Social Security’s retirement trust fund just six years away — and with it a deep 22% benefit cut — policymakers should urgently begin the work of enacting trust fund solutions,” The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan policy group, said in a statement Wednesday.
“Given the short time horizon, this should include consideration of COLA changes for current beneficiaries,” the group said. “But it must also include consideration of new or increased revenue sources as well as benefit reforms phased in for future beneficiaries.”

sources.news_title: Social Security Announces 3.6% COLA for 2027 — Here’s How Much More Retirees Will Get
sources.text:
Social Security’s 2027 cost-of-living adjustment is official — and millions of Americans now know exactly how much relief is headed their way.
The Social Security Administration announced Wednesday that benefits will rise 3.6% next year, lifting the average retirement check by roughly $75 per month.
That is real money for families living on fixed incomes.
But it is also a reminder of just how stubborn inflation remains.
The Associated Press broke the news shortly after the agency released the final number:
BREAKING: Social Security recipients will get a 3.6% cost-of-living boost in 2027, reflecting an average increase of $75 per month. https://t.co/cXKYCcco56
— The Associated Press (@AP) October 14, 2026
The increase will begin with January 2027 benefits for nearly 72 million Social Security recipients.
About 7.3 million people who receive Supplemental Security Income will see their higher payments arrive on December 31, 2026.
Some Americans receive both programs, so the combined total is about 76 million people rather than the sum of those two groups.
The Social Security Administration says the average retirement benefit will climb by about $75 a month. That works out to roughly $900 over a full year, though each person’s actual increase depends on the size of his or her current benefit.
A retiree receiving $1,500 per month would see a gross increase of about $54.
A $2,000 monthly benefit would rise by about $72, while a $3,000 benefit would increase by roughly $108.
The agency says nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will receive the adjustment beginning in January. Increased payments for roughly 7.3 million SSI recipients will begin one day earlier, on December 31, because January 1 is a federal holiday.
Individual COLA notices will begin appearing online in late November. Beneficiaries who use a personal “my Social Security” account can review the exact new benefit amount there instead of estimating from the national average.
The agency’s own announcement put the scale of the adjustment in plain terms:
❗BREAKING❗76 million Americans will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in their monthly Social Security benefits and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments in 2027. Learn more: https://t.co/ZFjSgZZqm4
— Social Security (@SocialSecurity) October 14, 2026
The 3.6% adjustment is larger than the 2.8% increase beneficiaries received for 2026. It is also the biggest annual Social Security increase since the 8.7% surge that took effect in 2023.
Federal law ties the annual COLA to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, better known as the CPI-W.
Officials compare the average CPI-W reading from July, August and September with the average from the same three months one year earlier. If prices rise, benefits rise by the same percentage, rounded to the nearest tenth of one percent.
That formula is automatic. Congress does not take a fresh vote on the increase each year.
The final piece arrived Wednesday morning, when the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the broader consumer price index was up 3.7% over the year ending in September. The CPI-W rose 3.9% over that same 12-month span, although the COLA calculation uses the three-month quarterly averages rather than one month’s year-over-year reading.
That distinction matters.
A 3.6% COLA does not mean every price rose exactly 3.6%, and it does not guarantee that every retiree will feel 3.6% better off.
Housing, food, electricity, insurance and medical costs can hit seniors much harder than the national average. When those essentials rise faster than the formula, the extra money can disappear before it ever feels like a raise.
CBS News summarized the enormous reach of Wednesday’s announcement:
More than 75 million Americans will get a 3.6% boost to their monthly Social Security benefits next year, due to a cost-of-living adjustment announced Wednesday by the Social Security Administration. https://t.co/1WTQaba8XT
— CBS News (@CBSNews) October 14, 2026
There is another number beneficiaries should watch: the 2027 Medicare Part B premium.
For many retirees, that premium is deducted directly from their Social Security payment. The announced COLA is a gross benefit increase, so a higher Part B premium can reduce how much of the raise actually lands in a recipient’s pocket.
Social Security will begin posting individual COLA notices online in late November through personal “my Social Security” accounts. Paper notices will follow by mail.
The agency’s 2027 fact sheet also confirms several other changes that will affect workers and beneficiaries.
The maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax will increase from $184,500 in 2026 to $192,300 in 2027.
Workers younger than full retirement age who claim benefits can earn up to $25,560 next year before the retirement earnings test begins withholding benefits. Social Security deducts $1 in benefits for every $2 earned above that limit.
For people who reach full retirement age during 2027, the earnings limit rises to $67,920. The withholding rate for earnings above that threshold is $1 for every $3 until the month full retirement age is reached.
The maximum federal SSI payment will increase to $1,029 per month for an eligible individual and $1,544 for an eligible couple, before any reductions for countable income.
Those details make Wednesday’s announcement bigger than one headline number.
The COLA changes checks. The taxable maximum changes how much higher-income workers pay into the system.
The earnings limits change the math for people who continue working while collecting retirement benefits.
For recipients, the smartest next step is simple: check the personalized notice when it arrives, compare the new gross benefit with any Medicare deduction, and build the 2027 budget around the net amount.
A $75 average increase will be welcome.
After years of elevated prices, however, nobody should confuse an inflation adjustment with a windfall.
Join the conversation!
Please share your thoughts about this article below. We value your opinions, and would love to see you add to the discussion!

2027 Social Security COLA announcement: Official percentage and how much your checks will increase by
The U.S.’s Social Security Administration reveals the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027.
Show key events only
2027 cost-of-living adjustment: latest news

- $1,000: Increases to $1,036 (+$36)

ICYMI: What does a 3.6% COLA mean in actual dollars?
The headline figure is 3.6%, but what does that actually mean for your bank account?
For someone currently receiving $2,000 a month in Social Security retirement benefits, the increase works out to $72 extra per month, bringing the payment to $2,072.
That's an additional $864 over a full year, before any changes to Medicare deductions or taxes.
The exact dollar increase will depend on each beneficiary's existing payment.
The average Social Security check will get a $75 per month boost next year with the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment announced by the SSA today. However, the added income may not go as far as is hoped. Other cost increases could eat away at the extra money they will receive next year.
Social Security payroll tax cap jumps $7,800
The SSA announced other changes to Social Security in 2027 along with the cost-of-living adjustment. Among those was that the payroll tax cap will jump $7,800 next year to $192,300. That's a 4.2% increase compared to the 3.6% given to Social Security benefits.
Now that the figure has been announced, beneficiaries can calculate how the adjustment will impact their checks and prepare for the changes. Here are 3 important dates to keep in mind about the 2027 COLA and Social Security payments.
Do you need to apply for the 3.6% Social Security increase?
No. Beneficiaries do not need to submit an application, contact the Social Security Administration or pay anyone to receive the annual cost-of-living adjustment.
The increase is applied automatically to eligible benefits.
The SSA generally provides personalized COLA notices toward the end of the year, including through the Message Center of beneficiaries' my Social Security accounts.
Be particularly cautious of unsolicited messages claiming that you must provide bank details, make a payment or click a link to activate the increase.
There is no COLA activation fee.
ICYMI: Who exactly is impacted by the Social Security COLA?
The COLA will affect payments sent out to recipients of Social Security retirement, disability and survivor benefits.
According to the latest figures released by the SSA, there were around 71.5 beneficiaries of the Social Security program as of August 2026:
Retirement benefits: 57.8 million
Disability benefits: 8 million
Survivor benefits: 5.8 million
The COLA is also applied to payments issued under the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program. While also run by the SSA, SSI is separate to Social Security; it's a needs-based scheme for certain low-income Americans.
As of August 2026, SSI had almost 4.8 million beneficiaries.
Higher than expected 2027 Social Security COLA puts pressure on Congress to make reforms
Estimates in the run-up to the Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) increase for 2027 ranged from 3.4% to 3.6%. In the end, a spike in inflation last month brought the number in at the higher number.
This is well above the 2.8% Social Security beneficiaries received at the beginning of this year and the biggest increase since 2022. It is also much higher than the 2.7% Social Secuirty Trustees had projected when they made their last report on the health of the trust fund that supports payments to beneficiaries.
Under their current forecast, the program's trust fund will run out of money in six years if Congress doesn't make changes to shore up Social Security's finances. When the trust fund becomes insolvent, it will result in an estimated 22% benefit cut across the board.
The 2027 COLA has been announced at 3.6%, slightly above The Senior Citizens League's final prediction of 3.5%, which will translate to an average increase of approximately $75 per month for retired workers.
While all benefits will see the same percentage increase, not all Social Security recipients will receive the same dollar amount increase.
With inflation continuing to squeeze household budgets, next year's Social Security checks will arrive with a bigger bump, and the payment schedule is already locked in.
ICYMI: When exactly will the 2027 COLA take effect?
The adjustment will be applied to Social Security and SSI benefits from January 2027's monthly payments.
The SSA's January distribution schedule is:
Social Security
Thursday, Dec. 31, 2026: Beneficiaries since pre-May 1997/who also get SSI
Wednesday, Jan. 13, 2027: Beneficiaries born 1st-10th of any month
Wednesday, Jan. 20, 2027: Beneficiaries born 11th-20th of any month
Wednesday, Jan. 27, 2027: Beneficiaries born 21st-31st of any month
SSI
Thursday, Dec. 31, 2026: All SSI beneficiaries
2027 COLA will affect payments to 76 million Americans
The waiting is over and the Social Security Administration's cost-of-living adjustment has been officially announced. At 3.6%, it will be the fifth highest since 1990.
The boost to monthly payments will affect nearly 76 million recipients of retirement, disability, spousal, and survivor benefits as well as Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits.
Not just retirees: Who else qualifies for the 3.6% increase?
Although retirement checks attract most of the attention, the annual cost-of-living adjustment extends beyond retired workers.
The increase also applies to Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI), survivor benefits and Supplemental Security Income (SSI).
That means eligible disabled workers, surviving spouses, children receiving survivor benefits and people receiving SSI can also benefit from the adjustment.
The actual dollar increase will vary depending on the type and amount of benefits received. Check at the official site.
What will the 2027 3.6% Social Security COLA mean for you
The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) on Wednesday. The final number surpassed the most recent forecasts coming in at 3.6%. However, there is a lot of confusion around how this boost to monthly payments to keep them in line with inflation will affect different Social Security benefits.
CFP Devin Carroll posted a video in which he resolves some of these doubts and misconceptions. 
When will I receive my first increased Social Security payment?
There's an important distinction between the date the COLA is announced, today, and when beneficiaries actually receive the money.
The 3.6% increase applies to Social Security benefits beginning in January 2027.
Most retirement beneficiaries will see the adjustment reflected in their regular January payment, according to the SSA's established payment schedule.
Supplemental Security Income recipients will receive their first increased payment on December 31, 2026, because January 1 is a federal holiday.
Social Security COLA: How much will your check increase?
Here's what the newly announced 3.6% adjustment would mean for different monthly benefit amounts:

What does a 3.6% COLA mean in actual dollars?
The headline figure is 3.6%, but what does that actually mean for your bank account?
For someone currently receiving $2,000 a month in Social Security retirement benefits, the increase works out to $72 extra per month, bringing the payment to $2,072.
That's an additional $864 over a full year, before any changes to Medicare deductions or taxes.
The exact dollar increase will depend on each beneficiary's existing payment.
Early forecasters predicted that it would surpass the 2.8% boost Social Security benefits received at the beginning of 2026. And sure enough, the 2027 COLA will be 3.6 percent, after considering government inflation data.
This prediction would translate to a $75 boost per month on the current monthly average of $1,940.08.
Calculate how the Social Security 3.6% 2027 COLA will change your benefit next year
For those who want to get an idea ahead of time of how the 2027 COLA could increase their current benefit payment there is a simple calculation to get an idea. Based on the SSA's announcement, you need to multiply your current benefit by 1.036.
For instance, if your monthly payment is $1,200, you would multiply that figure by 1.036, which equals $1,243, an increase of $43.

sources.news_title: US retirees to get another $75 a month for 2027 Social Security
sources.text:
US retirees to get another $75 a month for 2027 Social Security
Monthly checks for nearly 72 million Americans receiving Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6% in 2027, the most in four years.
The cost-of-living adjustment, known as COLA, will apply to Social Security benefits starting in January and increase the average benefit for retired workers by $75 per month to $2,170, the Social Security Administration said Wednesday. Higher payments for Supplemental Security Income recipients will begin on Dec. 31.
The annual adjustment carries particular weight for retirees who depend on Social Security for a large portion of their income.
It also comes against a backdrop of shifting retirement finances, as older Americans increasingly draw on investment accounts to support their spending. For top earners, those flows were equivalent to nearly 15% of annual spending in 2025, up from 8% in 2019, according to the JPMorganChase Institute.
The annual COLA, designed to ensure that the purchasing power of Social Security beneficiaries isn’t eroded by inflation, is calculated using the consumer price index.
Separate data out earlier Wednesday showed a gauge of inflation picked up in September to the fastest pace in five months.
The cost-of-living adjustment comes just weeks before the midterm elections, with affordability a central concern and older Americans among the most reliable voter block.
The SSA bases its annual COLA calculation on the percentage change in the CPI for urban wage earners and clerical workers in the third quarter compared with a year earlier. Those workers cover about 30% of the population, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Based on the annual adjustment, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax will also increase next year to $192,300 from $184,500.

sources.news_title: 2027 COLA is 3.6% for many retirees, but some feds will see a smaller adjustment
sources.text:
2027 COLA is 3.6% for many retirees, but some feds will see a smaller adjustment
A 2027 COLA of 3.6% will be added to Social Security payments and retirement benefits in January. But FERS annuitants will see a smaller 2.6% adjustment.
Many federal retirees will see a 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) of 3.6% added to their Social Security benefits and retirement annuities beginning in January.
The Social Security Administration’s announcement Wednesday of the 2027 COLA amount follows the Bureau of Labor Statistics‘ release of the September Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). About 76 million Americans, including retirees and individuals with disabilities, receive an annual COLA added to their Social Security benefits.
It’s a larger adjustment than what retirees and beneficiaries saw for 2026. Most annuitants received a 2.8% COLA this past January. It’s also slightly higher than the Senior Citizens League’s projection of a 3.5% COLA, but on par with AARP’s forecast of a 3.6% adjustment.
The annual COLA is meant to keep federal retirees’ and Social Security recipients’ benefits on pace with rising inflation. But not every beneficiary receives the same amount.
Civil Service Retirement System (CSRS) annuitants receive the full COLA added to their federal retirement payments, but those in the Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS) often receive a reduced adjustment.
The exact difference depends on how large the COLA is in a given year, based on the following formula:
COLA over 3%: FERS annuitants receive 1% less than COLA
COLA between 2% and 3%: FERS annuitants receive 2% COLA
COLA less than 2%: FERS annuitants receive full COLA
For 2027, the above formula means FERS retirees will see a 2.6% adjustment to their annuities. CSRS retirees will get the full 3.6%.
While the impact of a smaller COLA may appear minimal in any given year, federal advocacy organizations have argued that over time, the difference can add up. After many years, reduced COLAs can create a difference of thousands of dollars.
The National Active and Retired Federal Employees Association (NARFE) said the reduced COLA for FERS retirees doesn’t keep pace with inflation or rising federal health insurance premiums.
“FERS retirees will have their COLAs reduced by an entire percentage point, reducing the real value of their annuities,” NARFE National President William Shackelford said. “Inflation impacts these FERS retirees the same way as all other retirees, yet they are forced to accept a diet COLA.”
At the same time, some lawmakers have been attempting to eliminate the difference for FERS retirees. A pending House bill called the Equal COLA Act would allow for a full COLA each year on FERS annuities. The legislation was introduced in January 2025 and currently has 90 cosponsors, but the bill has so far not seen any movement.
“The Equal COLA Act would remedy this inequity,” Shackelford said. “FERS retirees deserve full protection to maintain the purchasing power of their annuity throughout retirement.”
COLA increases have averaged to about 3.1% over the last 10 years, but retirees have seen a wide range of percentages for the annual cost-of-living adjustment. Most notably, the COLA spiked to 8.7% in 2023, marking the largest increase in more than four decades.
Updated Wednesday afternoon with more details.

sources.news_title: Social Security recipients to get 3.6% cost of living boost
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, with some recipients complaining that is not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the 73 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
The agency's commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients "greater financial stability."
Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year's end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA "doesn't even meet what they're going to do for changes to Medicare," she told The Associated Press.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans' healthcare programs. She said that was "catastrophic."
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.
"There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment critically important," said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment "a pittance," given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
"We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn't offset what our COLA allowance is," he said.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn't adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees' report states that Social Security's combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same "would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation," they wrote in The New York Times.
The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy.
The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the payroll tax cap would add roughly $3 trillion into the program over the next 10 years.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program.
The Trump administration, as part of Republicans' tax and spending bill, gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren't able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don't pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold.
Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

sources.news_title: Inflation sizzled in September — and Social Security benefits will get a boost
sources.text:
Nights are getting colder, but inflation is heating up.
A report from the Labor Department on Wednesday showed consumer prices in September were up 3.7% from a year ago. That's a larger annual increase than the previous month.
A spike in energy prices tied to the U.S. war with Iran drove the cost of living higher. Prices jumped 0.6% between August and September.
"It's not looking good," said economist Brian Bethune of Boston College. "The main problem, of course, that everybody knows is gasoline prices. But also heating oil."
Heating oil is a close cousin of diesel fuel. The cost of the fuel oil has jumped 74% in the last year, which is hard on families in New England who rely on heating oil to stay warm.
Stripping out volatile energy and food prices, what's known as "core inflation" was 2.6% in September. That's also a bigger annual increase than was tallied in August.
The artificial intelligence boom has raised the cost of memory chips, affecting all sorts of consumer electronics. Apple, for example, raised the price of older-model iPhones last month by $100 apiece.
Social Security recipients will get a raise
Shortly after the inflation report was released, the Social Security Administration announced that benefits will increase by 3.6% next year. The annual cost-of-living adjustment is based on prices in July, August and September.
The jump in benefits amounts to an extra $75 a month for the average Social Security recipient.
Advocates for seniors welcomed the increase.
"It helps millions of Americans keep up with rising costs for groceries, routine bills, healthcare and other everyday expenses," said AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan.
Loading...
But critics complain that the cost-of-living adjustment doesn't reflect seniors' actual expenses, which often include higher costs for healthcare.
"It won't be enough for most seniors to even tread water financially," said Max Richtman, president of the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare.
Treading water would be an improvement for most workers, whose paychecks are not keeping pace with today's rising prices.
Prices are climbing faster than paychecks
Average wages in September rose just 3%, so the typical worker's buying power has eroded over the last year.
"People are kind of saying, 'Something isn't right with that,'" Bethune said. "I'm working harder. I'm more productive. And this is not a square deal."
Inflation is not nearly as high as it was in 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. But every time prices start to level off, the economy is rattled by a new supply shock, such as President Trump's double-digit tariffs or the war with Iran.
Beth Hammack, who heads the Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank, worries the cumulative effect of these shocks could make inflation more entrenched. Hammack told a group of economists this week about a Cleveland-area retailer she'd heard from who is raising prices not just to cover today's costs but the higher costs that may come in the future.
"This could be a sign that an inflationary mindset is taking hold," Hammack said. "When people expect higher prices, they make decisions with this in mind. It can become a self-fulfilling prophecy that makes it harder for monetary policy to bring inflation back down."
Policymakers at the Federal Reserve will weigh the new inflation data when they meet in two weeks to discuss interest rates. Investors now see about a 50-50 chance the Fed will raise its benchmark rate in October in an effort to combat inflation.

sources.news_title: 2027 COLA Is 3.6%: How Much More Federal Retirees Will Receive
sources.text:
Millions of Social Security recipients and retired federal employees now know how much their retirement payments will increase in 2027. The answer is good news for retirees facing higher prices, although some federal retirees will receive a smaller increase than others.
Based on inflation figures released October 14 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is 3.6% for Social Security recipients and Civil Service Retirement System (CSRS) retirees. Eligible Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS) retirees will receive 2.6%.
The increase is larger than the 2.8% COLA paid in 2026 and the largest annual adjustment since 2023.
For federal retirees, the new figures mean higher monthly annuity payments beginning in January. How much higher depends on their retirement system and current annuity.
How Much More Will Federal Retirees Receive?
Using the estimated average annuities from FedSmith’s September 17 COLA article, here is what the 2027 COLA means for an average federal retiree:
| Retirement system | 2027 COLA | Approximate monthly increase | Annual increase | 
|---|---|---|---|
| CSRS | 3.6% | $216 | $2,592 | 
| FERS | 2.6% | $62 | $744 | 
These estimates assume average monthly annuities of approximately $6,000 for CSRS and $2,400 for FERS. Actual increases depend on each retiree’s gross annuity and eligibility.
A CSRS retiree receiving $5,000 per month, for example, would see an increase of approximately $180, bringing the monthly annuity to $5,180. A FERS retiree receiving $3,000 per month would see an increase of approximately $78, bringing the monthly annuity to $3,078.
These figures are before deductions for federal income taxes, health insurance premiums and other withholding.
For retirees receiving both a FERS annuity and Social Security, the increases apply separately. Their Social Security benefits receive the full 3.6% adjustment, while their eligible FERS annuity receives 2.6%.
Why FERS Retirees Receive a Smaller COLA
The difference between CSRS and FERS cost-of-living adjustments dates to 1986, when Congress created FERS to replace CSRS.
CSRS retirees generally receive the full increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), the same inflation measure used for Social Security benefits. FERS retirees are subject to a modified formula, sometimes called the “diet COLA.”
Under the Office of Personnel Management’s COLA rules:
- When inflation is 2% or less, eligible FERS retirees receive the full adjustment.
- When inflation is more than 2% but no more than 3%, FERS retirees receive 2%.
- When inflation exceeds 3%, the FERS adjustment is one percentage point below the full inflation adjustment.
With the CPI-W up 3.6%, eligible FERS retirees therefore receive 2.6%.
Congress designed FERS as a three-part retirement system that combines a smaller federal pension with Social Security and the Thrift Savings Plan (TSP). The reduced pension COLA was one of the differences built into that system.
How the 2027 COLA Was Calculated
The COLA calculation is based on the CPI-W, published monthly by BLS.
Although news reports frequently cite the broader Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), that is not the index used to determine Social Security and federal retirement COLAs. Instead, the calculation compares the average CPI-W for July, August and September of the current year with the average for the same three months of the preceding year.
Here are the figures used to determine the 2027 adjustment:
| Month | CPI-W | 
|---|---|
| July 2026 | 327.104 | 
| August 2026 | 328.481 | 
| September 2026 | 330.654 | 
| 2026 third-quarter average | 328.746 | 
| 2025 third-quarter average | 317.265 | 
The calculation is:
(328.746 − 317.265) ÷ 317.265 × 100 = 3.619%
Rounded to the nearest tenth of one percent, the 2027 COLA is 3.6%.
The September CPI-W was the final figure needed to complete the calculation. The October 14 BLS inflation report showed the CPI-W increased 3.9% over the preceding 12 months. That figure differs from the 3.6% COLA because it compares September to September rather than comparing the averages for the two third quarters.
How Does the 2027 COLA Compare to the Past 10 Years?
The 2027 adjustment is higher than most annual increases over the past decade but substantially less than the unusually large adjustments during the inflation surge of 2022 and 2023.

|---|---|---|
| 2017 | 0.3% | 0.3% | 
| 2018 | 2.0% | 2.0% | 
| 2019 | 2.8% | 2.0% | 
| 2020 | 1.6% | 1.6% | 
| 2021 | 1.3% | 1.3% | 
| 2022 | 5.9% | 4.9% | 
| 2023 | 8.7% | 7.7% |

| 2025 | 2.5% | 2.0% |

| 2027 | 3.6% | 2.6% | 
Sources: Social Security Administration historical COLA data and OPM’s FERS adjustment formula. Years show when increases were paid. FERS percentages assume eligibility for a full annual COLA.
The highest COLA during this period was 8.7% in 2023, reflecting the sharp inflation that followed the COVID-19 pandemic and associated economic disruptions. Retirees received only a 0.3% adjustment in 2017.
The 2027 increase is the third-largest adjustment in the 11-year period shown.
What About Social Security Benefits?
Social Security recipients will also receive the 3.6% increase. A retiree currently receiving $2,100 per month would see an increase of approximately $76, bringing the monthly benefit to about $2,176. A $3,000 monthly benefit would rise by approximately $108.
The Social Security COLA becomes effective with December 2026 benefits, which are generally paid in January 2027. Federal retirement annuity increases also generally appear in payments received in January.
Retirees should remember that an increase in Medicare Part B premiums could reduce the net increase in Social Security payments. The COLA applies to gross benefits, not necessarily the amount deposited into a recipient’s bank account.
The Bottom Line for Federal Retirees
The 2027 COLA provides a larger increase than retirees received in either 2025 or 2026. It will help offset higher living costs, but whether retirees actually gain purchasing power will depend on what happens to inflation, insurance premiums, taxes and other household expenses during 2027.
For now, retirees have the information needed to begin planning their budgets for the coming year.

sources.news_title: Social Security Benefits to Rise 3.6% in 2027, but Retirees Warn Inflation Will Erase Gains
sources.text:
More than 70 million Americans will receive higher Social Security payments next year, with an average monthly increase of $75, although rising healthcare, housing and everyday living costs threaten to offset the financial relief.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment in 2027, the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday, October 14, providing millions of retirees and disabled Americans with higher monthly payments as inflation continues squeezing household budgets.
The increase will add approximately $75 per month, or $900 annually, to the average retirement benefit. The adjustment will take effect in January for approximately 72 million Social Security beneficiaries, while nearly 7.3 million Supplemental Security Income recipients will begin receiving higher payments December 31.
According to Reuters’ coverage of the announcement, the adjustment exceeds the 2.8% increase granted for 2026 and represents the largest annual benefit increase since 2023.
Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano said the adjustment would provide beneficiaries with “greater financial stability” as the agency continues administering retirement, disability and survivor benefits.
The annual cost-of-living adjustment, known as COLA, is calculated using changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers during the third quarter of each year.
Wednesday’s announcement followed a Labor Department report showing that consumer prices increased 0.6% in September, bringing annual inflation to 3.7%.
Gasoline prices rose 9.1% during the month, while housing, medical services and other essential expenses continued increasing.
Despite the larger benefit adjustment, some retirees say the additional payments will do little to offset the rising cost of healthcare and household necessities.
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree living near Rochester, Minnesota, expressed concern about increasing Medicare expenses, particularly following the scheduled expiration of a temporary federal subsidy program designed to limit prescription drug premium increases.
Ufkin told The Associated Press that one medication she and her husband take could increase from $11 to $200 per month per prescription.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she said.
She described the anticipated prescription drug increase as “catastrophic.”
Other retirees cited growing property taxes and higher prices for food, transportation and utilities.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old Buffalo, New York, resident who retired at age 55, said he recently returned to work to help cover living expenses.
He described the 3.6% increase as “a pittance,” pointing to a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his community.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” Jakubczak said.
Senior advocacy organizations have also warned that Social Security adjustments may not fully reflect the expenses older Americans face.
AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan said many retirees depend heavily on Social Security because they have limited personal savings.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” she said.
A September AARP survey found that approximately three-quarters of respondents aged 50 and older believed a projected 3.5% increase would be insufficient to keep pace with rising prices.
The Social Security Administration also announced that the maximum amount of annual earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes will increase from $184,500 in 2026 to $192,300 in 2027.
The higher threshold means workers earning above the current limit will pay Social Security taxes on a larger portion of their income.
Meanwhile, the program continues facing substantial long-term financial challenges.
According to the 2026 Social Security trustees’ report, the combined reserves of the retirement and disability trust funds are projected to be depleted in 2034 unless Congress makes changes.
At that point, incoming revenue would be sufficient to cover approximately 83% of scheduled benefits. The retirement trust fund alone is projected to exhaust its reserves in 2032, when continuing income would cover approximately 78% of scheduled payments.
The projections do not mean Social Security would disappear, but they indicate that lawmakers must address the funding gap to prevent future benefit reductions.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, have proposed raising or eliminating the payroll tax earnings cap to increase revenue.
The Peter G. Peterson Foundation estimates that eliminating the cap could generate approximately $3 trillion over 10 years, although such proposals face disagreements over taxes and program financing.
Recent federal policy changes have also affected Social Security’s financial outlook.
Legislation signed under former President Joe Biden eliminated the Windfall Elimination Provision and Government Pension Offset, increasing benefits for approximately 2.8 million retirees, including former public employees.
President Donald Trump’s tax legislation introduced a temporary deduction for eligible Americans aged 65 and older. However, the deduction is subject to income limits and does not benefit all Social Security recipients.
For current beneficiaries, the immediate concern remains whether next year’s increase will provide meaningful financial relief.
Although the 3.6% adjustment will raise monthly payments, higher Medicare costs and continued inflation could absorb much of the increase for retirees living on fixed incomes.
With Social Security’s long-term funding challenges unresolved, the announcement also renews attention on the difficult decisions facing Congress over the future of America’s largest retirement benefits program.

The Social Security Administration announced the official annual cost-of-living-adjustment on Wednesday, increasing benefits by 3.6% in 2027.
Tens of millions of retirees will see a modest increase in benefits in January when the new COLA is added to Social Security payments. The 3.6% rise is an additional $75 on average per month, intended to help older adults meet higher prices for food, fuel, and other goods and services.
Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are
The agency's commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.” However, some recipients say it's not enough and won't offset rising prices.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics' released September 2026 inflation data showing the consumer price index rose 3.7% last month, a sign that high prices remain an economic challenge for Americans. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, up from 0.4% the previous month.
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA won't even put a dent on her healthcare costs, which are set to increase in January after the Trump administration announced it was ending a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin told The Associated Press that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told the AP.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after the Republican administration made changes to older Americans' healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”
U.S. & World
Another change set to take effect next year is an increase in the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax. That is slated to increase to $192,300 from $184,500 in 2027, the agency announced.
What is the Social Security COLA for 2027?
Millions of Social Security recipients will get a 3.6% increase in their benefits in 2027. That's about $75 per month for the average recipient, according to government estimates.
The maximum benefit for a retired worker who claims at full retirement age will go up to $4,188 per month in 2027, up from $4,152 per month in 2026, according to the Social Security Administration. The average benefits for all retired workers will be $2,107 in 2027, up from $2,095 in 2026. A retired couple would see an increase of $147, going from $3,208 to $3,355.
| Estimated Average Monthly Social Security Benefits Payable in January 2027 |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
|  | Before 3.6% COLA | After 3.6% COLA | 
| All Retired Workers | $2,095 | $2,170 | 
| Aged Couple, Both Receiving Benefits | $3,238 | $3,355 | 
| Widowed Mother and Two Children | $3,932 | $4,074 |

The agency will begin notifying recipients about their new benefit amount by mail starting in early December. Adjusted payments to nearly 7.5 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income will begin on December 31.
Those with my Social Security accounts can view their COLA notices online.
Higher disability benefits threshold
Individuals receiving Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) can work while maintaining their benefits, but their earnings must remain below the agency's limits.
Workers who are not blind may earn up to $1,770 a month in 2027, up from $1,690 in 2026, before their eligibility is affected. For blind workers, the limit will increase to $2,950 per month.
The thresholds for a trial work period — when beneficiaries can test their ability to work while still being considered disabled — will also rise, from $1,210 per month to $1,270.
Is the COLA enough? Some seniors call it 'a pittance'
For some older adults, the COLA increase in a drop in the bucket as inflation eats away at any gains.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York, who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance," given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is," he said.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
How does Social Security work?
The Social Security program pays roughly $1.4 trillion in benefits to more than 71 million people each year, including including retirees and low-income individuals with disabilities.
The short answer is that taxes fund Social Security. The government uses taxes from working people to pay benefits to people who have already retired, people who are disabled, the survivors of workers who have died and dependents of beneficiaries.
Social Security is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers. While the money is used to pay people currently receiving benefits, any unused money goes to the Social Security trust fund. Some of the money in the trust, together with the Social Security contributions of people in the workforce, pay for future benefits.
To determine what amount of Social Security you'll receive, the government calculates a percentage of your highest wages from your top 35 years of earning, factoring in when you choose to start receiving benefits.
Why are Social Security benefits adjusted and how is COLA calculated?
Policymakers say the COLA works to preserve the purchasing power of Social Security benefits, and shouldn’t be seen as a pay hike for retirees.
COLA is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W. The consumer price index, which measures a basket of common products as well as various energy goods, increased 4.3% in August and 3.7% in September.
At one time Congress had to approve inflation increases, but starting in the mid-1970s lawmakers turned that function over to nonpartisan experts within the government bureaucracy. The annual review is now tied to changes in an official measure of inflation and proceeds automatically and with no political brinksmanship
Is the Social Security trust running out of money?
Future problems with the fund have long been predicted, largely because of demographic shifts. As birthrates decline, fewer people become workers, which results in fewer payments of payroll taxes. Meanwhile, more Baby Boomers are retiring and collecting Social Security.
The annual Social Security and Medicare trustees report said the program’s trust fund will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. If the trust fund is depleted, the government will be able to pay only 81% of scheduled benefits, the report said. So while Social Security won't go "bankrupt," a 20% cut in payments would be devastating to recipients, said John Hishta, AARP's senior vice president for campaigns.
“That’s a car payment, that’s utility costs, that's monthly grocery bills,” Hishta added.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Social Security benefits will rise 3.6% in 2027, but that may not be enough to offset healthcare costs
sources.text:
Monthly checks for the nearly 76 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits will rise by 3.6% in 2027. The increase, announced on Oct. 14, 2026, is the largest since the one that took effect in 2023.
This cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is how the government tries to make sure that the value of Social Security benefits keeps up with inflation. Without it, the same payment would cover less of what recipients are spending on medical care, housing, groceries, clothing and other necessities.
I am a finance professor, and one of the topics I research is how inflation affects retirees’ investment choices. And I believe the upcoming bump doesn’t capture the inflation challenges that many people who receive Social Security benefits face.
The percentage increase in Social Security benefits depends in part on the annual inflation rate as of September 2026. It stood at 3.7% that month, as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a government agency, also announced on Oct. 14.
But the size of the increase is only part of the issue. The index used to set the COLA reflects what working people buy, not retirees, and that is a mismatch at the heart of a long-running debate over how the adjustment should be measured.
Calculating the COLA
The government has annually increased Social Security benefits to keep up with inflation since 1975. Congress previously had to pass a law each time it increased benefits. As a result, years could pass without an adjustment, despite climbing prices.
The metric that the government uses is its consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers, known as the CPI-W. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks changes in the prices of goods and services that working households typically buy to calculate this index.
The Social Security Administration then compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August and September with the average for those same months in the prior year to set the COLA adjustment, which kicks in the following January.
If the economy contracts and prices fall, however, benefits stay the same. That happened in 2009, 2010 and 2015.
Spending much of the bump on premiums
One big problem with this calculation is that it understates healthcare inflation.
Out-of-pocket health costs, including Medicare premiums, deductibles and copayments for medical care and prescription drugs, typically consume nearly 30% of Social Security benefits, according to research from the nonpartisan Center for Retirement Research at Boston College.
For example, the government deducts Medicare Part B premiums directly from many retirees’ Social Security checks. The standard monthly Part B premium rose by US$17.90 in 2026, from $185 to $202.90. That increase alone consumed roughly one-third of the average $56 monthly gain in benefits from the 2026 COLA.
More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as most Americans getting Social Security benefits are, helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation.
Finding other options
Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the Senior Citizens League and the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees. Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education and transportation than people with jobs.
There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the consumer price index for Americans 62 and older, known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite some efforts in Congress to make the switch.
The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care. People 65 and older spend more than twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates.
Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014. It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W.
But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment. The CPI-E has increased less than CPI-W in some years. What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose.
This article was originally published on Oct. 13, 2026. It has been updated with the latest cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security benefits.
