More money, more problems.
Though the upcoming October 14 announcement of the US Bureau of Labor Statistics’ September inflation report — which reveals the last data point that will set Social Security’s latest cost of living adjustment (COLA) — will likely translate into a “raise” of sorts for the program’s 71 million beneficiaries next year, the potential benefit cuts that could eventually accompany this bump may be brutal.
The 2027 COLA adjustment, which will be announced at 8:30 a.m. ET this Wednesday, is projected by The Senior Citizens’ League (an advocacy group) to increase by 3.5%, per The Independent.
Though the bump sounds like a big win at first glance (indeed, the projected increase would be one of the largest of the past 35 years, according to The Motley Fool), the benefit cuts that may indirectly result — like potentially smaller SNAP food assistance allotments, higher Medicaid Part B premiums and less overall purchasing power for Social Security beneficiaries — could significantly hamper the announcement’s surface-level benefits in the not-so-distant future.
These potential negative effects are mainly tied to projected issues with the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund (OASI), which is one of the two main financial accounts that support Social Security, and its dwindling asset reserves.
As of now, the fund, which was established in 1939 and pays benefits to eligible retired workers and eligible family members of workers who’ve died, has an unfunded obligation of a whopping $29.3 trillion. Though these funds are currently forecast to be exhausted by the fourth quarter of 2032, the high projected COLA bump could mean that the reserve will drain even faster, leading to substantially smaller Social Security checks if Congress does not intervene.
If the law remains unchanged, continuing income would cover around 78% of potential benefits, according to the 2026 OASDI Trustees Report.
Social Security beneficiaries should not panic just yet, however. These potential cuts are not guaranteed — nor are they directly tied to the COLA adjustment (and will therefore not be announced this Wednesday).
But those who still find themselves worrying over how the COLA bump may negatively impact their Social Security down the line can still take some steps to ease their financial anxiety.
Beyond keeping an eye on benefit changes in real time by checking in with state benefit agencies, Supplemental Security Income (SSI) notices and Medicaid and Medicare agencies, Social Security beneficiaries can estimate their monthly income after premiums, taxes and other assistance changes to track a full, accurate picture of their finances.

sources.news_title: What US Recipients Could Learn From Wednesday's Social Security 2027 COLA Announcement
sources.text:
What US Recipients Could Learn From Wednesday's Social Security 2027 COLA Announcement
The official cost-of-living adjustment is expected on 14 October 2026, while projected Part B and Part D costs could limit beneficiaries' gains
Millions of Americans will learn on 14 October 2026 how much their Social Security benefits are expected to rise next year, although higher Medicare costs could offset part of the increase.
Per AL.com, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) is scheduled to release September inflation data at 08:30 Eastern Time on 14 October 2026. Thereafter, the Social Security Administration (SSA) is expected to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA).
The Senior Citizens League (TSCL) forecasts a 3.5% increase, above the 2.8% adjustment for 2026, but the official figure has yet to be confirmed.
The group estimates that a 3.5% adjustment would add $67.90 (approximately £51.32) to the average monthly Social Security benefit. On its figures, an average payment of $1,940.08 (£1,466.31) would rise to $2,007.98 (£1,517.63).
For someone receiving $2,000 (£1,511.60) a month, a 3.5% increase would mean an additional $70 (£52.91), bringing the monthly payment to $2,070 (£1,564.51).
These are illustrative calculations based on the TSCL's forecast, not confirmed 2027 payment amounts. Individual increases would depend on existing benefits.
How the Increase is Calculated
The annual COLA is intended to help Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments keep pace with inflation. The SSA calculates the adjustment using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W).
Specifically, it compares the average CPI-W for July, August and September with the average for the same three months in the previous year. The percentage increase in that quarterly average determines the COLA, rather than the inflation rate for any single month. If the index does not increase, there is no COLA under the standard formula.
Some SSI recipients will receive two payments in October, but neither is an extra benefit. The regular October payment is followed by the November payment on 30 October because 1 November falls on a Sunday. This is a calendar adjustment, not a bonus, and it is separate from the 2027 Social Security COLA, The Hill noted.
Why a Higher Benefit May Feel Smaller
For beneficiaries who have their Medicare Part B premiums deducted directly from Social Security payments, an increase in premiums can reduce the amount of their COLA that they actually receive.
A Medicare report projects a standard monthly Part B premium of $209.50 (£158.34) for 2027, up $6.60 (£4.99) from $202.90 (£153.35) in 2026. The trustees also project an annual Part B deductible of $292 (£220.69), compared with $283 (£213.89) in 2026. These 2027 Part B figures are projections, not final premiums or deductibles.
Prescription drug coverage under Medicare Part D could bring additional costs. The standard deductible is set to rise from $615 (£464.82) in 2026 to $700 (£529.06) in 2027. The annual out-of-pocket limit is also set to increase from $2,100 (£1,587.18) to $2,400 (£1,813.92).
These figures describe the standard Part D benefit structure; actual costs will depend on a beneficiary's plan, covered medicines and prescriptions. The deductible and out-of-pocket limit are separate from the monthly Part B premium.
Even if the COLA reaches 3.5%, beneficiaries may therefore see a smaller improvement in their disposable income once healthcare expenses and other rising living costs are taken into account.
When the Higher Payments Arrive
Most Social Security recipients will receive their first payment reflecting the 2027 COLA in January 2027. SSI recipients will receive their adjusted January payment on 31 December 2026 because 1 January is a federal holiday.
Social Security payments normally scheduled for the third day of the month will also arrive on 31 December in this instance. The usual payment date, 3 January 2027, falls on a Sunday, and the preceding days include the New Year's Day holiday and a Saturday.
Meanwhile, in the TSCL's 2026 survey, 89% of respondents said the 2026 COLA was too low, while 44% reported relying entirely on Social Security for income.
TSCL executive director Shannon Benton has argued that the CPI-W does not adequately reflect older Americans' spending patterns. The concern is that a measure based on urban wage earners and clerical workers may not capture the particular pressures older people face from healthcare and other essential expenses.
The official 2027 adjustment will become clear after the September inflation data are released. Until then, the 3.5% figure remains a forecast, and the effect on each recipient's finances will depend on their benefit amount and any changes in healthcare costs.

sources.news_title: Social Security 2027 COLA: Trump Tax Cuts vs. Biden Benefits - FINCHANNEL
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — Social Security’s 2027 COLA is approaching its final calculation as retirees face two separate financial developments: a projected increase in monthly benefits and a tax break enacted by President Donald Trump that federal trustees say reduces revenue supporting the retirement program.
The Senior Citizens League, a nonpartisan advocacy organization, projects a 3.5 percent cost-of-living adjustment. The official percentage remains undetermined ahead of the September inflation report, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics is scheduled to release on October 14 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern time. The Senior Citizens League
Trump’s principal enacted tax change for older Americans provides an additional deduction for eligible taxpayers age 65 and older. Former President Joe Biden’s most consequential recent Social Security legislation increased benefits for people whose public pensions had reduced their Social Security payments.
Both measures provide financial relief to affected households. Their financing costs enter the program through different channels: Trump’s legislation reduces tax receipts, while the law Biden signed increases benefit spending.
Social Security 2027 COLA follows an existing formula
The annual adjustment is calculated under a longstanding statutory system. The president does not select the percentage.
Social Security compares the average Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W, for July, August and September with the corresponding average from the previous year. The resulting increase determines the COLA, subject to the program’s calculation rules.
Automatic inflation adjustments began in 1975. Before then, Congress enacted general benefit increases through legislation. ssa.gov
If the projected 3.5 percent adjustment is confirmed, a beneficiary receiving exactly $2,000 a month would receive a $70 gross monthly increase. That is an illustrative calculation, rather than an estimate of the average beneficiary’s payment.
Actual dollar increases vary with existing benefits. The amount deposited into a bank account also depends on deductions, including Medicare premiums and any federal income-tax withholding.
Calling the adjustment a presidential bonus assigns political ownership to an automatic calculation. Economic policies can influence prices, but the COLA formula itself has continued across Republican and Democratic administrations.
The Biden-era increases were larger
The same mechanism produced substantial increases during Biden’s presidency, when inflation accelerated.
Adjustments first reflected in January payments were 5.9 percent in 2022, 8.7 percent in 2023 and 3.2 percent in 2024. The adjustment for January 2025 was 2.5 percent, determined before Trump returned to office. Benefits rose 2.8 percent in January 2026. These payment-year figures follow Social Security’s historical COLA series, which lists adjustments by their December effective dates. ssa.gov
A confirmed 3.5 percent increase for 2027 would exceed the adjustments paid in 2024, 2025 and 2026, while remaining below those paid in 2022 and 2023.
The Senior Citizens League advocates changing the inflation measure used for benefits, arguing that the spending patterns of working households differ from those of older Americans. Its COLA policy position calls for a calculation that better reflects seniors’ expenses. The Senior Citizens League
Trump’s tax relief has eligibility limits
Trump campaigned on eliminating taxes on Social Security benefits. The legislation he signed on July 4, 2025, instead provides an additional deduction alongside broader income-tax changes.
Under IRS eligibility rules, qualifying taxpayers age 65 and older may claim an additional $6,000 deduction for tax years 2025 through 2028. A married couple can claim $12,000 if both spouses qualify.
The deduction begins phasing out when modified adjusted gross income exceeds $75,000 for an individual or $150,000 for joint filers. Internal Revenue Service
A deduction reduces taxable income; its dollar value depends on the taxpayer’s circumstances. It does not add $6,000 to an annual Social Security benefit, and beneficiaries younger than 65 do not qualify solely because they receive retirement, disability or survivor payments.
The existing rules governing taxable Social Security benefits remain in place. Depending on income and filing status, up to 85 percent of benefits can be included in taxable income. That percentage describes the taxable portion of benefits, rather than an income-tax rate. Internal Revenue Service
The White House defended the legislation as fulfilling Trump’s pledge, citing a Council of Economic Advisers estimate that 88 percent of seniors receiving Social Security would pay no tax on their benefits. That is an administration estimate about tax outcomes under the measure.
Biden expanded benefits for public-pension recipients
Biden signed the bipartisan Social Security Fairness Act on January 5, 2025.
The law repealed the Windfall Elimination Provision and Government Pension Offset. Those provisions reduced certain retirement, disability, spousal or survivor benefits for people receiving pensions from employment outside Social Security coverage.
Affected groups included some teachers, firefighters, police officers and other public employees. Eligibility depends on an individual’s employment and benefit history.
The Trump administration implemented the law. Social Security reported that, by July 7, 2025, it had completed sending more than 3.1 million payments totaling $17 billion to eligible beneficiaries. The repeal applied to benefits payable after December 2023. SSA
The expansion also increased projected costs. In its analysis of the legislation, the Congressional Budget Office said repealing the provisions would permanently increase scheduled benefit spending and widen the existing gap between expenditures and revenues. Congressional Budget Office
Biden’s fiscal 2025 budget proposed strengthening Social Security by requiring greater contributions from the highest-income Americans, opposing benefit cuts and privatization, and improving benefits for financially vulnerable recipients. Those were budget policy principles, rather than an enacted comprehensive financing overhaul. bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov
The economic cost extends beyond next year’s increase
The 2026 trustees report identifies reduced fertility assumptions, lower immigration assumptions and Trump’s tax legislation as principal reasons the program’s long-term financial outlook deteriorated.
The trustees say the tax law’s lower rates and larger deductions reduce income taxes collected on Social Security benefits. Some of that revenue supports the retirement and disability trust funds.
Their report highlights also show that Social Security’s total costs exceeded total income by $160 billion in 2025, with reserves covering the difference.
Inflation affects both sides of the accounts. COLAs increase benefit obligations, while wages and employment affect payroll-tax receipts. The effect on financing therefore depends on earnings, employment, demographics and tax policy alongside inflation.
The trustees calculate a 75-year unfunded obligation of $29.3 trillion. This is a present-value estimate of the projected financing gap over the period, after accounting for starting reserves, rather than an amount immediately due. ssa.gov
Under their intermediate assumptions, the retirement and survivor trust fund would exhaust its reserves in the fourth quarter of 2032. Continuing income would then cover 78 percent of scheduled benefits.
A hypothetical combination with the disability fund would extend reserve availability to the third quarter of 2034, with 83 percent payable afterward. Combining the funds would require legislation, according to the trustees’ summary. ssa.gov
What is the Social Security COLA for 2027?
The Senior Citizens League projects 3.5 percent. As of October 12, the official adjustment remains undetermined pending September CPI-W data.
Did Trump authorize the projected increase?
The percentage follows an existing inflation formula. Trump’s senior tax deduction is a separate policy.
Has federal taxation of Social Security ended?
The statutory benefit-taxation rules remain. Eligible taxpayers age 65 and older can use the additional deduction to reduce taxable income.
How did Biden’s policy differ?
Biden signed legislation removing two provisions that reduced benefits for certain public-pension recipients. Trump implemented that expansion and signed separate tax relief.
Will Social Security stop paying benefits in 2032?
The trustees project that retirement-fund reserves will be depleted then under their intermediate assumptions. Payroll taxes and other continuing receipts would still finance benefits, but projected income would cover 78 percent of scheduled retirement and survivor payments without a change in law.
Can a larger COLA produce a smaller increase in the bank deposit?
Yes. Medicare premiums and other deductions affect the net payment. The FINANCIAL has separately reported on Medicare-related payments administered through Social Security. The official 2027 COLA calculation awaits the September inflation release on October 14.

sources.news_title: Major Social Security announcement expected this week. What it could mean for recipients
sources.text:
Editor's Note: The video in this story is from a previous report.
A major social security announcement is expected this week and it will have big implications on what recipients can expect for 2027.
Stream NBC 5 for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
The Social Security Administration is expected to announce its cost-of-living, or COLA, increases for 2027 on Wednesday. The announcement will decide how Social Security payments are adjusted each year to account for cost of living changes and inflation.
Here's what to know.
When is the Social Security COLA announcement?
The official announcement is slated for Oct. 14, the agency said.
Notices last year became available online to most beneficiaries in the Message Center of their my Social Security account.
Local
"The purpose of the COLA is to ensure that the purchasing power of Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits is not eroded by inflation," the administration's website states.
How is the COLA calculated?
According to the agency, the COLA update "is based on the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) from the third quarter of the last year a COLA was determined to the third quarter of the current year."
The CPI-W "is determined by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the Department of Labor."
How much of an increase is expected for 2027? Latest predictions and how much they could mean for checks
Oftentimes, predictions will be made about where the COLA will be come December.
The Senior Citizens League announced last month that it predicted the adjustment will sit at 3.5%, which if it took effect now would equate to $67.90 more in payments.
"The current average beneficiary receives $1,940.08 in their monthly Social Security check. With a 3.5 percent COLA, that would rise to $ 2,007.98," TSCL reported.
Meanwhile, Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare analyst, told USA Today in August her predictions sat at 3.4%.
Those numbers are both down from predictions earlier this summer, which peaked at 3.8%.
“The biggest thing we’re watching with the COLA announcement coming are short-term shocks to the economy that push inflation way up or down in the next 30 days. Of the three CPI-W figures used to calculate the COLA, two are already in," TSCL Executive Director Shannon Benton said in a release.
What about inflation?
The U.S. reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting in the Middle East. More of the same is expected for September with all sides in the Iranian conflict unwilling to concede ground.
The Labor Department is expected to report Wednesday that its consumer price index rose by two-tenths of a percent month over month and rose 3.6% compared with a year ago at this time.
A day later, the department will release its producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers. Same story there.
Economists expect an increase from the 5.4% registered in August, which was up from 4.8% in July. Last week, PepsiCo said it was raising prices on Doritos and other favorites, citing rising costs for fuel, aluminum and commodities.

sources.news_title: Social Security COLA announcement could come as soon as Wednesday
sources.text:
Social Security COLA announcement could come as soon as Wednesday
Social Security recipients across the United States should soon know how much of an increase they will see in their monthly checks next year.
Big picture view:
On Wednesday, October 14, the Bureau of Labor Statistics will publish its September 2026 Consumer Price Index (CPI). That report contains the last bit of data needed by the Social Security Administration (SSA) to determine its 2027 Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA).
When is the Social Security COLA announced?
Any COLA change could be announced as soon as Wednesday. The SSA has only stated that the COLA for 2027 would be announced in October of this year. However, once the BLS data is released, the agency will have all of the information it needs. In 2025, both the CPI data and the adjustment announcement came on the same day.
How much will the increase be?
There is no official indication of how much more recipients will get. The annual adjustment for a coming year is based on the year-to-year Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) for July, August, and September of the current year. The CPI-W for July was 3.4%, while August’s increase was 3.5%, according to BLS numbers.
RELATED: Pumpkin spice season is back, but it can cost extra; See how much
By the numbers:
Following the release of the August CPI-W, the Senior Citizens League predicted that the COLA would be 3.5% next year. According to its numbers, the average recipient is currently getting $1,940.08 per month, and a 3.5% increase would push that number to $2,007.98.
The backstory:
If the COLA were 3.5% in 2027, that would be a sharp rise from the 2.8% adjustment made last year. After making the announcement last year, the SSA stated that people who have a personal Social Security account would be able to see their individual adjustment notices for that year immediately on its website, and notices would be sent by mail in December.

sources.news_title: Social Security COLA 2027: Why a $73 monthly boost could spell trouble ahead of October 14 announcement
sources.text:
Social Security COLA 2027: Why a $73 monthly boost could spell trouble ahead of October 14 announcement
Social Security COLA 2027 could reach 3.5%, adding $73 monthly for retirees. Here's why the October 14 announcement could raise funding concerns.
The US Social Security Administration is expected to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) after the September inflation report is released on October 14. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics will publish the report at 8:30 am ET, providing the final inflation data needed to calculate the increase.
More than 71 million traditional Social Security beneficiaries could receive one of the biggest annual benefit increases in the last 35 years in 2027. However, while larger monthly payments could help beneficiaries manage higher expenses, they could also put more pressure on the programme's already strained finances, according to The Motley Fool.
The Senior Citizens League (TSCL), a nonpartisan advocacy group for older Americans, and Mary Johnson, a Social Security and Medicare policy analyst, are both projecting a 3.5% COLA for 2027, according to The Motley Fool. This is an estimate, not the final announced increase.
If the 3.5% estimate is correct, the average retired worker could receive an additional $73 per month in Social Security benefits. That would mean about $876 more over a full year, based on the estimated monthly increase.
A 3.5% increase would tie for the sixth-largest Social Security COLA since 1993. It would also mark the sixth consecutive year with a benefit increase of at least 2.5%, a streak that has not occurred in 30 years.
Also read: Why did I get $90 from Social Security? Trump Medicare payment explained
Why Social Security benefits could rise in 2027
Trump's tariffs have pushed up the cost of consumer goods. His trade policies began affecting prices in mid-2025. The tariffs introduced on “Liberation Day” also contributed to higher consumer prices and helped support the 2.8% Social Security COLA provided in 2026.
The US Supreme Court struck down the “Liberation Day” tariffs in February 2026. However, the effects of earlier tariffs on consumer prices may continue, while the Trump administration introduced broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from more than 80 countries in late July, The Motley Fool reported.
The Iran war has also added to inflation pressures. After Trump approved attacks against Iran on February 28, Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz to most commercial vessels, disrupting the movement of a major share of the world's crude oil.
Why a bigger Social Security COLA could create problems
While a higher COLA can help older Americans manage rising living costs, it can also increase the amount Social Security pays out in benefits. The Motley Fool warned that unusually large annual increases could worsen the programme's long-term financial challenges.
The Social Security Board of Trustees has warned about the programme's long-term funding shortfall every year since 1985. The programme's projected long-term unfunded obligation reached $29.3 trillion in 2026, according to The Motley Fool. This figure represents the projected gap between future income and expenses over the 75-year period covered by the Trustees' calculations.
Social Security has accumulated reserves from income collected in earlier years. By law, these reserves are invested in special-issue, interest-bearing US government bonds. However, the OASI trust fund's reserves are projected to run out by the fourth quarter of 2032.
Also read: Social Security COLA 2027: Why Medicare deductions could reduce retirees' monthly benefit increase
Social Security is not expected to simply go bankrupt or stop making all payments when its reserves run out. More than 91% of the programme's income comes from the 12.4% payroll tax on earned income. As long as people continue working and paying payroll taxes, the programme will continue receiving money to pay eligible beneficiaries.
The bigger risk is a possible reduction in benefits. If the OASI trust fund's reserves are exhausted, incoming revenue is projected to be insufficient to pay all scheduled benefits. The resulting shortfall could require benefit cuts estimated at 22%.
How the 2027 COLA could worsen the funding gap
The Social Security Board of Trustees considers several factors when estimating the programme's future finances. These include birth rates, net migration, death rates and the annual cost-of-living adjustments given to beneficiaries.
If the projected 3.5% COLA becomes official, the increase could add to Social Security's expenses more than the Trustees' relatively modest assumptions anticipate. The Motley Fool warned that this could cause the OASI trust fund's reserves to run out sooner than currently projected.
Inflation could also remain a problem beyond 2026. The effects of tariffs and the Iran war could continue into 2027, keeping pressure on consumer prices. If inflation remains elevated, it could also lead to another relatively large COLA in 2028. This would potentially increase Social Security's benefit expenses further, adding to the programme's long-term funding challenges.
The central concern is that larger Social Security checks may offer short-term relief while increasing pressure on the programme's long-term finances. If inflation remains high and annual benefit increases stay elevated, the need for future benefit cuts could arrive sooner or the cuts could be larger than currently projected, The Motley Fool warned.
What to watch before the October 14 announcement
The September inflation report, scheduled for October 14 at 8:30 a.m. ET, is the final data point needed to calculate the 2027 Social Security COLA. The report will help determine the official adjustment rather than leave beneficiaries relying on estimates.
Beneficiaries should remember that the projected 3.5% increase and the additional $73 per month are estimates. The final adjustment could differ depending on the inflation figures used in the calculation.
The announcement will provide a clearer picture of how much monthly benefits are expected to rise in 2027. However, the longer-term issue will remain: whether Social Security can continue paying scheduled benefits without major changes to its finances.

Social Security's 3.5% COLA Bump in 2027 Would Be Largest in 4 Years -- But Soaring Medical Costs Could Wipe Out Every Penny
sources.text:
Social Security’s 3.5% COLA Bump in 2027 Would Be Largest in 4 Years — But Soaring Medical Costs Could Wipe Out Every Penny
Social Security's biggest raise in four years sounds like good news until you see what Medicare does to it before the money ever hits your bank account.
On October 14, the Social Security Administration will announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for about 70 million beneficiaries. The Senior Citizens League projects a 3.5% raise, up from 2.8% for 2026. On a $2,000 monthly check, that works out to about $70 more per month before Medicare takes its cut.
That last part is where the real story is, since the Medicare deduction comes out of the same check and the 2027 Part B premium has not been set. AARP reported this week that the Part B premium is expected to rise in 2027.
Two Months of Data Point to a Bigger Raise
The COLA formula relies on a specific comparison. It measures the average Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) for July, August and September against the same quarter a year earlier. With two of the three months reported, the measure is tracking toward 3.3%. The August reading of 328.5 rose 0.4% in a single month. September data will decide whether the final figure comes in near 3.3% or the League’s 3.5%. Either one beats this year’s 2.8%.
Medicare Premiums Eat the Raise First
Last year shows how it plays out. The standard Part B premium rose from $185.00 in 2025 to $202.90 in 2026, an increase of $17.90 a month, or about 9.7%. The Part B deductible climbed to $283, and the Part A hospital deductible rose to $1,736. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) blamed the premium jump mainly on “projected price changes and assumed utilization increases”. The agency said the premium would have been about $11 a month higher without new limits on spending for skin substitutes.
If the 2027 premium rises by the same amount, it would take about 26% of the projected $70 raise. That happens before a retiree fills a single prescription or pays a copay.
Households See Medical Inflation the Index Misses
On paper, medical inflation is soft. The medical care part of the broader Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose just 1.6% in the year through August. Households see it very differently. The latest New York Fed Survey of Consumer Expectations shows Americans expect medical care prices to rise 9.2% over the next year. That is the highest of any category in the survey and far above the 3.9% they expect for overall inflation. Rent expectations are at 6.8%.
The survey shows how all adults feel, so it is neither an official forecast nor a retiree-specific measure. Still, the gap explains the frustration. Retirees pay for care through premiums, deductibles and out-of-pocket costs that reset every January, and those bills can rise much faster than the medical price index suggests. CPI-W is based on the spending of working households. They put a smaller share of their budgets toward health care than retirees do. That is a long-running flaw in the way Social Security adjusts for inflation.
Two Numbers to Watch Before January
The first number comes with the September CPI-W data and the October 14 announcement. The second is the 2027 Part B premium, which CMS usually releases in November. The 2026 figures came out on November 14, 2025. If the next increase comes close to last year’s $17.90, a 3.5% COLA will look much smaller in the January deposit.
For investors approaching retirement, the lesson goes beyond Social Security. Portfolio income has to keep pace with real costs. Whether from dividends or bond coupons, it must keep up with the expenses its owner actually faces, including medical bills and Medicare premiums. Matching headline CPI is not enough. A retirement plan built on the official index will underestimate the expenses that matter most heavily after 65.

sources.news_title: Social Security 2027 Updates Include 3.6% COLA and Higher Earnings Limits » ¡Que Onda Magazine!
sources.text:
The latest Social Security 2027 updates include a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for retirement, disability and Supplemental Security Income benefits. The increase will affect approximately 76 million Americans.
Social Security beneficiaries will receive the adjustment with payments issued in January 2027. Higher SSI payments will begin Dec. 31, 2026, because Jan. 1 is a federal holiday.
Social Security 2027 COLA Raises Average Benefits
The Social Security Administration calculates the annual adjustment using inflation data. It compares the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers during the third quarter of each year.
The 3.6% increase is higher than the 2.8% adjustment provided for 2026.
An average retired worker’s monthly benefit will increase from approximately $2,095 to $2,170. That represents an average increase of $75 per month.
An older couple receiving benefits will see its average combined payment rise from $3,238 to $3,355. The average benefit for a disabled worker will increase from $1,642 to $1,701.
Actual increases will vary because Social Security applies the adjustment to each person’s benefit amount. The figures announced by the agency are national averages.
SSI Payments Increase in 2027
The maximum federal SSI payment will increase to $1,029 per month for an eligible individual. The maximum for an eligible couple will rise to $1,544.
However, the SSI resource limits will not change. The limit remains $2,000 for an individual and $3,000 for a couple.
SSI payments can also vary based on income, living arrangements and state supplements.
Earnings Limits Rise for Working Beneficiaries
People receiving retirement benefits before reaching full retirement age can continue working. However, Social Security may temporarily withhold benefits when earnings exceed certain limits.
The annual earnings limit for workers below full retirement age will increase to $25,560 in 2027. That equals $2,130 per month.
Social Security will withhold $1 in benefits for every $2 earned above that limit.
For workers reaching full retirement age during 2027, the limit will increase to $67,920. The agency will withhold $1 for every $3 earned above the limit before the worker reaches full retirement age.
The earnings test ends during the month a beneficiary reaches full retirement age. There is no earnings limit after that point.
Withheld benefits are not permanently lost. Social Security recalculates the monthly benefit after the person reaches full retirement age.
Social Security Taxable Wage Cap Increases
The maximum amount of earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes will increase from $184,500 to $192,300.
Employees will continue paying a 6.2% Social Security tax on covered earnings up to that limit. Employers pay the same percentage.
The Medicare tax rate remains 1.45% for employees and employers, with no earnings cap. Self-employed workers generally pay the combined employee and employer portions.
The amount needed to earn one Social Security work credit will increase from $1,890 to $1,970. Workers can earn up to four credits annually.
Disability Thresholds Also Change
The substantial gainful activity threshold for nonblind disabled workers will increase to $1,770 per month. The threshold for blind workers will rise to $2,950.
The trial work period threshold will increase to $1,270 per month. These figures can affect disability eligibility and work incentive rules.
The maximum benefit for a worker retiring at full retirement age will increase from $4,152 to $4,188 per month. That maximum applies only to workers with sufficient earnings at or above the taxable limit.
Medicare Premium Could Affect Net Payments
Medicare had not announced its 2027 premium changes when Social Security released the COLA. Many beneficiaries have their Medicare Part B premium deducted directly from their Social Security payment.
As a result, the increase in a beneficiary’s net deposit may be smaller than 3.6%. The final amount will depend partly on the 2027 Medicare premium.
Personalized COLA notices will become available through my Social Security accounts in late November. Beneficiaries who have not selected paperless notices will receive a mailed notice in December.
The Social Security Administration’s 2027 fact sheet provides the complete list of updated amounts. Beneficiaries should rely on official notices and avoid anyone requesting payment for COLA information or benefit assistance.

sources.news_title: Social Security Benefits Are Going Up in 2027 — But Is It Enough?
sources.text:
Monthly checks for the nearly 76 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits will rise by 3.6 percent in 2027. The increase, announced on Oct. 14, 2026, is the largest since the one that took effect in 2023.
This cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is how the government tries to make sure that the value of Social Security benefits keeps up with inflation. Without it, the same payment would cover less of what recipients are spending on medical care, housing, groceries, clothing, and other necessities.
I am a finance professor, and one of the topics I research is how inflation affects retirees’ investment choices. And I believe the upcoming bump doesn’t capture the inflation challenges that many people who receive Social Security benefits face.
The percentage increase in Social Security benefits depends in part on the annual inflation rate as of September 2026. It stood at 3.7 percent that month, as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a government agency, also announced on Oct. 14.
But the size of the increase is only part of the issue. The index used to set the COLA reflects what working people buy, not retirees, and that is a mismatch at the heart of a long-running debate over how the adjustment should be measured.
Calculating the COLA
The government has annually increased Social Security benefits to keep up with inflation since 1975. Congress previously had to pass a law each time it increased benefits. As a result, years could pass without an adjustment, despite climbing prices.
The metric that the government uses is its consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers, known as the CPI-W. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks changes in the prices of goods and services that working households typically buy to calculate this index.
The Social Security Administration then compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August, and September with the average for those same months in the prior year to set the COLA adjustment, which kicks in the following January.
If the economy contracts and prices fall, however, benefits stay the same. That happened in 2009, 2010, and 2015.
Spending much of the bump on premiums
One big problem with this calculation is that it understates healthcare inflation.
Out-of-pocket health costs, including Medicare premiums, deductibles and copayments for medical care, and prescription drugs, typically consume nearly 30 percent of Social Security benefits, according to research from the nonpartisan Center for Retirement Research at Boston College.
For example, the government deducts Medicare Part B premiums directly from many retirees’ Social Security checks. The standard monthly Part B premium rose by $17.90 in 2026, from $185 to $202.90. That increase alone consumed roughly one-third of the average $56 monthly gain in benefits from the 2026 COLA.
More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as most Americans getting Social Security benefits are, helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation.
Finding other options
Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the Senior Citizens League and the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare, say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees. Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education, and transportation than people with jobs.
There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the consumer price index for Americans 62 and older, known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite some efforts in Congress to make the switch.
The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care. People 65 and older spend more than twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates.
Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014. It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing, and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W.
But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment. The CPI-E has increased less than CPI-W in some years. What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose.
Pankaj Agrrawal is a professor of finance at the University of Maine.

Social Leadership And Big Security Benefits To Rise By 3.6 Pc In US Next Year
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Social Security benefits in the United States will rise by 3.6 percent in 2027, giving retired workers an average increase of about $75 a month, the Social Security Administration announced.
The cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will affect nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries, including retirees, disabled workers and their families. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments will also increase for about 7.3 million recipients. Because some people receive both benefits, the combined number of beneficiaries is about 76 million.
The higher Social Security payments will begin in January 2027, while increased SSI payments will start on December 31, 2026.
The average monthly retirement benefit for a retired worker is projected to rise from $2,095 to $2,170. For an older couple in which both partners receive benefits, the average payment will increase from $3,238 to $3,355.
The average monthly benefit for a disabled worker is expected to rise from $1,642 to $1,701. For SSI recipients, the maximum federal monthly payment for an individual will increase from $994 to $1,029, while the amount for an eligible couple will rise from $1,491 to $1,544.
Beneficiaries will receive notices explaining their new payment amounts online in late November and by mail in December. Actual payments may vary depending on individual circumstances, and Medicare premium deductions may affect the amount deposited.
The 2027 adjustment follows a 2.8 percent increase in 2026. COLA is calculated using changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), based on inflation data compiled by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The adjustment is made automatically under federal law.
The administration also announced changes to earnings limits for 2027. The maximum amount of earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes will rise from $184,500 to $192,300. For beneficiaries below full retirement age, the annual earnings limit will increase from $24,480 to $25,560.
The changes will also affect eligible Indian American retirees and other beneficiaries in the United States. Benefit amounts and eligibility depend on individual work records and applicable program rules. (IANS)

sources.text:
Social Security Benefits to Rise 3.6% in 2027, Largest Increase Since 2023
Average retirement payments are expected to increase by about $75 a month, while Medicare premiums and the taxable earnings cap are also projected to rise.
BALTIMORE — The Social Security Administration announced Wednesday that benefits will increase 3.6 percent in 2027, the largest cost-of-living adjustment since 2023.
The adjustment will raise average monthly retirement benefits by about $75, from roughly $2,095 to $2,170, the agency said. Nearly 72 million Social Security recipients will see higher payments beginning in January 2027. About 7.3 million Supplemental Security Income recipients will receive increased payments starting Dec. 31, 2026.
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said.
The COLA is based on the increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers for the third quarter of 2026. The higher figure reflects elevated inflation this year, driven in part by rising energy prices following the Iran-related conflict and disruptions to oil supplies.
Previous adjustments were 2.8 percent in 2026, 2.5 percent in 2025, and 3.2 percent in 2024. The 2023 COLA was 8.7 percent amid the post-pandemic inflation spike.
AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said the increase is important because many older Americans face rising costs for groceries, healthcare, and everyday expenses. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget noted that the adjustment will boost average benefits by about $900 per retiree annually, with larger increases for higher-benefit recipients.
Medicare Part B premiums, which are deducted from many Social Security checks, are projected to rise $6.60 to $209.50 in 2027, according to the Medicare trustees' report. The final premium amount has not yet been announced.
The Social Security taxable earnings base will also rise from $184,500 to $192,300 in 2027. The agency said beneficiaries can view their new benefit amounts in their online accounts beginning in late November.

sources.text:
Washington, Oct 15 (SocialNews.XYZ) The United States has announced a 3.6 per cent increase in Social Security benefits for 2027, providing an average additional $75 a month to retired workers as millions of Americans struggle with rising living costs.
The Social Security Administration (SSA) said on Wednesday (local time) that nearly 72 million beneficiaries will receive higher payments beginning in January, while approximately 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income (SSI) will see their increases reflected in payments beginning December 31.
The annual cost-of-living adjustment, commonly known as COLA, is designed to help protect the purchasing power of retirees, people with disabilities and other eligible beneficiaries against inflation.
The adjustment will affect approximately 76 million Americans across the two programmes, with some individuals receiving benefits under both.
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said.
"Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people," he added.
According to official figures, the estimated average monthly retirement benefit will rise from $2,095 to $2,170 in January 2027.
For retired couples where both spouses receive benefits, the average combined monthly payment is expected to increase from $3,238 to $3,355.
The average monthly benefit for workers receiving Social Security Disability Insurance will increase from $1,642 to $1,701.
The adjustment also raises federal SSI payment standards, with the maximum monthly payment for an eligible individual increasing from $994 to $1,029.
For an eligible couple, the corresponding amount will rise from $1,491 to $1,544.
The administration said beneficiaries with personal online Social Security accounts will be able to view their updated benefit notices beginning in late November.
Those who have not enrolled in paperless notifications will receive their notices by mail during December.
The personalised notices will explain the revised monthly payment, the date it takes effect and any applicable deductions.
Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare will also receive information about changes to their premiums, which can affect the amount deposited into their accounts each month.
The administration said information about Medicare changes for 2027 would be available through the official Medicare website.
The 3.6 per cent adjustment is higher than the 2.8 per cent increase implemented for 2026, reflecting changes in consumer prices over the relevant measurement period.
The annual adjustment is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, compiled by the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics.
The increase is automatic under federal law and does not require separate congressional approval.
The Social Security Administration also announced changes to several earnings-related thresholds for 2027.
The maximum annual earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes will increase from $184,500 to $192,300.
For beneficiaries below full retirement age who continue working, the annual earnings limit before benefit withholding begins will rise from $24,480 to $25,560.
The increase will also be relevant to eligible Indian-American retirees and other beneficiaries of Indian origin who receive US Social Security payments. Eligibility and payment amounts depend on individual contribution records and programme rules, rather than nationality alone.

sources.news_title: SOCIAL SECURITY CHECKS GOING UP: 3.6% Increase Announced for 2027, but Millions of Seniors Say Rising Costs Will Swallow the Extra Money
sources.text:
Millions of Americans receiving Social Security benefits will see their monthly payments increase by 3.6% beginning in January 2027, federal officials announced Wednesday, providing an average increase of approximately $75 a month as retirees and disabled Americans continue struggling with rising prices for food, healthcare, housing and other necessities.
The Social Security Administration said the annual cost-of-living adjustment, commonly known as COLA, will affect approximately 72 million Social Security recipients and nearly 7.3 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income, although some individuals qualify for both programs.
The increase is intended to help beneficiaries maintain their purchasing power as inflation continues to affect household budgets. However, many older Americans say the additional money will provide little meaningful relief, particularly as Medicare expenses, prescription drug costs and property taxes continue climbing.
The announcement comes just weeks before the November midterm elections, with inflation and the cost of living remaining major concerns for voters across the country.
Under the new adjustment, a beneficiary receiving approximately $2,083 a month would see that payment rise by about $75, bringing the monthly benefit to roughly $2,158. Actual increases will vary depending on each recipient’s existing benefit amount.
Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano welcomed the adjustment, saying it would provide beneficiaries with “greater financial stability.”
The annual increase is calculated using a federal inflation measure designed to reflect changes in consumer prices. The formula automatically adjusts benefits to account for inflation, although critics argue that it does not adequately reflect the spending patterns of retirees, who often devote a larger portion of their income to healthcare and housing.
The adjustment comes amid renewed inflationary pressures, including higher energy costs. Government figures released last month showed that inflation accelerated in August as gasoline prices rose following renewed military conflict involving the United States and Iran.
The Social Security Administration also announced that the maximum amount of annual earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes will increase from $184,500 in 2026 to $192,300 in 2027.
The payroll tax, which is paid by workers and their employers, provides the primary funding for Social Security retirement and disability benefits. Earnings above the annual taxable maximum are not subject to the Social Security portion of the payroll tax.
For some retirees, however, the increase in benefits is expected to be largely consumed by higher medical expenses.
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree living near Rochester, Minnesota, said the additional Social Security income would do little to offset the healthcare costs she and her husband anticipate facing next year.
Ufkin expressed concern about the scheduled expiration of a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program at the end of 2026, which she expects will result in higher prescription drug and insurance expenses.
Although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected relatively modest premium increases for most beneficiaries, Ufkin said her family’s individual circumstances could produce much larger expenses.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
According to Ufkin, a medication taken by both her and her husband is expected to increase in price from $11 per monthly prescription to $200 per prescription.
She described the anticipated increase as “catastrophic.”
Advocates for older Americans say such concerns illustrate why even a relatively substantial annual adjustment may fail to improve the financial circumstances of retirees living on fixed incomes.
AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan warned that many seniors are entering 2027 with limited savings and growing anxiety about their ability to meet everyday expenses.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” she said.
Another retiree, 68-year-old Jaime Jakubczak of Buffalo, New York, said he had been forced to return to work after retiring at age 55 because his expenses had become increasingly difficult to manage.
Jakubczak pointed particularly to property taxes, which he said have become a significant burden. His community is considering an additional 3.9% property tax increase, further reducing the benefit of the Social Security adjustment.
He described the 3.6% increase as “a pittance,” arguing that the higher payments would be quickly absorbed by rising prices for groceries, gasoline, healthcare and local taxes.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
A September survey conducted by AARP found widespread skepticism among older Americans about whether the annual Social Security increase would adequately compensate for inflation.
Approximately three-quarters of respondents age 50 and older disagreed with the suggestion that a 3.5% adjustment for 2027 would be enough to keep pace with rising consumer prices.
Beyond the immediate debate over the size of the increase, Social Security faces a much larger financial challenge that Congress has yet to resolve.
According to the program’s June 2026 trustees’ report, Social Security’s combined retirement and disability trust fund reserves are projected to run out in 2034 if lawmakers fail to enact changes.
At that point, continuing payroll tax revenue and other income would be sufficient to pay approximately 83% of scheduled benefits, potentially leaving millions of retirees facing significant reductions in their expected payments.
The outlook is even more pressing for the trust fund specifically responsible for retirement and survivor benefits. That fund is projected to exhaust its reserves in 2032, when incoming revenue would cover approximately 78% of scheduled payments.
Lawmakers from both parties have proposed various measures to strengthen Social Security’s finances, although no comprehensive solution has been enacted.
Among the proposals is legislation supported by Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio that would increase the amount of earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes.
The senators argued in a June opinion article that eliminating the existing taxable earnings ceiling and treating higher incomes similarly to other wages “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation.”
The proposal would represent a major change to the current financing system, under which earnings above the annual payroll tax cap are exempt from Social Security taxes.
The Peterson Foundation has estimated that eliminating the ceiling could generate approximately $3 trillion in additional revenue over a decade.
Such proposals remain politically contentious, particularly among Republicans who have traditionally opposed tax increases on higher-income Americans.
Recent administrations have also approved measures intended to provide additional financial relief to retirees, although some of those changes have added to the program’s long-term financial obligations.
Under legislation enacted during Trump’s presidency, Americans age 65 and older became eligible for a temporary additional federal income tax deduction, subject to income limitations.
The deduction applies to eligible taxpayers’ income generally, rather than exclusively to Social Security benefits. As a result, retirees whose incomes are already too low to generate federal income tax liability may receive little or no benefit from the provision.
Americans who begin collecting Social Security before age 65 are also ineligible for the age-based deduction, while higher-income retirees may be excluded because of the provision’s income restrictions.
Separately, legislation signed by President Joe Biden in January 2025 eliminated the Windfall Elimination Provision and Government Pension Offset, two longstanding federal rules that had reduced Social Security benefits for certain retirees receiving public-sector pensions.
That change increased payments for approximately 2.8 million Americans, including retired teachers, firefighters, police officers and other public employees whose benefits had previously been reduced.
For recipients preparing for the 2027 increase, the Social Security Administration says personalized notices detailing new benefit amounts will become available online beginning in late November, with mailed notices following in December.
Recipients who maintain a personal my Social Security account can review their adjusted benefits electronically. The agency has also encouraged beneficiaries to enroll in digital notifications by November 18 to receive their information earlier.
The higher payments will begin in January for Social Security beneficiaries, while individuals receiving Supplemental Security Income will receive their first increased payment on December 31, 2026.

sources.news_title: Social Security Benefits to Rise 3.6% in 2027, Adding About $75 a Month
sources.text:
The Social Security Administration announced the increase Wednesday, saying it will affect about 73 million people receiving Social Security benefits and nearly 7.5 million people receiving Supplemental Security Income. Some people receive both types of payments.
The adjustment, commonly known as COLA, is designed to help benefits keep pace with inflation. Social Security payments will reflect the increase beginning in January 2027, while higher SSI payments are scheduled to begin Dec. 31, 2026.
But some older adults and people with disabilities say the increase will do little to ease financial pressure as the cost of necessities continues to climb.
The announcement comes weeks before the November midterm elections, putting the finances of older Americans and the future of Social Security back into focus as voters weigh the economy and household costs.
Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano said the adjustment would provide recipients with “greater financial stability.”
Rising prices continue to strain older Americans
For retirees living on fixed incomes, the annual adjustment can help offset increases in everyday expenses. But the benefit increase does not guarantee that recipients will gain purchasing power, particularly when costs for housing, groceries, transportation and health care rise.
Inflation accelerated in August as gasoline prices climbed amid renewed fighting between the United States and Iran. The latest price increases have added pressure to household budgets, including those of retirees who have limited opportunities to increase their income.
The 2027 adjustment is larger than the 2.8% increase recipients received in 2026. Still, its effect will vary depending on each person’s monthly benefit and how quickly their expenses rise.
The increase is calculated using a measure of inflation known as the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W. The formula compares price changes during the third quarter of the current year with the same period a year earlier.
Because the formula tracks spending patterns among urban wage earners and clerical workers rather than retirees specifically, advocates have questioned whether it fully reflects the expenses older Americans face.
Social Security faces a long-term funding challenge
The benefit increase comes as Social Security faces a funding shortfall that Congress has yet to resolve.
The June 2026 trustees’ report projected that Social Security’s combined trust funds, which support retirement and disability benefits, would be unable to pay all scheduled benefits beginning in 2034 if lawmakers do not act.
After the funds are depleted, continuing tax revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits under the report’s projections. That would not mean Social Security would stop paying benefits altogether, but recipients could face across-the-board reductions if Congress does not change the program’s finances.
The outlook has renewed calls for lawmakers to address the system’s long-term funding needs without reducing benefits for current or future retirees.
In June, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, proposed lifting the cap on earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes. Under current rules, wages above an annual threshold are not subject to the Social Security portion of the payroll tax.
The taxable maximum is scheduled to rise to $192,300 in 2027, up from $184,500 in 2026.
Warren and Moreno argued in an opinion article in The New York Times that applying the payroll tax to more earnings could generate substantial revenue and extend the program’s solvency.
The proposal reflects a broader debate over whether Social Security’s funding gap should be addressed primarily through higher revenue, benefit changes or a combination of measures.
The Peter G. Peterson Foundation estimates that eliminating the payroll tax cap could bring roughly $3 trillion into the program over a decade. The proposal remains politically contentious, particularly among Republicans who have traditionally opposed tax increases on higher-income earners.
Recent policy changes affect benefits and taxes
Changes enacted under both the Trump and Biden administrations have altered how some older Americans receive benefits or pay taxes, while leaving the broader funding challenge unresolved.
President Donald Trump’s tax and spending legislation created a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and older. The deduction applies to qualifying income beyond Social Security benefits, but it does not benefit everyone equally. Older adults who do not owe federal income tax may receive little or no additional benefit from the deduction, while eligibility limits restrict its availability to some higher-income taxpayers.
Former President Joe Biden signed legislation in 2025 repealing the Windfall Elimination Provision and Government Pension Offset. Those provisions had reduced Social Security payments for certain people with pensions from work not covered by Social Security, including many former public employees and some spouses or surviving spouses.
The repeal increased benefits for roughly 2.8 million people, according to previous reporting by The Associated Press.
Although these changes have affected individual recipients, they have not eliminated the need for a broader agreement on Social Security’s long-term finances.
What recipients should know about the 2027 increase
The 3.6% adjustment will be applied to eligible Social Security benefits and SSI payments according to the program’s rules. The average $75 monthly increase is an estimate, not a guaranteed amount for every recipient.
Actual increases will depend on each person’s current benefit. Changes in Medicare premiums, taxes and other deductions can also affect how much money beneficiaries ultimately have available.
The increase will provide additional income to millions of retirees and people with disabilities, but its practical impact will depend on whether it keeps pace with their individual expenses.
Meanwhile, Congress faces continued pressure to address Social Security’s projected funding shortfall before the trust funds can no longer cover all scheduled payments. Without legislative action, the system’s incoming revenue would be insufficient to pay the full benefits currently promised after the projected depletion date.

In 2026, the cost of living adjustment was 2.8%; in 2025, the COLA was 2.5%; in 2024, the COLA was 3.2%; in 2023, the COLA was 8.7%.
In addition, workers will see a 7.65% tax rate in 2027 which is a combined rate of 6.2% for Social Security old age, survivors and disability insurance, OASDI, and a rate of 1.45% for Medicare hospital insurance, HI. For those who are self-employed, the tax rate will be 15.30% – rates match the rates seen in 2026.
Social Security taxes will apply to $192,300 for Social Security OASDI, a $7,800 increase from the limit of $184,500 in 2026.

sources.news_title: Social Security's 3.6% COLA may fall short for retirees. How advisors can help
sources.text:
- Key insight: Benefit increases mask a widening purchasing power gap for retirees, as cost-of-living adjustments often fail to keep pace with inflation.
- Supporting data: The 3.6% COLA set to start in January 2027 lags the 3.7% CPI-U inflation rate for the 12 months ending in September 2026.
- Expert quote: "This is a free reason to call your clients and demonstrate the value you're adding." — Sri Reddy, Principal Financial Group
Today the Social Security Administration announced the largest cost-of-living adjustment since 2023, but for retirees, the benefits bump is unlikely to keep up with inflation. For advisors, it's an opportunity to review retirement income plans, assess how rising costs affect budgets and discuss potential spending adjustments.
The 3.6% COLA will take effect in January 2027 for nearly 72 million beneficiaries and will translate to an average monthly benefit increase of $75. It is likely to lag inflation as measured by the consumer price index for all urban consumers (CPI-U), which rose by 3.7% for the 12 months ending in September. Both the COLA and CPI-U were announced Oct. 14. Last year's COLA bump was 2.8%. 
If inflation outpaces the COLA, beneficiaries lose purchasing power. In 2026, spikes in Medicare premiums eroded the Social Security COLA, and Medicare premiums are usually deducted directly from Social Security checks.
COLA announcements can create natural openings to talk with clients about how their retirement income is holding up against rising costs.
"This is a free reason to call your clients and demonstrate the value you're adding," said Sri Reddy, Principal Financial Group's senior vice president of retirement and income solutions.
Advisors should review what portion of clients' monthly income comes from Social Security and discuss whether their plans need to change based on the COLA news, he said.
"Do you want me to match a Social Security adjustment for COLA, or do you want to keep it level because you feel like you can save money elsewhere, or do you need more for some other reason?" Reddy added. "It's just a great conversation to have and also while reminding them how their account has done and overall performance of the relationship."
Those conversations can extend past income projections to practical cost-saving considerations, he said. Clients might consider buying ground turkey instead of beef, traveling during off-peak times or visiting Brussels instead of Paris, for example.
READ MORE: What Social Security uncertainty means even for wealthy clients
The SSA bases the annual COLA on a different calculation of CPI, the consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers (CPI-W), which rose by 3.9% over the previous 12 months — an even higher rate than the CPI-U.
Executive Director Shannon Benton of the nonprofit, nonpartisan Senior Citizens League said in a statement ahead of the announcement that seniors would likely be disappointed with the COLA over the long term.
"Older Americans allocate their budgets differently than people still in the workforce, so inflation hits them differently," she added. "The CPI-W captures the experience of urban wage earners, which doesn't represent the average senior's budget."
The annual cadence of the adjustments also creates challenges and "puts life on hold for a lot of seniors," Benton said. "When prices rise, they don't rise next January when your benefit check goes up. They rise right now."
READ MORE: Maximize tax-free Social Security income with this IRA withdrawal strategy
What the COLA means for clients' retirement budgets
Rather than focus on the headline percentage, advisors should help clients understand what the COLA means for their individual budgets, said Matthew Smart, chief investment officer of Chicago-based wealth management firm WWM Investments.
"Don't spend too much time, as a recipient of Social Security, on the headline number," Smart said. "You always have to go back to a financial plan and do our best to do the projections. An increase is good, but when you put these percentages in dollars, sometimes, it makes you feel a little bit different, right? Some people might say, 'Oh, man, an extra $73 a month. That's going to actually cover the physical therapy that I'm doing,' or something like that."
The impact depends on how clients spend their money. The COLA will likely fall short for those whose budgets are overloaded with expenses like healthcare.
"If your living expenses are more heavily comprised of the faster growing expense items — say healthcare, for example — then your COLA increase will not cover the entire increase in living expenses," Greg Welborn, principal at Pasadena, California-based financial planning and investment management firm First Financial Consulting, told Financial Planning in a statement.
In contrast, retirees whose expenses are more heavily weighted toward rent or fixed-rate mortgage payments and groceries may fare better.
"Take a nuanced view of your living expenses, and be prepared to make adjustments in key areas, not just across the board," he said.

sources.news_title: Social Security 3.6% COLA increase accelerates date when benefits will fall 25%
sources.text:
Nearly 72 million Social Security recipients will see a 3.6% increase in their monthly checks starting in January 2027, the Social Security Administration announced Wednesday, giving retirees their largest benefit boost since 2023 while accelerating long-term solvency pressures on the program’s trust funds.
The annual cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, will raise the average retiree benefit by roughly $75 per month, or about $900 a year, according to the agency.
The increase follows government inflation data released Wednesday for September. The COLA is calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), averaging price changes from July, August, and September of 2025 against the same period in 2026.
The 2027 adjustment is 0.8 percentage points higher than the 2.8% COLA enacted for 2026 and modestly above the 3.4% average over the past decade.
To help fund the system, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax will increase 4% in 2027, rising from $184,500 to $192,300.
Strain on Trust Funds
While the adjustment provides immediate relief for seniors facing elevated living costs, policy analysts warn it adds sudden fiscal weight to a system running cash deficits since 2021.
The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget noted the 3.6% figure comes in 0.9 percentage points higher than recent projections by Social Security Trustees. Because benefit outlays will outpace prior forecasts, the higher checks will speed up the drain on asset reserves.
Under current baselines before Wednesday’s announcement:
- Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) Trust Fund: Projected by the Board of Trustees and the Congressional Budget Office to be depleted by fiscal year 2032.
- Combined OASDI Trust Funds: Projected to run dry by 2034.
- Potential Cuts: If the trust funds hit insolvency, current law triggers an automatic, across-the-board benefit reduction of 22% to 28%.
The Social Security Administration’s chief actuary will publish an official evaluation of how the 3.6% COLA alters the depletion timeline in the next annual Trustees Report.
Social Security crisis looms
Progressive Democrat Lisa McCormick has been calling on Congress to protect the retirement security of millions of Americans for more than eight years, when she proposed “scrapping the cap” on taxable earnings, as part of her 2018 challenge to disgraced former US Senator Bob Menendez.
McCormick said the move would require very wealthy Americans to contribute to Social Security at the same tax rate as the rest of the population, but the incumbent had failed to work for it during his 25 years in Congress.
Almost a year ago, Republican former Senator Mitt Romney shifted his long-held opposition to raising or eliminating the Social Security taxable earnings cap, writing in a The New York Times Op-Ed that rising economic inequality and the program’s looming fiscal cliff changed his perspective.
“The way to fix this problem is by eliminating the cap on taxable income. This action alone would put Social Security on a solid financial foundation, ensuring that benefits remain secure, even if they are increased, or the retirement age is lowered,” said McCormick. “If we ‘scrap the cap,’ very wealthy Americans would contribute to Social Security at the same tax rate as the rest of us and the system would again be financially stable.”
“While 94 percent of U.S. workers shell out payroll taxes on every dollar in their paycheck, the very richest Americans avoid contributions to Social Security on most of their money due to the program’s cap on taxable earnings,” said McCormick.
High Inflation vs. Senior Budgets
For many older Americans, the adjustment may not fully cover the rising price of essential goods and healthcare.
The CPI-W tracks spending patterns for working-age employees rather than older adults. Healthcare spending accounts for 14% of total household spending for Medicare enrollees — more than double the burden of other households, according to health research non-profit KFF.
“For most people, the COLA just isn’t enough to keep up with what they see as rising costs in their life,” said Bill Sweeney, AARP’s senior vice president for government affairs. “When they go to the grocery store or fill up their tank with gas or get a notice that their rent is going up, it’s almost always higher than those numbers.”
A recent AARP survey found that only 23% of adults over age 50 believe a 3.5% COLA keeps pace with inflation.
Net gains will also depend on Medicare costs. The Medicare Board of Trustees projects monthly Part B premiums, which are typically deducted directly from Social Security checks, will rise from $6.60 to $209.50 in 2027.
Final Medicare premium figures will be released later this fall. This year, premiums went up about $528, or $44 per month.
Historical Perspective
Automatic COLAs were enacted under President Richard Nixon in 1972 and took effect in 1975 to ensure benefit levels kept pace with inflation.
| Period / Year | COLA Rate | Context | 
| 1980 | 14.3% | All-time high during severe stagflation | 
| 2010, 2011, 2016 | 0.0% | Zero increase due to flat inflation | 
| 2017 | 0.3% | Lowest non-zero increase on record | 
| 2023 | 8.7% | Post-pandemic inflation spike | 
| 10-Year Average | 3.4% | Baseline multi-year average | 
| 2027 (Announced) | 3.6% | Largest adjustment since 2023 |

sources.text:
By Leada Gore
al.com
(TNS)
Social Security benefits will rise by 3.6% in 2027, the biggest boost in four years, according to the Social Security Administration’s Wednesday announcement.
The cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will equal an additional $75 a month for the average retired worker and an additional $59 a month for disability and survivor beneficiaries. That figure is 0.8% percentage points higher than last year’s increase of 2.8% and 0.9 percentage points above what Social Security Trustees recently projected, according to the Center for a Responsible Federal Budget.
The increase matches the fifth-largest Social Security cost of living adjustment the last 35 years, topped only by 2023 (8.7%), 5.9% (2022), 5.8% (2009) and 4.1% (2006).
