Social Security COLA for 2026 is 2.8%
Retirement September 30, 2026
History of Social Security COLAs
Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 3.6% COLA beginning in January 2027. Increased payments to about 7.3 million people receiving SSI will begin on Dec. 31 since the normal payment date—Jan. 1, 2027—is a federal holiday.
The COLA will equal an additional $75 a month for the average retired worker and an additional $59 a month for disability and survivor beneficiaries. That figure is 0.8% percentage points higher than last year’s increase of 2.8% and 0.9 percentage points above what Social Security Trustees recently projected, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.
The increase matches the fifth-largest Social Security cost of living adjustment the last 35 years, topped only by 2022 (8.7%), 5.9% (2021), 5.8% (2008) and 4.1% (2005), based on date of announcement. The increases went into effect the following year.
The news comes after the last set of inflation data—September’s Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W)—was released. The yearly COLA is determined by comparing the CPI-W for July, August and September to the same period of time last year.
The purpose of the COLA is to ensure the purchasing power of Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) is not eroded by inflation, which has remained stubbornly high throughout 2026. Congress enacted the COLA provision as part of the 1972 Social Security Amendments, and automatic changes began in 1975. Before that, benefits were increased only when Congress enacted special legislation.
Last month, experts with The Senior Citizens League estimated the COLA would be 3.5%, the highest number since 2023.
Medicare costs
A portion of the Social Security increase will be lost to rising Medicare costs.
The latest Medicare Trustees Report projects the standard Part B premium at $209.50 for 2027, a $6.60 monthly increase from the current $202.90. Part B premiums are deducted directly from Social Security checks, reducing the amount of monthly benefits.
The annual Part B deductible is projected to increase from $283 to about $292.
Costs related to Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage are also expected to increase. Standard deductions are projected to rise to $700, up from $615, with out-of-pocket limits increasing from $2,100 to $2,400.

sources.news_title: Social Security Benefits Will Rise 3.6% In 2027. Here’s What That Means For You
2027 Social Security COLA: 3.6 Percent Benefit Increase
sources.text:
2027 Social Security COLA: 3.6 Percent Benefit Increase
Author: The United States Social Security Administration
Published: 14 Oct 2026
Publication Type: Announcement
Table of Contents:
Synopsis - Definition - Overview - FAQs - Insights, Updates - Related Content
Synopsis
This report covers the Social Security Administration’s announcement of a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment for 2027. The increase applies to Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) and Supplemental Security Income (SSI), and it raises the average retirement benefit by about $75 a month. Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see higher payments starting in January 2027. About 7.3 million SSI recipients will get their increased payments on December 31, 2026. Some people receive both benefits, so about 76 million Americans are affected in total. By law, the adjustment follows the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which is measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This makes it a formula-based figure rather than a discretionary one. The update matters most to retirees, seniors on fixed incomes, people with disabilities, and surviving family members who rely on these monthly checks for rent, food, utilities, and medical costs. Because it comes straight from the agency that pays the benefits, it gives readers a reliable number to plan their 2027 household budget around.*
At a Glance
- 1 - People not enrolled in paperless notices will get their COLA notice by mail in December.
- 2 - Medicare enrollees can see their 2027 premium amount in the my Social Security Message Center starting in late November.
- 3 - To see the COLA notice online, people without a personal my Social Security account must create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18.
- 4 - The new COLA notice is a simplified one-page letter written in plain, personalized language. It lists exact dates and dollar amounts for the new benefit and any deductions.
Topic Definition
- Cost-of-Living Adjustment (COLA)
- A Cost-of-Living Adjustment, or COLA, is an annual increase in Social Security and Supplemental Security Income payments that helps benefits keep pace with inflation. Under the Social Security Act, the adjustment is calculated automatically from the rise in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The average CPI-W for July, August, and September is compared with the same three months of the previous year. If prices have gone up, benefits rise by that percentage starting in January. If prices have not gone up, benefits stay the same. Beneficiaries do not need to apply to receive a COLA.
Overview
Social Security Announces 3.6 Percent Benefit Increase for 2027
The Social Security Administration (SSA) on 14 October, 2026, announced a 3.6 percent benefit increase for 2027. Social Security benefits include Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI), and Supplemental Security Income (SSI). On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month.
Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2027. Increased payments to about 7.3 million people receiving SSI will begin on December 31, 2026. (Note: Some people receive both Social Security benefits and SSI).
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," said Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano. "Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people."
Individuals with personal my Social Security accounts can view their COLA notice online starting in late November-up to three weeks earlier than receiving a paper notice in the mail. Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account's Message Center. Individuals who do not have a personal account will need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see their COLA notice online. Create an account today at www.ssa.gov/myaccount.

Information about Medicare changes for 2027 will be available at www.medicare.gov For Medicare enrollees, the 2027 premium amount will be available via my Social Security Message Center starting in late November. Individuals who have not opted to receive messages online will receive their COLA notice by mail in December.
The Social Security Act provides for how the COLA is calculated. The Social Security Act ties the annual COLA to the increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) as determined by the Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Frequently Asked Questions
NOTE: Researched FAQs by Disabled World (DW)
Do I need to apply to receive the 2027 Social Security COLA?
No. The cost-of-living adjustment is applied automatically to all eligible Social Security and SSI payments, so beneficiaries do not need to file any forms or contact the agency to receive it.
Why will SSI recipients receive their January 2027 payment on December 31, 2026?
SSI is normally paid on the first day of the month, but when that day falls on a weekend or a federal holiday such as New Year’s Day, the payment is sent on the business day before it.
How do Medicare premiums affect the size of my COLA increase?
Medicare Part B premiums are usually deducted directly from Social Security benefits, so a premium increase can reduce the net gain from the COLA. A hold harmless rule protects most beneficiaries from seeing their net payment go down because of a premium increase.
Which months of inflation data are used to calculate the COLA?
The COLA compares the average CPI-W for July, August, and September of the current year with the average for the same three months of the prior year, and the percentage increase becomes the new adjustment.
Can Social Security benefits go down if inflation falls?
No. If the CPI-W does not increase from one year to the next, there is no COLA for that year, but benefit amounts are not reduced.
Is the COLA increase subject to federal income tax?
The COLA is part of your regular benefit, so it is taxed the same way. Up to 85 percent of Social Security benefits may be taxable depending on combined income, while SSI payments are not taxable.
Could a higher Social Security payment affect other assistance programs?
Possibly. Some means tested programs, such as SNAP, housing assistance, and certain Medicaid categories, count Social Security income, so a higher benefit can change eligibility or benefit levels. Beneficiaries should report the new amount to those programs when asked.
When will Social Security retirement payments with the new COLA arrive in January 2027?
Most beneficiaries are paid on the second, third, or fourth Wednesday of the month based on their birth date, while people who started benefits before May 1997 or who receive both Social Security and SSI are generally paid on the third of the month.
Insights, Analysis, and Developments
Editorial Note: A 3.6 percent raise sounds simple, but the amount that actually reaches a bank account depends on what comes out first. For most retirees the largest deduction is the Medicare Part B premium, which often goes up in the same year. That is why the 2027 premium figure due in late November matters as much as the COLA itself. The formula also deserves a closer look. The CPI-W tracks spending by working households rather than older adults, and advocates for seniors have long argued that it underweights costs such as health care and housing, where retirees spend a larger share of their income. Anyone on a fixed income, especially people with disabilities and older adults living alone, should read their personalized notice carefully when it arrives and compare the net payment with their actual monthly bills, instead of assuming the full percentage will cover rising prices.*

sources.news_title: Oswego County TodayGillibrand Calls For Legislation To Improve Social Security Benefits Following Announcement Of 2027 Cola
sources.text:
Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) called for passage of her legislation to strengthen Social Security benefits following the release of the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). The Social Security Administration (SSA) announced this morning that Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6% in 2027.
“Our seniors have spent a lifetime of hard work paying into Social Security, but their checks simply aren’t keeping up with rising costs,” said Senator Gillibrand. “This year’s cost-of-living adjustment is not enough to make up for skyrocketing costs for groceries, gas, heating, and healthcare in President Trump’s America. As the top Democrat on the Senate Aging Committee, I’m fighting to pass the Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act to protect and expand Social Security benefits long-term by changing the formula used to calculate COLAs to better account for the expenses that seniors face.”
The 3.6% COLA comes as rising costs are making it harder for American seniors to make ends meet. Already, New Yorkers have paid over $5,500 more due to President Trump’s reckless policies. In September alone, inflation rose to 3.7%.
The 2027 COLA will amount to an increase of about $75 per month. 80 percent of current Social Security recipients say a similar increase would not adequately compensate for the rising cost of living.
Senator Gillibrand’s Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act—which was introduced last year—would direct SSA to adjust benefits based on the Consumer Price Index for Americans aged 62 or older (CPI-E), rather than the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners (CPI-W). The CPI-E more accurately accounts for the actual costs incurred by older Americans, such as medical expenses and prescription drug costs—making it a more reflective index to use when calculating benefits.
Additionally, this week, Senator Gillibrand sent a letter to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics urging the administration to improve data collection for the CPI-E. This letter follows the Trump administration’s attempt to cut funding to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) in Fiscal Year 2027, as well as reports that staffing cuts at BLS have already eroded the reliability of economic data.
The text of the Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act can be found here. Senator Gillibrand’s letter to the Bureau of Labor Statistics can be found here.
In addition to the Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act, Senator Gillibrand has proposed multiple pieces of legislation to help ensure that seniors can continue to get the full benefits they are owed and to reverse disastrous Trump administration cuts to SSA:
- The Social Security Expansion Act would extend the solvency of Social Security for 75 years by requiring the wealthiest American households to pay their fair share of payroll taxes. Under the current formula, a CEO making $20 million a year pays the same amount into Social Security as individuals making $184,500 a year. This legislation would lift the cap on Social Security, requiring income above $250,000 to be subject to the Social Security payroll tax and thus increasing the amount paid into the Social Security trust fund to increase its longevity.

News
Social Security announces 3.6 percent increase for 2027
The Social Security Administration announces a 3.6 percent benefit increase for 2027, impacting millions of beneficiaries.
VICKSBURG, Miss. (VDN) — The Social Security Administration (SSA) has announced a 3.6 percent benefit increase for 2027. Social Security benefits include Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI), and Supplemental Security Income (SSI). On average, Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month.
Nearly 72 million beneficiaries will see a 3.6 percent cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2027. Increased payments to about 7.3 million people receiving SSI will begin on December 31, 2026. (Note: Some people receive both benefits and SSI).
“Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” said Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano. “Under President Donald J. Trump, Social Security is delivering better, faster, higher-quality service for the American people.”
Individuals with personal my Social Security accounts can view their COLA notice online starting in late November—up to three weeks earlier than receiving a paper notice in the mail. Account holders can also choose to receive text or email alerts when a new message, including their COLA notice, is available in their personal my Social Security account’s Message Center. Individuals who do not have a personal account will need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by November 18 to see their COLA notice online. Create an account today at www.ssa.gov/myaccount.
Individuals who have not enrolled in paperless notices in their online account will receive their COLA notice by mail in December.
Beneficiaries will receive a simplified, one-page COLA notice, which uses plain and personalized language, and provides exact dates and dollar amounts of an individual’s new benefit amount and any deductions.
Information about Medicare changes for 2027 will be available at www.medicare.gov. For Medicare enrollees, the 2027 premium amount will be available via my Social Security Message Center starting in late November. Individuals who have not opted to receive messages online will receive their COLA notice by mail in December.
The Social Security Act provides for how the COLA is calculated. The Social Security Act ties the annual COLA to the increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) as determined by the Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics.
For additional information, visit www.ssa.gov/cola.

Social Security Administration says cost-of-living adjustment will rise 3.6% in 2027
Social Security benefits will increase 3.6% beginning in January for more than 70 million recipients, the Social Security Administration (SSA) said on Wednesday.
The cost-of-living adjustment for 2027, known as COLA, came in markedly higher than the prior year's hike of 2.8%.
The annual uptick in Social Security benefits aims to keep payments on pace with inflation, which surged in the spring after the outbreak of the Iran war.
The rise in Social Security payments for 2027 amounts to an average increase of about $75 a month for each recipient, the SSA said.
The announcement on Wednesday came after inflation data for September showed price hikes had climbed to a four-month high due in large part to a surge in gasoline costs. The fresh reading marked the final piece of data necessary for SSA to calculate COLA for 2027.
“Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability,” Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a statement.
The agency will also hike the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security tax, elevating the taxable income limit from $184,500 to $192,300.
Recipients can check their online accounts with Social Security for notifications of their new benefit amount beginning in late November, the agency said. Notices will be sent to recipients by mail starting in early December.

sources.news_title: Social Security Recipients to See Their Biggest Raise in Years: 2027's COLA Will Be 3.6%
sources.text:
Social Security Recipients to See Their Biggest Raise in Years: 2027's COLA Will Be 3.6%
The Social Security Administration has announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment to the benefits that retirees, spouses and disabled Americans will receive in 2027.
The adjustment, referred to as the COLA, will provide an average increase of $75 to the monthly checks of 76 million recipients, according to the announcement Wednesday. It is tied for the fifth-largest adjustment in the past 35 years.
The 2027 COLA beats the 2.8% increase recipients got for 2026, but retirees don't necessarily see it as getting a "raise." The COLA is meant to help benefits maintain their purchasing power as prices rise.
Must Read
- You're probably eligible to save money on car insurance. Compare rates for your ZIP code with this free — and fast — tool from Money.
- Investors have historically used gold to hedge against inflation — and that trend still continues today. Get in on the action with American Hartford Gold's free guide.
- Meet your financial goals faster: Take this free, no-obligation quiz to get matched with an advisor today.
Social Security beneficiaries had strong reason to expect a larger-than-usual COLA for 2027 given the flare-up in inflation this year, especially at the gas pump. Airfare and fuel oil costs have spiked, in part due to global conflicts including the war in Iran, and retirees are also facing rising costs for healthcare, public transportation, electronics and grocery staples like beef and fish.
So will the 3.6% increase be enough?
Here's what you need to know about the 2027 Social Security COLA:
How was the Social Security COLA calculated?
The COLA is calculated using government inflation data for the third quarter, which spans from July to September.
The consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers, or the CPI-W, showed 3.9% annual inflation in the September update released Wednesday. During those months, average gas prices ranged from around $3.80 to $4.50 per gallon, driving much of the uptick in inflation.
The calculation is a relatively simple comparison of third-quarter average CPI-W readings year-over-year. The CPI-W was 327.104 in July, 328.481 in August and 330.654 in September. The average for those months (328.746) compares to last year's third-quarter average of 317.265. The COLA is that difference (11.482), expressed as a percentage (3.6%) of last year's average.
How much will Social Security benefits increase in 2027?
The average Social Security retirement payment will rise from $2,095 to $2,170, an increase of $75, according to a fact sheet published Wednesday.
For comparison, the 2026 COLA delivered an average Social Security retirement payment increase of $56.
On Jan. 1, an increase in Medicare Part B premiums will also take effect for millions of retirees, and these premiums are usually withheld from Social Security benefits. The standard Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 per month and could rise to $209.50 next year, according to a projection in the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report.
The premium adjustment is typically announced in November.
Will the 2027 COLA be enough?
In a CNBC interview Monday, Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano was asked whether the increase will be enough for beneficiaries facing rising costs for groceries, healthcare and energy. Bisignano argued that the COLA is a sign the Trump administration is keeping its promises on Social Security and said Wednesday would be a "good day" for beneficiaries.
"The promise was to protect and preserve, and we've been running that platform since I've been here with the president. And we're going to do it Wednesday — there'll be a cost-of-living adjustment," he said, adding that he received thank-you notes for the COLA last year. "People are very, very grateful for it, and they look forward to it."
The COLA is automatic, and the same formula has been used for over 40 years.
Advocacy groups representing older Americans, like The Senior Citizens League, say retirees are dissatisfied with recent COLAs and continue to worry about their ability to afford climbing household costs.
"Another year, another COLA that falls short of expectations," Shannon Benton, executive director of the group, said in a news release Wednesday. "When inflation spikes due to a geopolitical event like the Iran war, seniors pay the price. Prices go up today, but benefits stay the same for months due to an outdated COLA methodology."
Social Security beneficiaries also remain concerned about the inflationary effects of the Trump administration's trade policies. New York Fed researchers recently estimated that consumer goods prices are about 2% higher than they would have been without tariffs.
The AARP said the COLA, which it lobbied to create in 1972, provides critical financial support for beneficiaries: "Without it, millions more older Americans would be living in poverty," AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement.
The nonprofit's survey data finds that 76% of respondents said the projected COLA would not be enough. Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security policy analyst, agreed.
"That may get us one fill-up at the gas station," Johnson said in a release Wednesday.
The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) took the opposite view, arguing that the program cannot afford large COLAs as trust fund insolvency looms. The think tank's calculations show that the COLA will increase benefits by more than $2,200 next year for the richest retirees.
"Lawmakers should consider reforming future COLAs," a CRFB blog post read Wednesday. "This could be done by adopting the more accurate chained CPI or by adopting a COLA Cap that puts a dollar limit on the COLA."
Who gets the Social Security COLA
When the 3.6% COLA kicks in, it will boost benefits for everyone currently collecting Social Security. That's about 58 million people who receive retirement benefits, 5.8 million who receive survivor benefits and 8 million beneficiaries who get disability insurance.
The COLA also applies to Supplemental Security Income, or SSI. About 7.3 million people receive SSI, which is intended to help adults and children with little to no income and resources who are blind, disabled, or age 65 and up. (Many of these beneficiaries receive SSI and Social Security benefits.)
When will the 2027 COLA take effect?
Social Security retirement benefits are paid monthly in batches on the third day of the month and the second, third and fourth Wednesdays. The payment schedule is based on birthdates.
The 2027 COLA will take effect on the last day of 2026. Some payments are scheduled to go out Dec. 31 because Jan. 1 and Jan. 3 are a federal holiday and a Sunday, respectively.
Most retirees will notice the COLA increase later in the month in their Jan. 13, Jan. 20 or Jan. 27 payments.
The full 2027 Social Security payment schedule can be found on the Social Security Administration's website.
The Social Security Administration said it will send out notices with new benefit amounts starting in December. Beneficiaries with a "my Social Security" account will be able to access their COLA notice online and can opt in to receive text or email alerts when it's available.

sources.news_title: Social Security COLA 2027: Welcome 3.6% Boost Explained
sources.text:
Social Security COLA 2027 will increase monthly benefits by 3.6%, giving the average retired worker about $75 more per month starting in January. The increase is welcome relief for millions of Americans facing higher grocery, housing and health care costs, but it is not a bonus or a cure for lost purchasing power. It is an inflation adjustment, and the amount people actually keep will depend in part on their Medicare premiums and other household expenses.
By Michelle Laguerre | October 14, 2026
What the 2027 Social Security COLA means for your check
The Social Security Administration’s newly announced 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is larger than the 2.8% adjustment for 2026. The Associated Press reports that approximately 73 million Social Security recipients and nearly 7.5 million Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients are affected. Some people receive both, so the figures should not simply be added together as a count of unique Americans.
The Associated Press reports an average increase of about $75 per month for retired workers, or roughly $900 across a full year. Individual increases vary because they are calculated from each person’s benefit before applicable deductions. People who receive retirement, survivor and disability benefits can also be affected.
| Current monthly benefit | Illustrative 3.6% increase | Illustrative new gross benefit | 
|---|---|---|
| $1,000 | $36 | $1,036 | 
| $1,500 | $54 | $1,554 | 
| $2,000 | $72 | $2,072 | 
| $2,500 | $90 | $2,590 | 
| $3,000 | $108 | $3,108 | 
Examples are simple estimates before rounding, taxes, Medicare premiums and other deductions. Your official notice determines your actual amount.
How is the COLA calculated?
Federal law ties the adjustment to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. The government compares average index levels in July, August and September against the same quarter a year earlier. This system automatically adjusts benefits when the index rises. It does not measure each retired person’s exact household budget. See the Social Security Administration’s COLA explanation.
The good news: Where the 3.6% increase helps
For households with little room in their budgets, even a modest increase matters. An extra $36 to $108 a month in the examples above can help cover a utility bill, food, a prescription or a ride to a medical appointment. Because the COLA is automatic, beneficiaries generally do not need to apply for it.
There are broader advantages, too. Annual inflation protection keeps a fixed benefit from remaining unchanged while average prices rise. The higher payments also put money into local economies, where beneficiaries buy groceries, pay rent and use services. In Utica, Rome and the Mohawk Valley, the issue is particularly practical for residents living on a pension and Social Security rather than a paycheck.
Another important point: A larger adjustment does not mean the recipient has become wealthier. Its purpose is to preserve buying power against measured inflation, not to create a real increase in living standards.
The downside: Why some retirees may still fall behind
There is no single inflation experience. A homeowner with a paid-off mortgage faces different costs from a renter. A person who drives often may notice gasoline more than someone who depends on public transportation. Older people who use more medical care can feel price increases that do not track neatly with the CPI-W basket.
AARP has warned about retirement insecurity. Its CEO, Myechia Minter-Jordan, highlighted the fact that roughly one in five older Americans has no retirement savings in coverage of the announcement. For people relying heavily on their monthly check, a higher benefit can be swallowed by rising essentials before they experience much relief.
Will Medicare take part of the increase?
For many beneficiaries, Medicare Part B premiums are deducted directly from Social Security payments. A projected standard Part B premium of $209.50 for 2027, $6.60 above the 2026 amount of $202.90, has appeared in pre-announcement estimates. That figure is a projection, not a final premium determination. Other Medicare coverage and prescription drug costs depend on the enrollee’s plan and situation.
If the $6.60 projection proves correct, a retiree receiving a $75 gross COLA increase and paying the standard Part B premium would keep about $68.40 more a month from those two changes alone. This is an illustration, not a personalized net-benefit quote. Review the final Medicare announcement and annual notice rather than budgeting from a forecast.
Pros and cons of the Social Security COLA 2027 increase
| Pros | Cons and limitations | 
|---|---|
| Automatic inflation adjustment without a new application | CPI-W may not match an older household’s spending | 
| About $75 more monthly for the average retired worker | Health costs and other bills can absorb the increase | 
| Helps retirement, survivor and disability beneficiaries | A percentage increase means smaller checks receive smaller dollar gains | 
| Supports spending in local communities | Does not by itself fix Social Security’s financing gap | 
The larger concern: Social Security’s 2032 funding warning
The 2026 Social Security trustees report projects that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) trust fund can pay full scheduled benefits until 2032. If Congress does not change the law, continuing income at reserve depletion would cover about 78% of scheduled OASI benefits. Put another way, that is a projected 22% shortfall, not a prediction that all checks suddenly disappear. The separate disability trust fund has a different financial outlook. The combined trust funds are projected to be able to pay full scheduled benefits through 2034, although combining funds for payment purposes would require a change in law.
The trustees state: “Legislative action will be needed to prevent OASI reserve depletion.” Read the official 2026 trustees findings for the underlying projections.
Lawmakers face difficult choices. Proposals include raising additional payroll-tax revenue, changing the earnings subject to Social Security tax, adjusting some benefit formulas or combining measures over time. Advocates for more revenue argue that retirees should not bear the burden of repairing a program they paid into. Those who favor slowing benefit growth warn that new taxes also carry costs for workers and employers. No single option is free of trade-offs. The 2027 COLA itself should not be confused with a congressional solution to long-term financing.
What people in Upstate New York should do next
The announcement deserves attention well beyond Washington. In Oneida and Herkimer counties, even a small difference between a gross increase and take-home payment can shape decisions about heat, groceries and health care during winter. Beneficiaries should take a few practical steps:
- Check your benefit and annual COLA notice using your secure my Social Security account.
- Compare the gross benefit with the actual deposit after Medicare, tax withholding and other deductions.
- Review Medicare coverage during the annual open enrollment period, October 15 through December 7, and compare each plan’s premiums, medicines, network and total costs at Medicare.gov.
- Ask about help paying Medicare costs through New York’s free HIICAP insurance counseling program.
- Be alert for scams. You do not need to pay anyone or disclose banking information to claim an automatic COLA.
A needed increase, and an unfinished responsibility
The 3.6% adjustment should help millions of households start 2027 with a little more breathing room. Its limits deserve equal attention. Inflation does not affect everyone equally, and the program’s projected financing shortfall cannot be wished away. Americans should review their notices, compare actual health coverage costs and ask elected representatives how they plan to protect both promised benefits and the system that delivers them. A secure retirement should not depend on guessing how much of next year’s increase will survive the next round of bills.
Sources: Social Security Administration COLA information; Associated Press, October 14, 2026; 2026 Social Security Trustees Report; Medicare premium projection context.

Just Days Away: Social Security to Announce 2027 COLA Increase – Herb Weiss
By Herb Weiss, contributing writer on aging issues
In just a few days, nearly 279,000 Rhode Islanders who rely on Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) will learn how much their monthly checks will increase in 2027 when the Social Security Administration (SSA) announces next year’s cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). Social Security recipients will see the increase in January, while SSI recipients will receive their adjusted payments on Dec. 31, 2026, because New Year’s Day is a federal holiday. The additional income will help them keep pace with rising costs.
Older Rhode Island beneficiaries will be joining 75 million Americans—including roughly 71 million Social Security beneficiaries and between 7.3 and 7.5 million SSI recipients—awaiting this highly anticipated news.
SSA is expected to announce the official 2027 COLA on Wednesday, Oct. 14, following the release of September inflation data by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
According to the Virginia-based The Senior Citizens League (TSCL), the SSA’s COLA for 2026 was 2.8 percent, somewhat higher than the 2.5 percent COLA implemented at the start of 2025. TSCL predicts that the COLA for 2027 will tick up to 3.5 percent. AARP experts project an even higher COLA increase for 2027 than TSCL estimates, at 3.6 percent.
Congress enacted the COLA provision as part of the 1972 Social Security Amendments, and automatic annual COLAs began in 1975, says SSA, noting that before then Congress could only increase this benefit through special legislation. The new provision tied COLAs to the annual increase of the Consumer Price Index (CPI-W).
SSA calculates the COLA by comparing the average CPI-W for July, August and September with the average for the same three months of the previous year. The percentage is rounded to the nearest tenth of one percent and determines the annual adjustment.
With the 3.5 percent projection, the average beneficiary’s monthly benefit increases by $67.90. The current average beneficiary receives $1,940.08 in their monthly Social Security check. With a 3.5 percent COLA, that would rise to $ 2,007.98, estimates TSCL
If TSCL’s calculation holds, the 2027 COLA would land right in the middle of the ranking historically—ranking 19th among all COLA adjustments since the federal government started using its current inflation math in 1977. By comparison, the recent boost seniors received at the start of 2026 was a bit more modest, tying for 27th place.
“The biggest thing we’re watching with the COLA announcement coming are short-term shocks to the economy that push inflation way up or down in the next 30 days. Of the three CPI-W figures used to calculate the COLA, two are already in,” said TSCL Executive Director Shannon G. Benton in a statement releasing the 2027 estimated projections.
“No matter if the COLA announcement comes in slightly higher or slightly lower than our prediction, seniors will probably end up disappointed in the long run,” said Benton, noting that older Americans allocate their budgets differently than people still in the workforce, so inflation hits them differently. The consumer price index (CPI) captures the experience of urban wage earners, which doesn’t represent the average senior’s budget, she adds.
“The COLA only happening once a year puts life on hold for a lot of seniors. When prices rise, they don’t rise next January when your benefit check goes up. They rise right now. We need to consider COLAs that compound quarterly or monthly so seniors can keep up throughout the year when inflation comes in above Federal Reserve targets, like in 2026,” adds Benton.
Advocates Push for CPI-E Index
In a recent AARP Sept. 11 blog post, “Social Security COLA 2027: An Early Look at How Much Payments Could Increase,” writer Deirdre Shesgreen interviewed Rich Johnson, the vice president for financial security at the AARP Public Policy Institute. Johnson emphasized that the organization’s COLA forecast is meant to give older adults a head start on managing their 2027 finances. “Family budgets have been under increasing pressure because of rising prices,” Johnson noted. “The sooner that we can give them reliable information as to how much their benefits might [increase next year], the sooner they can start planning,” he said.
“Most seniors depend on Social Security for some or all of their income, and the program’s annual Cost of Living Adjustments (COLAs) for inflation help keep them from falling behind,” says Max Richtman, President & CEO, National Committee to Preserve Social Security & Medicare, noting that even the estimated 3.5-3.6% increase will barely be enough for seniors to tread water.
“That’s because the COLA is based on an inflation index that does not account for the impact of inflation on seniors’ true expenses, especially health care costs – which are rising faster than the general inflation rate,” said Richtman, calling for the adoption of the CPI-E (Consumer Price Index for the Elderly). This CPI index is designed to better reflect older American’s spending patterns.
“What we know is that when the COLA is announced, it will be far too low to make up for the crushing prices everybody is facing right now. But seniors and those on fixed incomes are being crushed the hardest,” said Alex Lawson, Executive Director of Social Security Works.
His concerns come as Census Bureau figures show that the poverty rate among Americans aged 65 and older rose from 9.4 percent in 2020 to 15.4 percent in 2025, according to the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which accounts for medical expenses and other living costs.
“And still Republican proposals, when we see them, include provisions to cut back on the COLA, which is just a cruel benefit cut. We need to expand Social Security, increase benefits, raise the COLA, and pay for it by having billionaires pay the same rate on all of their income into Social Security. Just like the rest of us do,” argued Lawson.
Improving SSA’s Benefit Calculation Formula
TSCL advocates for the Social Security 2100 Act, legislation championed by Congressman John Larson (D-Connecticut), first introduced in 2017 and reintroduced in 2026.
Lawmakers reintroduced this legislative proposal to provide long-term relief to seniors losing buying power due to high inflation. The bill would raise benefits by 2%, set the new minimum benefit to 125% of the Federal poverty line, change the COLA calculation to the CPI for the Elderly (CPI-E), and improve the benefits calculation formula, said TSCL.
“Although the Social Security 2100 Act is unlikely to pass in the current Congress, it should. The bill is the gold standard for Social Security reform and accomplishes the majority of changes older Americans want to see in the program,” says TSCL’s Benton in a statement released on July 14. “The reality is that poverty is increasing rapidly among American seniors, who make up the fastest-growing portion of the homeless population. Adjusting the minimum benefit to above the Federal poverty line would almost certainly slow this trend, although more holistic efforts may be required to stop it entirely,” she says.

sources.news_title: Social Security COLA 2027: Why a $73 monthly boost could spell trouble ahead of October 14 announcement - THE LOCAL REPORT ARTICLES
sources.text:
The US Social Security Administration is expected to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) after the September inflation report is released on October 14. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics will publish the report at 8:30 am ET, providing the final inflation data needed to calculate the increase.
More than 71 million traditional Social Security beneficiaries could receive one of the biggest annual benefit increases in the last 35 years in 2027. However, while larger monthly payments could help beneficiaries manage higher expenses, they could also put more pressure on the programme’s already strained finances, according to The Motley Fool.
The Senior Citizens League (TSCL), a nonpartisan advocacy group for older Americans, and Mary Johnson, a Social Security and Medicare policy analyst, are both projecting a 3.5% COLA for 2027, according to The Motley Fool. This is an estimate, not the final announced increase.
If the 3.5% estimate is correct, the average retired worker could receive an additional $73 per month in Social Security benefits. That would mean about $876 more over a full year, based on the estimated monthly increase.
A 3.5% increase would tie for the sixth-largest Social Security COLA since 1993. It would also mark the sixth consecutive year with a benefit increase of at least 2.5%, a streak that has not occurred in 30 years.
Also read: Why did I get $90 from Social Security? Trump Medicare payment explained
Why Social Security benefits could rise in 2027
Trump’s tariffs have pushed up the cost of consumer goods. His trade policies began affecting prices in mid-2025. The tariffs introduced on “Liberation Day” also contributed to higher consumer prices and helped support the 2.8% Social Security COLA provided in 2026.
The US Supreme Court struck down the “Liberation Day” tariffs in February 2026. However, the effects of earlier tariffs on consumer prices may continue, while the Trump administration introduced broad tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on goods from more than 80 countries in late July, The Motley Fool reported.
The Iran war has also added to inflation pressures. After Trump approved attacks against Iran on February 28, Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz to most commercial vessels, disrupting the movement of a major share of the world’s crude oil.
Why a bigger Social Security COLA could create problems
While a higher COLA can help older Americans manage rising living costs, it can also increase the amount Social Security pays out in benefits. The Motley Fool warned that unusually large annual increases could worsen the programme’s long-term financial challenges.
The Social Security Board of Trustees has warned about the programme’s long-term funding shortfall every year since 1985. The programme’s projected long-term unfunded obligation reached $29.3 trillion in 2026, according to The Motley Fool. This figure represents the projected gap between future income and expenses over the 75-year period covered by the Trustees’ calculations.
Social Security has accumulated reserves from income collected in earlier years. By law, these reserves are invested in special-issue, interest-bearing US government bonds. However, the OASI trust fund’s reserves are projected to run out by the fourth quarter of 2032.
Also read: Social Security COLA 2027: Why Medicare deductions could reduce retirees’ monthly benefit increase
Social Security is not expected to simply go bankrupt or stop making all payments when its reserves run out. More than 91% of the programme’s income comes from the 12.4% payroll tax on earned income. As long as people continue working and paying payroll taxes, the programme will continue receiving money to pay eligible beneficiaries.
The bigger risk is a possible reduction in benefits. If the OASI trust fund’s reserves are exhausted, incoming revenue is projected to be insufficient to pay all scheduled benefits. The resulting shortfall could require benefit cuts estimated at 22%.
How the 2027 COLA could worsen the funding gap
The Social Security Board of Trustees considers several factors when estimating the programme’s future finances. These include birth rates, net migration, death rates and the annual cost-of-living adjustments given to beneficiaries.
If the projected 3.5% COLA becomes official, the increase could add to Social Security’s expenses more than the Trustees’ relatively modest assumptions anticipate. The Motley Fool warned that this could cause the OASI trust fund’s reserves to run out sooner than currently projected.
Inflation could also remain a problem beyond 2026. The effects of tariffs and the Iran war could continue into 2027, keeping pressure on consumer prices. If inflation remains elevated, it could also lead to another relatively large COLA in 2028. This would potentially increase Social Security’s benefit expenses further, adding to the programme’s long-term funding challenges.
The central concern is that larger Social Security checks may offer short-term relief while increasing pressure on the programme’s long-term finances. If inflation remains high and annual benefit increases stay elevated, the need for future benefit cuts could arrive sooner or the cuts could be larger than currently projected, The Motley Fool warned.
What to watch before the October 14 announcement
The September inflation report, scheduled for October 14 at 8:30 a.m. ET, is the final data point needed to calculate the 2027 Social Security COLA. The report will help determine the official adjustment rather than leave beneficiaries relying on estimates.
Beneficiaries should remember that the projected 3.5% increase and the additional $73 per month are estimates. The final adjustment could differ depending on the inflation figures used in the calculation.
The announcement will provide a clearer picture of how much monthly benefits are expected to rise in 2027. However, the longer-term issue will remain: whether Social Security can continue paying scheduled benefits without major changes to its finances.

sources.news_title: A Bigger Social Security COLA Might Sound Like a Win - But There's a Catch
sources.text:
A larger Social Security check can look like a win, although the reason behind the increase may make it feel a little less generous. By the time that bigger COLA arrives, inflation may have already pushed many of your everyday costs higher, giving those extra dollars some catching up to do.
A 3.5% or 3.6% increase could still be welcome, but how much it helps depends on what happens to the expenses you pay each month. If you are balancing those costs with your retirement goals, here's what a bigger COLA could actually mean for your buying power.
Get a protection plan on all your appliances
Did you know if your air conditioner stops working, your homeowner’s insurance won’t cover it? Same with plumbing, electrical issues, appliances, and more.
A home warranty from Choice Home Warranty could pick up the slack where insurance falls short.
For a limited time, you can get your first month free with a Single Payment home warranty plan.
What a 3.5% COLA could add to your check
Social Security compares the average CPI-W reading from July, August, and September with the same period a year earlier to set the COLA.
The Senior Citizens League currently estimates a 2027 increase of roughly 3.5%. On the average retired-worker benefit of about $2,088 as of August 2026, a 3.5% COLA would add around $73 a month, or roughly $877 over a full year.
By the time that higher payment reaches your account, many of the costs behind the increase have already gone up. If a $500 monthly expense rose by the same 3.5% as the projected COLA, it would cost about $517.50, so some of the additional Social Security income would simply be catching up with higher prices.
Your own expenses may be rising faster than 3.5%
Your own expenses may be rising faster than the national inflation rate, depending on where most of your money goes. Overall consumer prices were up about 3.5% in August 2026 from a year earlier, but some costs retirees deal with rose much faster.
- Energy prices rose 16.3%, with gasoline up 27.4%.
- Hospital services rose 5.2%, while home health care climbed 10.6%.
- Food prices increased 2.7%, and shelter costs were up 3.0%.
- Prescription-drug prices fell 2.9% nationally, though your own pharmacy costs still depend on the medications you take and your Part D coverage.
If you spend heavily on energy or healthcare, your personal costs could be rising much faster than 3.5%. Someone paying $300 a month for energy-related expenses would be spending about $49 more after a 16.3% increase, which would eat up roughly two-thirds of that $73 monthly COLA increase.
Medicare could take part of the COLA increase before you receive it
Because Part B premiums are deducted directly from most Social Security checks, part of that $73 could be gone before the money reaches your account.
The standard premium rose from $185 in 2025 to $202.90 in 2026, a 9.7% increase, while the COLA that January was 2.8%. The Senior Citizens League found that Part B premiums grew faster than the COLA in seven of the past 10 years.
If the 2027 Part B premium rises by $10, that $73 increase would fall to about $63 before taxes or other deductions.
If you’re over 50, take advantage of massive discounts and financial resources
Over 50? Join AARP today— because if you’re not a member you could be missing out on huge perks. When you start your membership today, you can get discounts on things like travel, meal deliveries, eyeglasses, prescriptions that aren’t covered by insurance and more.
Start your membership by creating an account here and filling in all of the information (Do not skip this step!) Doing so will allow you to take up to 25% off your AARP membership, making it just $15 the first year with auto-renewal.
A higher benefit could also bring more of it into taxable income
A larger COLA can push more of your Social Security into taxable income because the federal thresholds ($25,000 for single filers, $32,000 for married couples filing jointly) haven't changed since the 1980s.
If you were just below one of those limits last year, a higher Social Security benefit could move you above it even when nothing else about your income changes. Depending on your total income, up to 50% or 85% of your benefits may then be included in taxable income.
The Center for Retirement Research has pointed to these unchanging thresholds as one reason more retirees can end up paying tax on their benefits over time. Your COLA rises with inflation, while the tax limits don't, so each increase can bring more people into taxable territory.
How to make the COLA work for your specific budget
Take your actual monthly costs and note which categories climbed the most over the past year. If your energy and medical costs rose faster than 3.5%, the COLA may not cover the ground you've lost in those areas. If housing costs barely changed, you may have a little more of the increase left for other expenses.
Once your Social Security notice and Medicare premium are official, look at the change in your net deposit. If a $73 gross increase turns into $58 after Medicare, you can use that $58 when you plan your 2027 budget.
Why the COLA may still fall behind some retirement costs
Social Security adjusts your benefit for inflation each year, which gives it an edge over income sources like pensions and annuities that may stay the same as prices rise.
The problem, though, is that the COLA follows the CPI-W, and that index reflects spending by working households rather than the way many retirees spend their money. The Senior Citizens League estimates that Social Security benefits have lost about 13.7% of their buying power since 2016 when compared with costs that tend to take up more of an older household's budget.
So even when your benefit rises, the increase may not fully match the expenses that are climbing fastest for you.
Retirement News: Almost 80% of Americans fear a retirement age increase — here’s the real reason why
Bottom line
A bigger COLA can put more money in your Social Security check, even if rising costs claim part of the increase before you get much use from it. Once Medicare and taxes come out, the amount left is what you really have to work with.
Building your budget around that amount can help you cover costs that have gone up while finding ways to save money in retirement. Even though the increase might be smaller than you expected, those added dollars can still make a few monthly expenses easier to cover.
